He took conception in a brahmin family in Sāvatthī and was named the youth Mogharāja. King Kaṭṭhavāhana, having performed extraordinary meritorious deeds under the Blessed One Kassapa, wandered through the realms of devas and humans for one buddhantara with his retinue. Before the appearance of our Blessed One, he took conception in the house of the royal chaplain in Sāvatthī and was named the youth Bāvarī. Later, that youth Bāvarī mastered the three Vedas and lived teaching the arts to sixteen thousand young brahmins. Then, during the reign of King Pasenadi of Kosala, upon the death of his father, he was given the position of royal chaplain. At that time, this youth Mogharāja also studied the arts under the brahmin Bāvarī.

Then one day, the brahmin Bāvarī went into seclusion and, while looking for the essence in the arts he had mastered, he did not see any essence for the hereafter. Thinking, 'I shall go forth as an ascetic and seek the essence for the hereafter,' he approached King Kosala and asked permission to go forth. Having been granted permission by the king, he departed to go forth, surrounded by sixteen thousand young brahmins. King Kosala also sent a minister along with him, giving him a thousand coins, saying, 'In the place where the teacher goes forth, arrange a dwelling place for him.' While searching for a pleasant place to live, the brahmin Bāvarī moved away from the Middle Country and had a dwelling place built for himself on the banks of the Godhāvarī River, in the border region between the territories of King Assaka and King Muḷaka.

Then a man went to see the matted-hair ascetics and, with their permission, built a dwelling for himself on the land belonging to them. Seeing what that man had done, another hundred families built a hundred houses. All of them gathered and said, 'We are living on the land belonging to the venerable ones; there is no reason to live here for free. We shall give you something so that you may live in comfort.' Thus, each person offered one coin...
258:
...and placed it at the dwelling place of the brahmin Bāvarī. All the coins brought there amounted to about one hundred thousand. The brahmin Bāvarī asked, 'For what purpose have these been brought?' They replied, 'Venerable sir, it is for the sake of an offering so that you may live in comfort.' He said, 'If I had desired silver and gold, I would not have gone forth, abandoning a great mass of wealth. Take your coins and go.' They replied, 'We have already relinquished these to the venerable sir and shall not take them back. We shall bring them every year in this same manner. May the venerable sir take these and give them as alms.' The brahmin consented and bestowed them as gifts to the poor, wayfarers, and beggars. His reputation as a donor who gave repeatedly became well-known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Then, in the village named Dunniwiṭṭha in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, the wife of a brahmin born in the lineage of the brahmin Jūjaka repeatedly urged her husband, saying, 'Bāvarī, it is said, is giving alms. Go and bring gold and silver from him.' Being thus urged by her and unable to resist, he went to Bāvarī. The brahmin Bāvarī, having finished giving alms, had entered his leaf-hut and was lying down, reflecting on his generosity, when that brahmin arrived. Upon arrival, he said, 'Brahmin, give me a gift! Brahmin, give me a gift!' Bāvarī said, 'Brahmin, you have come at the wrong time. I have already given to all the beggars who arrived; there are no coins left now.' He replied, 'Brahmin, I do not need many coins. For you who give such a great amount in alms, it is impossible to be without coins. Give me five hundred coins.' Bāvarī said, 'Brahmin, I do not have even five hundred. You will receive them when the next time for giving alms arrives.' He said, 'How can I come at your next time of giving?' Then, making a mound of sand at the door of Bāvarī’s leaf-hut, scattering red flowers all around, and moving his lips as if chanting a mantra, he said, 'May your head split into seven pieces!'

The brahmin Bāvarī thought, 'This wandering brahmin of great austerity, having taken up ascetic practices, says to me that on the seventh day my head shall split into seven pieces. And I do not have the five hundred coins to be given to this brahmin. Surely, he will kill me.' Thus, while he lay there with the shaft of sorrow pierced within him, at the end of the night, at dawn, Bāvarī’s mother, who had been reborn as a deity, appeared. Seeing her son pierced by the shaft of sorrow, she came and spoke thus:
259:
“Dear son, this brahmin knows neither the head nor the splitting of the head; you too do not know that a Buddha has arisen in the world. If you have any doubt, go to the presence of the Blessed One and ask; that Blessed One will explain this matter to you.” From the moment the Brahmin Bāvarī heard the words of the deity, he felt relieved. At dawn the next day, he called all his disciples and said, “Sons, it is said that a Buddha has arisen in the world. Go quickly and find out whether he is indeed a Buddha or not, then return and inform me. I shall go to the presence of the Blessed One. However, I am old and the danger to my life is difficult to know. Go to the presence of that Blessed One and ask questions using these signs.” Thus, he prepared and gave them the questions concerning the splitting of the head.

Then he thought, “All these youths are wise. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One and reaching the completion of their duties as monks, they might or might not return to me.” Then, he gave instructions to his nephew, the youth Ajita: “You, however, should certainly return to me. Come back and tell me of the virtues you have attained.” Then, those sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics, making the youth Ajita their leader along with the sixteen chief disciples, set out on their journey saying, “We shall ask questions of the Blessed One.” Wherever they arrived, they were asked, “Venerables, where are you going?” They replied, “We are going to ask questions in the presence of the Ten-Powered One,” and they gathered followers from the outskirts, traveling a distance of many hundreds of leagues. The Blessed One thought, “On the day they arrive, there will be no opportunity for others; this place is suitable for this assembly.” He then went and sat upon the Back Rock (Piṭṭhipāsāṇa) at the Rock Shrine (Pāsāṇacetiya). The youth Ajita, together with his followers, ascended that Back Rock and, seeing the perfection of the Blessed One’s physical body, thought, “This man must surely be a Buddha who has removed the veil in this world.” He proceeded while mentally asking the questions sent by his teacher.

On that day, the assembly gathered at that place extended for twelve leagues. Among those sixteen chief disciples, the youth Mogharāja was stiff with pride, thinking, “I am wiser than all.” It occurred to him, “This youth Ajita is the eldest of all; it is not proper for me to ask my questions before him...”
260:
...(thinking it) improper, he felt ashamed and did not ask his question first. After Ajita had finished asking, he became the second to ask the Blessed One. The Blessed One thought, “The youth Mogharāja is stiff with pride; his wisdom has not yet reached maturity. It is proper to restrain his pride.” Thus, He said, “Wait, Mogharāja, let others ask their questions first.” Having received this rebuke from the Blessed One, the youth Mogharāja thought, “For so long, I have wandered thinking there is no one wiser than I. Buddhas do not speak without knowing. The Teacher must have seen a fault in my question,” and he remained silent. When eight people had asked their questions in succession, he could no longer restrain himself and stood up again as the ninth. The Blessed One rebuked him once more.

He remained silent again, thinking, “Now I shall not be able to even be the most junior in the Saṅgha.” He then asked his question as the fifteenth person. Then, the Blessed One, knowing that his wisdom had matured, answered the question. At the conclusion of the teaching, Mogharāja, along with his retinue of one thousand matted-hair ascetics, attained Arahantship. In this same manner, the remaining fifteen thousand matted-hair ascetics also attained Arahantship. All of them became ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ monks, bearing miraculously created bowls and robes. The remaining people (who attained lower stages like Sotāpanna) are not mentioned. From that time on, the Elder Mogharāja wore robes characterized by three types of coarseness. Thus, the story arose in the Pārayanavagga. Later, while the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana, when He was appointing the elders to their respective positions of eminence, He placed the Elder Mogharāja in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes in this Dispensation, saying, “Monks, among my monk disciples who wear coarse robes, Mogharāja is the foremost.”

## Commentary on the Fourth Vagga.
## The commentary on the Theragāthā, consisting of forty-one suttas, is finished.
261:
## 14. Etadagga Vagga
## (14) 5. Fifth Etadagga Vagga
## The Story of Mahāpajāpatigotamī Therī
In the first sutta of the Therī Pāḷi, the phrase "yadidaṃ mahāpajāpatigotamī" indicates that Mahāpajāpatigotamī Therī was the foremost among those of long standing (rattaññū).

Regarding her past deeds, the sequential account is as follows: During the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn into a family in the city of Haṃsāvatī. Later, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain nun to the foremost position of long standing. She performed a great meritorious deed and made an aspiration for that position. She practiced giving and guarded her virtue throughout her life, and after passing away from that life, she was reborn in the celestial realm. Again, during an interval between two Buddhas, she passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn in Bārāṇasī as the leader of five hundred slave women.

At that time, as the time for the rains retreat (vassa) approached, five Paccekabuddhas descended from the Nandamūlaka mountain cave to Isipatana. After wandering for alms in the city, they returned to Isipatana and thought, "Let us request manual labor for the construction of huts for the rains retreat." Why? Because a monk entering the rains retreat, even if practicing the Nālaka practice, must enter the retreat in a dwelling that is roofed with one of the five types of roofing—brick, lime, grass, or leaves—and fitted with a door. It was said: "Monks, one should not enter the rains retreat without a dwelling. Should one do so, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa)" (as stated in the Mahāvagga Pāḷi).

Therefore, when the time for the rains retreat is near, it is good if a dwelling is obtained. If not obtained, one should seek manual labor to have it built. If manual labor is not obtained, one should build it oneself; one must not enter the rains retreat without a dwelling. This is the nature of the Dhamma. Thus, those Paccekabuddhas, intending to "request manual labor," robed themselves and entered the city in the evening, standing at the door of a treasurer's (seṭṭhi) house. The head slave woman, while taking a water pot to the landing place, saw the Paccekabuddhas entering the city. When the treasurer heard the reason for the Paccekabuddhas' arrival, he said, "We have no opportunity; please move on."

Then, as those Paccekabuddhas were leaving the city, the head slave woman, entering the city with her water pot, saw them. She set down the water pot, paid homage, and with a bowed body and uplifted face, asked, "Venerable sirs, you have only just entered the city; why are you leaving already?" They replied, "We have come to request manual labor for huts for the rains retreat." She asked, "Venerable sirs, did you receive it?" They replied, "Lay follower, we did not."
262:
"Venerable sirs, must these huts be built only by the powerful, or can they be built by the poor as well?" she asked. "Anyone can build them," they replied. "Venerable sirs, very well, we will build them. Please accept my alms tomorrow," she invited. Then, taking her water pot again, she stood at the path to the landing place and said to each of the remaining slave women as they arrived, "Stay right here." When all the slave women had arrived, she asked, "Mothers, why will you always perform the work of slaves for others? Or do you wish to be free from slavery?" They replied, "Lady, we wish to be free this very day."

"If you so desire, there are Paccekabuddhas whom I have invited for tomorrow because they did not receive manual labor. Have your husbands provide manual labor for just one day," she said. Those slave women agreed, saying "Very well," and told their husbands when they returned from the forest in the evening. They said "Very well" and gathered at the door of the head slave man's house.

Then the head slave woman told them, "Brothers, provide manual labor for the Paccekabuddhas tomorrow," explaining the benefits. She even threatened those who were unwilling with stern words of advice, making everyone agree. The next day, after offering alms to the Paccekabuddhas, she gave a signal to all the slave men. They immediately entered the forest, gathered building materials, and forming groups of one hundred each, built a hut for each Paccekabuddha, complete with walkways and other surroundings. They provided couches, stools, drinking water, and utility water, and having obtained the Paccekabuddhas' commitment to stay there for the three months of the rains retreat, they arranged for alms in rotation. For any slave woman who could not provide alms on her turn, the head slave woman took from her own house and gave it.

Having looked after them for the three months of the rains retreat in this way, the head slave woman had a piece of coarse cloth prepared for each slave woman, totaling five hundred pieces of coarse cloth. She had those cloths exchanged and made into sets of triple robes (ticīvara) for the five Paccekabuddhas and offered them. While the women were watching, the Paccekabuddhas departed through the air to Gandhamādana Mountain.

All those five hundred slave women performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives and were reborn in the celestial realm. Among them, the head slave woman passed away from that celestial realm and was reborn in a weaver's village not far from Bārāṇasī, in the house of the head weaver. Then one day, the five hundred Paccekabuddhas, who were the sons of Queen Padumavatī, came to the palace gate at the invitation of the King of Bārāṇasī. Seeing no one to attend to them, they turned back and left through the city gate...
263:
(Those Paccekabuddhas) went to the village of the weavers. Upon seeing the Paccekabuddhas, that woman was filled with devotion and affection; she paid homage to all of them and offered alms-food. Having finished their meal, those Paccekabuddhas departed only for Mount Gandhamādana.

That woman, having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, wandered through the realms of gods and humans. Long before the appearance of our Buddha, she took conception in the house of King Mahāsuppabuddha in the city of Devadaha. They named the maiden Gotamī. She was the younger sister of Queen Mahāmāyā. When brahmins skilled in the Vedas examined her marks, they prophesied, "The children residing in the wombs of both these maidens will become Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti)." When the maidens reached of age, King Suddhodana performed the marriage ceremony for both and brought them to his palace.

Later, our Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita heaven and took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā. On the seventh day after the Bodhisatta was born, Queen Mahāmāyā passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. King Suddhodana then appointed Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the Bodhisatta's maternal aunt, to the position of Chief Queen. At that time, Prince Nanda was born. This Mahāpajāpatī entrusted Prince Nanda to nurses and she herself looked after the Bodhisatta.

At another time, after the Bodhisatta had made the Great Renunciation, attained Omniscience, and was working for the benefit of the world, he eventually reached Kapilavatthu and entered the city for alms. Then his father, King Suddhodana, became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) after hearing a Dhamma discourse in the middle of the street. Furthermore, on the second day, Prince Nanda ordained as a monk, and on the seventh day, Prince Rāhula ordained as a novice. At a later time, the Buddha was residing in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) near the city of Vesālī. At that time, King Suddhodana realized Arahantship under the white parasol and attained Parinibbāna. Then, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī conceived the desire to ordain.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of the preaching of the Kalahavivāda Sutta on the banks of the Rohiṇī River, five hundred Sakyan princesses, who were the attendants of the five hundred princes who had renounced the world and ordained, were all of one mind. Thinking, "We shall go to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and all of us will ordain in the presence of the Buddha," they made Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī their leader and desired to go to the Buddha to ordain. This Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī had previously requested ordination from the Buddha once but did not receive it. Therefore, she summoned a barber, had her hair cut off, donned saffron-colored robes, and taking all those Sakyan princesses with her, went to Vesālī. Having requested the Buddha through the Elder Ānanda, she received the status of a novice and a fully ordained nun through the Eight Heavy Rules (Garudhammas). All the remaining Sakyan princesses also received full ordination from the community of monks alone.
264:
Having gone to Vesālī and having requested the Buddha through the Elder Ānanda, she received both the initial and full ordination through the Eight Heavy Rules (Garudhammas). All the other (five hundred) princesses were also ordained at once (by the monks). This is just a summary here; in detail, this story has already appeared in the Vinaya Cūḷavagga (402, etc.).

Having thus attained ordination, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Buddha, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place; then the Buddha preached the Dhamma to her. She took a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Buddha and attained Arahantship. The remaining five hundred bhikkhunīs also attained Arahantship at the conclusion of the Nandakovāda Sutta. Thus did this story arise. Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing bhikkhunīs to various positions, he placed Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī in the foremost position among those of long standing (rattaññū).

## The Story of Khemā Therī
In the second sutta, it is about the bhikkhunī named Khemā. From this sutta onwards, regarding the matter of her questioning, I shall not say "this is the sequential talk," but in every instance, I shall speak only the words starting from the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra).

It is said that in the past, during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born in the city of Haṃsavatī as a servant to others. Then one day, seeing the Elder Nun named Sujātā, the Chief Disciple of that Buddha, walking for alms, she offered three sweet cakes (modaka). On that very day, she sold her hair to give an offering to the Elder Nun and made an aspiration: "In the time of a future Buddha, may I be one of great wisdom like you, venerable lady." Without being negligent in meritorious deeds throughout her life, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took conception in the palace of King Kiki of Kāsi and was born among seven sisters. For twenty thousand years, she practiced the maidenly holy life (komāri-brahmacariya) in the palace itself, and together with those sisters, she built and offered a monastery for the Buddha. Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans during the interval between two Buddhas, she took conception in a royal family in the city of Sāgala in the kingdom of Madda during the time of this Buddha; they named her Khemā. Her body's complexion was like the color of molten gold. When she reached of age, she went to the palace of King Bimbisāra.
265:
While the Blessed One was staying at the Veጷuvana Monastery near Rājagaha, Queen Khemā, being intoxicated with her own beauty, heard that "the Teacher points out the faults of beauty." Fearing that "He might point out the faults in my beauty as well," she did not go to see the Ten-Powered One. King Bimbisāra thought, "I am the chief attendant of the Teacher; it is not pleasing to me that the chief queen of an Ariya disciple like myself does not go to see the Ten-Powered One." The King had wise poets compose verses praising the Veጷuvana garden and said, "Sing these within the hearing of Queen Khemā." Having heard the praises of the garden, the Queen desired to go and asked the King for permission. The King said, "Go to the garden, but you shall not be allowed to return without seeing the Teacher." Without replying to the King's words, she set out on the journey. The King instructed the royal men accompanying the Queen, "If the Queen sees the Ten-Powered One on her return from the garden, that is well. If she does not, make her see Him by royal command." Then, after wandering in the garden all day, the Queen attempted to leave without seeing the Ten-Powered One. At that time, the King's men, even against the Queen's will, took her to the presence of the Teacher.

Seeing her coming, the Teacher, through His psychic power, created an illusion of a celestial maiden who appeared to be fanning Him with a palmyra fan. Seeing that maiden, Queen Khemā thought, "I am ruined by my pride. Women as beautiful as celestial maidens stand near the Ten-Powered One; I am not even fit to be a servant to these women. I am ruined by the power of an evil mind based on intoxication with pride." Taking that as an object of contemplation, she stood looking at that woman. Then, while the Queen was watching, by the power of the Teacher's determination, that woman appeared to pass through youth into middle age, and from middle age into old age, with wrinkled skin, grey hair, and broken teeth. Then, while the Queen was still watching, she collapsed along with the palmyra fan. At that moment, because Queen Khemā was endowed with the merit of past perfections, when this object of decay became clear to her, she thought, "Even such a body as this reaches such destruction; my body, too, will surely have such a nature." At the moment of her thinking thus, the Teacher spoke this Dhammapada verse:
266: "Just as a spider falls into the web it has made itself, so those infatuated with lust fall into the stream of craving they have created themselves. The wise, having cut even this stream of craving, go forth without longing, abandoning all suffering." At the end of the verse, while standing in the same posture, Queen Khemā attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). One who attains Arahantship while living in the household life must either attain Parinibbāna on that very day or go forth. Queen Khemā, knowing that her life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) would still continue, thought, "I will ask for permission to ordain," and after paying homage to the Blessed One, she went to the palace and stood without saluting King Bimbisāra. The King knew by her gesture, "This queen must have attained the Noble Dhamma." Then he asked her, "Queen, did you go to see the Teacher?" She replied, "Great King, your seeing is but a small seeing; I, however, have seen the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) well. Please grant me permission to ordain." The King, saying "Very well, Queen," accepted her request, and having her sent to the nunnery in a golden palanquin, he had her ordained. Then, her status as a great wise one became famous, saying, "The one named Khemā Therī attained Arahantship while still in the lay life." This is the story here. Later, while the Teacher was staying at Jetavana, when assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions, he placed Khemā Therī in the foremost position among those of great wisdom. ## The Story of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī In the third sutta, "Uppalavaṇṇā" is the name given to the elder nun because she possessed a complexion like the interior of a blue lotus. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a respectable family in Haṃsavatī. Later, going with a group of people to the Teacher and listening to the Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those with psychic powers. She then gave great offerings (mahādāna) for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and aspired for that position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life and wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she took rebirth in the palace of King Kikī of Kāsi in the city of Bārāṇasī during the time of Kassapa Buddha. Becoming one among seven sisters, for twenty thousand years...
267:
(For twenty thousand years) she practiced the holy life, built and offered a precinct to the Saṅgha of monks, and was reborn in the celestial realm.

Passing away from that celestial realm and returning to the human world, she was born in a village where she earned her living by manual labor. One day, while going to a field-watch hut, she saw a lotus flower blooming early in a pond along the way. She descended into the pond, took the lotus flower and a lotus leaf to hold popped rice, cut some stalks of hill-paddy in the field, and sat in the hut roasting the rice, counting five hundred grains of popped rice. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha, who had arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana, arrived and stood not far from her. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, she took the lotus flower along with the popped rice, came down from the hut, placed the popped rice in the Paccekabuddha’s bowl, and offered it after covering the bowl with the lotus flower.

Then, when the Paccekabuddha had gone a little way, the thought occurred to her: "Renunciants have no need for flowers; I will take the flower and wear it myself." So she went and took the flower from the Paccekabuddha’s hand, but then she thought again: "If the Noble One had no need for the flower, he would not have allowed it to be placed on top of the bowl; surely the Noble One must have a use for it." She went back again, placed it on top of the bowl, and asked for the Paccekabuddha’s forgiveness, making a wish: "Venerable Sir, by the result of this popped rice, may I have as many sons as the number of grains; by the result of this lotus flower, may a lotus flower spring up at every step I take wherever I am born." While she was watching, the Paccekabuddha traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana and placed that lotus as a foot-wipe near the staircase used by the Paccekabuddhas to ascend in the Nandamūlaka valley.

She too, by the result of that meritorious deed, was reborn in the celestial realm. From the time of her birth, a great lotus flower sprang up at every step she took. Passing away from that celestial realm, she was reborn inside a lotus in a lotus pond at the foot of a mountain. An ascetic lived depending on that pond. Going to the pond early in the morning to wash his face, he saw that lotus and thought: "This lotus is much larger than the others; while the others are blooming, this one remains a bud; there must be a reason for this." He descended into the water and took the lotus. As soon as he touched it, it bloomed. The ascetic saw a young girl lying inside the lotus. From the moment he saw her, he felt a fatherly love for her, and taking her along with the lotus to his leaf-hut, he laid her on a small couch.
268:
Then, by the power of her merit, milk appeared in her thumb. When that lotus withered, the ascetic brought another fresh flower and laid her in it. Later, from the time she was able to run and play about, a lotus flower sprang up at every step she took. Her body's complexion was like a heap of saffron. She did not reach the beauty of a goddess, but she surpassed the beauty of humans. She would remain in the leaf-hut when her father went to search for various fruits.

Then one day, when she had reached the age of maturity and her father had gone to search for fruits, a forest hunter saw her and thought: "Such a beauty does not exist among humans; I will investigate." He sat waiting for the ascetic's return. When she saw her father returning, she went to meet him, took the carrying pole and water jar from his hand, and performed the major and minor duties for her father as he sat down. Then the forest hunter, realizing she was indeed human, paid homage to the ascetic and sat down. The ascetic invited the forest hunter with various forest roots and fruits and drinking water, then asked: "Good man, will you stay in this very place or will you go?" The hunter replied: "Venerable Sir, I will go; what would I do here?" The ascetic said: "Will you be able to go from here and not tell others about what you have seen?" The hunter replied: "Venerable Sir, if you do not wish it, why would I speak of it?" After paying homage to the ascetic, he departed, making marks on branches and trees to recognize the path when he returned.

Going to Bārāṇasī, he saw the King. The King asked: "Why have you come?" He reported everything, saying: "Your Majesty, I am your forest hunter; I have come because I saw a wonderful jewel of a woman at the foot of the mountain." Hearing those words, the King went quickly to the foot of the mountain, established a camp nearby, and after performing the meal service for the ascetic along with the hunter and other men, he went to the ascetic, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat on one side. The King placed the requisites of a renunciant at the ascetic's feet and said: "Venerable Sir, what will you do in this forest? Let us go." The ascetic said: "Great King, you go." "Yes, I will go, Venerable Sir. However, we have heard that there is a person of a different nature near you; such a person is not suitable for renunciants. Venerable Sir, let her go with me." The ascetic replied: "The minds of humans are indeed ill-disposed; how, in the midst of many people, could this girl..."
269: "Venerable Sir, from the time we desire, we shall place her in the position of the head of the other women and look after her," they said. Hearing the King's words, the ascetic called his daughter by the name given in her childhood, "Dear daughter Padumavatī." At his first call, she came out of the leaf-hut, paid homage to her father, and stood there. Then the father said, "Dear daughter, you have reached maturity. It is no longer appropriate for you to stay in this forest since the King has seen you. Go with the King, my daughter." Padumavatī accepted her father's words, saying, "Very well, father," paid homage, and stood weeping. The King, thinking, "I will satisfy the heart of this maiden's father," placed her upon a pile of kahāpaṇas right there and consecrated her as the Chief Queen. Then the King took her and returned to his city. From the time of his arrival, he did not look at the other women but delighted only with Padumavatī. Those women, overcome by jealousy and wishing to cause a rift between her and the King, said, "Great King, this one is not of human birth. Where have you ever seen lotuses springing up in places where humans walk? Surely she is a yakkhiṇī. Cast her out, Great King." Hearing their words, the King remained silent. Later, a rebellion broke out in the border region. The King, thinking, "Padumavatī is heavily pregnant," left her in the city and went to the border. Then those women bribed Padumavatī's attendant and said, "As soon as this queen gives birth, remove the child, smear a log of wood with blood, and place it near her." Soon after, Padumavatī gave birth. Although Prince Mahāpaduma alone took conception in the womb, the remaining four hundred and ninety-nine children were born as saṃsedaja (moisture-born) when Prince Mahāpaduma came out of his mother's womb and lay down. Then, knowing that "this queen has not yet regained consciousness," the attendant smeared a log of wood with blood, placed it nearby, and gave a signal to those women. Those five hundred women each took one child and sent them to the craftsmen to be placed in caskets...
270:
(Those women) had the caskets brought, placed the children they had respectively obtained into those caskets, sealed them from the outside, and kept them.

When Queen Padumavatī regained consciousness, she asked the attendant, "Mother, what kind of child have I given birth to?" The attendant threatened the queen and said, "Where would you get a child from?" and placed the blood-smeared log before her, saying, "This log is the child that came out of your womb." Seeing that log, the queen was filled with grief and said, "Quickly split this log and remove it. If anyone sees it, it would be shameful." Hearing the queen's words, the attendant, as if wishing her well, split the log and threw it into the stove.

The King returned from the border and, waiting for the festival, established an encampment outside the city and stayed there. Then those five hundred women came to welcome the King and said, "Great King, you do not believe our words; what we say seems groundless. You should call the Chief Queen's attendant and question her. Your queen gave birth only to a log." Without investigating or reflecting on the matter, the King said, "She must be a non-human yakkhiṇī," and expelled Padumavatī from the palace. As soon as Padumavatī left the palace, the lotuses disappeared, and her complexion became dull and ruined. While she was walking alone along the road, an elderly woman saw her, felt a motherly affection for her, and asked, "Dear daughter, where are you going?" She replied, "I am a stranger, wandering in search of a place to stay." Then the old woman said, "Come here, daughter," gave her a place to stay, and prepared food for her.

While Queen Padumavatī was living with the old woman in this manner, those five hundred women, being of one mind, said to the King, "Great King, when you went to war, we made a vow to the deity of the Gaṅgā, saying, 'When our lord returns victorious from battle, we shall make an offering and play in the water.' O King, we wish to inform you of this matter." The King was pleased with their words and went to play in the Gaṅgā. Those women also took the caskets they had respectively obtained, concealing them. Upon reaching the river, they covered the caskets with cloth to hide them, entered the water, and released the caskets. All those caskets floated away together and got caught in a net spread downstream. After they had finished playing in the water...
271:
When the King came up from the water, those who were pulling up the nets saw the caskets and brought them to the King. Seeing the caskets, the King asked, "Friends, what is inside these caskets?" They replied, "Your Majesty, we do not know." The King had the caskets opened and looked inside; first, he had the casket of Prince Mahāpaduma opened. In the caskets of all those princes, on the very day they were laid there, milk flowed from their thumbs due to the power of their merit.

Sakka, the King of Devas, in order to remove the King's doubt, had letters inscribed inside the caskets: "These princes were born from the womb of Queen Padumavatī and are the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī. At that time, the five hundred women who were Padumavatī's rivals placed these princes in caskets and set them adrift in the water. Let the King know this matter." As soon as the caskets were opened, the King read the letters and saw the children. He picked up Prince Mahāpaduma and said, "Quickly harness the chariots! Prepare the horses! Today I shall enter the city and do what is pleasing (punishment) to certain women." He then ascended the palace, placed a bundle of a thousand pieces of gold on an elephant's neck, and had the drum beaten, proclaiming, "Whoever can show me Padumavatī, let that person take this thousand!"

Hearing those words, Padumavatī signaled to her mother who had raised her, "Mother, take the thousand from the elephant's neck." She replied, "I do not dare to take such wealth." When told a second and third time, she asked, "Mother, what shall I say when I take it?" Padumavatī said, "Say, 'My daughter sees Queen Padumavatī,' and take it." The old woman said, "Let it be so," and went to take the bundle of a thousand. Then people asked her, "Mother, do you see Queen Padumavatī?" She replied, "I do not see her, but they say my daughter sees her." They said, "Mother, where is that daughter?" and went with the old woman. Recognizing Padumavatī, they prostrated at her feet. Then, realizing "This is indeed Queen Padumavatī," they said, "Alas, a heavy deed has been done to this woman! Being the chief consort of such a King, she had to live in such a place without protection."

The King's men surrounded Padumavatī's house with white curtains, placed guards at the door, and informed the King. The King sent a golden palanquin. Padumavatī said, "I do not wish to go like this. From my dwelling place to the palace, let fine rugs decorated with noble figures be spread, and above, let a cloth canopy adorned with golden stars be fastened. If all the ornaments are sent to me, I shall go only on foot. Only by going thus will the citizens see my prosperity." The King commanded, "Do as Padumavatī wishes."

Then Padumavatī, having adorned herself with all the ornaments, stepped onto the road, saying, "I shall go to the palace." At that moment, wherever she stepped, Paduma lotuses burst through the fine rugs decorated with noble figures and bloomed. Showing her prosperity to the multitude, she ascended to the palace and had all the decorative rugs given to the old woman as payment for her upbringing. The King also summoned those five hundred women and said, "Queen, I give these women to you as your slave-maids."
272:
"Even though all the ornaments have been sent for my decoration, I shall go only on foot. Only by going thus will the citizens see my prosperity," she said. The King replied, "Do as Queen Padumavatī wishes." Then Queen Padumavatī, having adorned herself with all the ornaments, set out on the journey to the palace. At that moment, wherever the Queen stepped, Paduma lotuses burst through the fine rugs decorated with noble figures and bloomed. Showing her prosperity to the multitude, she ascended to the palace and had all the decorative rugs given to the old woman who had raised her as payment for her upbringing. The King also summoned those five hundred women and said, "Queen, I give these women to you as your slave-maids."

The Queen replied, "Very well, Great King. Let the whole city know that these women have been given to me." The King had the drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, "The five hundred women who wronged Queen Padumavatī have been given to her as her slave-maids." When the Queen knew that their status as slaves was recognized by the whole city, she asked the King, "Your Majesty, may I have permission to make my slaves free (bhujissa)?" The King said, "As you wish, Queen." This being so, she summoned the same drum-beater and had it proclaimed again: "All five hundred women given to Queen Padumavatī as slaves have been made free." After she had freed those women, she handed over the four hundred and ninety-nine sons to those very women to be raised, while she herself took only Prince Mahāpaduma.

Later, when those princes reached the age for playing, the King had various playgrounds constructed in the park. When they reached the age of sixteen, they were all together playing in the auspicious lotus pond covered with Paduma lotuses in the park. Seeing the newly bloomed lotuses and the old lotuses falling from their stalks, they thought, "Even in these inanimate lotuses, such old age occurs. What then of our bodies? This body, too, will surely have such a destiny." Taking this as their object of meditation, all the princes attained the knowledge of Paccekabuddhas. Rising one by one, they sat cross-legged upon the lotus pericarps. Then the King's men who had come with them, realizing that much of the day had passed, said, "Princes, please know the time." The princes remained silent.
273:
Those men went and informed the King, "O King, the princes are sitting on the lotus pericarps. Even though we spoke to them, they did not utter a single word." The King said, "Let them sit as they wish." Those princes remained sitting on the lotus pericarps throughout the night under guard until dawn. The next day, the men approached them and said, "O Princes, please know the time." The princes replied, "We are not princes; we are Paccekabuddhas." The men said, "Sirs, you speak a very heavy word. Those called Paccekabuddhas are not like you. They have hair and beards two inches long and wear the eight requisites on their bodies." Then the princes touched their heads with their right hands. At that very moment, their lay appearance disappeared, and the eight requisites appeared on their bodies. Then, while the great multitude was watching, they departed through the air to the Nandamūlaka mountain slope.

Queen Padumavatī, thinking, "I, who had many sons, have now become sonless," fell into deep grief and died from that very sorrow. She was reborn in a small village near the gate of the city of Rājagaha, in a life where she had to earn her living by working with her own hands. Later, she went to her husband's house. One day, while carrying rice gruel to her husband in the field, she saw eight Paccekabuddhas—out of the five hundred who had been her sons—traveling through the air at the time for alms-round. Seeing them, she went quickly and said to her husband, "Lord, look at the Paccekabuddhas! Let us invite these noble ones and offer them food." The husband said, "These are called 'monk-birds'; they wander about like this in other places too. They are not Paccekabuddhas." While they were talking, the Paccekabuddhas descended nearby. That woman offered her rice and food to them that day and said, "Venerable sirs, please accept my alms tomorrow as well, all eight of you." They said, "Laywoman, it is well. Let your hospitality be this much; prepare only eight seats. When you see many other Paccekabuddhas, let your heart be clear and confident." The next day, she prepared eight seats and arranged the offerings for the eight Paccekabuddhas and sat waiting.

The invited Paccekabuddhas gave a signal to the remaining Paccekabuddhas, "Sirs, do not go elsewhere today; all of you, show favor to your mother." Hearing their words, they all came together through the air and appeared at the door of their mother's house. Because she had been given a signal beforehand, she was not shaken even though she saw many Paccekabuddhas. All of them...
274:
She invited those Paccekabuddhas into the house and had them sit on the seats. While those Paccekabuddhas were sitting in order, the ninth one created eight other seats and sat himself in the chief seat. As the seats increased, the house also expanded. When all of them were seated, the woman gave the offerings prepared for the eight Paccekabuddhas to all five hundred as much as they desired. Then, bringing eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she placed them at the feet of the invited Paccekabuddhas and made a wish: "Venerable sirs, in every place I am reborn, may my body's complexion be like the color of the inner womb of these blue lotuses." The Paccekabuddhas gave their blessing to their mother and departed for Mount Gandhamādana.

That woman performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, and after passing away from that existence, she was reborn in the celestial realm. During the time of this Buddha's appearance, she took rebirth in a treasurer's family in the city of Sāvatthī. Because her complexion was like the interior of a blue lotus, they named her "Uppalavaṇṇā." When she reached the age of maturity, kings and treasurers from throughout the whole of Jambudīpa sent messages to the treasurer, saying, "Give your daughter to us." There was almost no one who did not send a request. Then the treasurer thought, "I will not be able to please everyone's mind; I will use a stratagem." He called his daughter and asked, "Dear daughter, will you be able to ordain as a nun?" Because she was in her final existence, her father's words were like oil cooked a hundred times poured upon her head. Therefore, she said to her father, "Father, I will ordain." The treasurer made offerings for her and, taking her to the nunnery, had her ordained. Not long after her ordination, her turn came to look after the Uposatha hall. She lit a lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and taking the flame of the lamp as her object of meditation, she looked at it repeatedly. She developed jhāna with the fire-kasina as its object and, using that very jhāna as a basis, attained Arahantship. Along with the fruit of Arahantship, she became proficient in the mastery of psychic transformations. Later, on the day the Blessed One performed the Twin Miracle, she uttered a lion's roar, saying, "Venerable Sir, I will perform a miracle." The Buddha, taking this matter as an occasion while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, and appointing the bhikkhunīs to various positions in order, placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those bhikkhunīs possessed of psychic powers.
275:
## The Story of Paṭācārā Therī

In the fourth sutta, with the passage "Vinayadharānaṃ yadidaṃ Paṭācārā," the Buddha shows that the Elder Paṭācārā is the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who are keepers of the Vinaya. This future Paṭācārā Therī was conceived in a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, she saw the Buddha appoint a bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who are keepers of the Vinaya. She performed great meritorious deeds and aspired for that very position. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was conceived in the palace of King Kikī of Kāsi. Being one among seven sisters, she practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) for twenty thousand years and donated a monastery precinct (pariveṇa) to the Saṅgha. After that, she was reborn in the deva realm and enjoyed celestial bliss for the interval between two Buddhas. In the time of our current Buddha, she was conceived in the house of a merchant (seṭṭhi) in the city of Sāvatthī.

Later, when the merchant's daughter reached marriageable age, she had an affair with a servant in her house. Later, when she was about to be sent to a family of equal status, she gave a signal to the man she had been with, saying: "From tomorrow onwards, you will not have the chance to see me even with a hundred gatekeepers. If you have the ability to act, take me and go now." The man replied, "Let it be so," and taking suitable jewelry and wealth, he took the merchant's daughter and lived in a small village about three or four yojanas away from the city.

Later, while living there, she became pregnant. When the pregnancy reached full term, she said, "Lord, this place is a place of no refuge for us. Let us go to my parents' house." The man delayed, saying, "We will go today, we will go tomorrow," being unable to go. Knowing his reason, she thought, "This fool will not take me," and while he was out, she set out on the journey alone, thinking, "I will go to my parents' house by myself." When the man returned and did not find her at home, he asked the neighbors and heard that she had gone to her parents' house. Thinking, "Because of me, this daughter of a good family has become helpless," he followed her tracks and caught up with her. She gave birth while still on the way. Then they returned, saying, "The purpose for which we were going has been fulfilled on the way; what is the use of going now?" Later, she became pregnant again, and the details should be understood in the same manner as before.
276:
While on the way, at the time of her delivery, a great storm arose from the four directions. She said to her husband, "Lord, a storm has arisen from the four directions at an unseasonable time; please strive to make a shelter for us." The man said, "I will do so," and made a small hut with sticks and branches. Thinking, "I will fetch grass for roofing," he went to cut grass at the base of a large anthill. Then, a cobra lurking in the anthill bit his foot, and he fell and died on that very spot.

The merchant's daughter waited all night, thinking, "He will come now, he will come now." She thought, "Surely, thinking I am helpless, that man must have abandoned me on the road and left." When it became light, she followed his tracks and saw him fallen at the base of the anthill. She lamented, "Because of me, my husband has perished." Carrying the younger child and having the older child hold onto her fingers, she continued her journey. On the way, she saw a shallow river and thought, "I am not able to take both children across at the same time." She left the older child on this bank, carried the younger child to the other bank, laid him on a swaddling cloth, and then stepped back into the river, thinking, "I will go and get the older child."

When she reached the middle of the river, a hawk, thinking "This is a piece of meat," came to snatch the infant. She waved her hands to drive the hawk away. Seeing her waving hands, the older child thought, "She is calling me," and entered the river, where he was swept away by the current. The hawk also snatched the infant and flew away before she could reach him. Overwhelmed by intense grief, she went along the way singing this lamentation:
"Both sons have perished; my husband died on the path."

Lamenting in this way, she reached the city of Sāvatthī. Although she went towards her family's home, due to her grief, she could not recognize her own house and asked, "In this place, there is a family of such a name; where is that house?" People told her, "What will you do by asking for that family? Their house collapsed due to a violent wind, and all of them perished right there. Now, they are cremating both the young and the old on a single funeral pyre. Look at that column of smoke." As soon as she heard those words...
277:
"What are you saying?" she said, and unable to keep her clothes on, she raised both arms and went to the cremation ground of her relatives, wailing and lamenting just as she was born from her mother's womb. Completing her lamentation song, she wailed:

"Both sons have died,
My husband died on the way;
Mother, father, and brother
Are burning on a single pyre."

Even when others gave her clothes, she tore them up again and again and discarded them. Then, wherever she was seen, crowds of people surrounded her as she wandered. At that time, they named her "Paṭācārā," saying, "This woman wanders without wearing a cloth (paṭa)." And because her shameless conduct was evident due to her nakedness, they named her Paṭācārā, meaning "one whose conduct (ācāra) has fallen."

One day, while the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma to a great multitude, she entered the monastery and stood at the edge of the assembly. The Teacher, suffusing her with loving-kindness, said, "Sister, regain your mindfulness; sister, regain your mindfulness." Upon hearing the Teacher's words, a strong sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) arose in her, and she sat down right there on the ground. A man standing nearby threw her an upper robe. She wore that cloth and listened to the Dhamma. The Teacher, by the power of her conduct, spoke these verses from the Dhammapada:

"Sons are no protection, nor father, nor kinsmen;
For one seized by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among relatives.
Knowing this fact, the wise man, restrained by virtue,
Should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna."

At the end of the verses, while standing there, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. She approached the Teacher, paid homage, and requested ordination. The Teacher permitted her ordination, saying, "Go to the nunnery and ordain." Soon after ordaining, she attained Arahantship. While learning the Buddha's words, she became an expert with mastery in the Vinaya Piṭaka. Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana monastery and assigning various ranks to the bhikkhunīs in order, he placed Theri Paṭācārā in the foremost (etadagga) position among the bhikkhunīs who are experts in the Vinaya.
278:
## The Story of Theri Dhammadinnā

In the fifth sutta, with the word "dhammakathikānaṃ," it is shown that Dhammadinnā is the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who teach the Dhamma. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born as a servant in the city of Haṃsavatī. She performed an extraordinary deed of merit for Sujāta Thera, the Chief Disciple of Padumuttara Buddha, and aspired for that specific rank. She performed meritorious deeds throughout her life and was reborn in the celestial realm. All the details should be understood according to the aspiration of Theri Khemā mentioned previously.

During the time of Phussa Buddha, she lived in the house of a treasurer appointed to manage the almsgiving of the three brothers, who were the Buddha's half-brothers. When asked to "give one," she gave two. Thus, giving without diminishing any merit, after ninety-two aeons had passed, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the palace of King Kikī of Kāsi, becoming one of the seven sisters. For twenty thousand years, she practiced the holy life and built a residential monastery (vasanapariveṇa) for the Saṅgha. Wandering through celestial and human realms during the interval between Buddhas (buddhantara), she took rebirth in a noble family during the time of this Buddha and later went to the house of the merchant Visākha. The merchant Visākha was a friend of King Bimbisāra; he went with the king to see the Buddha for the first time, heard the Dhamma, and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Later, he realized the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala).

On the day he attained the fruit of Non-returning, he returned home. When Dhammadinnā, standing at the head of the stairs, extended her hand, he did not take it and ascended the mansion. Even while eating, he did not say a single word like "Give this" or "Take this away." While Dhammadinnā was serving him with a ladle, she thought, "This merchant did not take my hand even though I offered it, and he says nothing while eating. What is my fault?" Then, after he had eaten, she asked, "Noble sir, what is my fault?"

"Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you. However, from today onwards, I am no longer fit to sit or stand near you, or to eat or consume food with you through the power of sensual intimacy. If you wish, stay in this house. If not, take as much wealth as you need and return to your family home."

"Noble son, if that is the case, I do not wish to live carrying on my head the sensual pleasures which are like the spit and vomit discarded by you. Please allow me to ordain." Visākha said, "Very well, Dhammadinnā," and after informing the King, he sent Dhammadinnā to the nunnery in a golden palanquin for her ordination.
279:
After ordaining, Dhammadinnā thought: "This merchant Visākha, while staying in the midst of his house, has already made an end of suffering. It is proper that I too, from the time I have received ordination, should make an end of suffering." She then went to her teachers and preceptors and said, "Ladies, my mind does not delight in a place crowded with people; I will go to a village dwelling."

The elder nuns, unable to restrain her mind because she had ordained after leaving a noble family, took her and went to a village dwelling. Because she had the habit of contemplating the conditioned formations in her past lives, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Then the thought occurred to her: "My task as a nun has reached its completion. What shall I do by staying here? I will go to Rājagaha. There, many of my relatives, depending on me, will perform meritorious deeds." Thus, taking the elder nuns with her, she returned to the city.

When the merchant Visākha learned of her return, he thought, "She has returned very quickly. Could she be dissatisfied with the holy life?" In the evening, he went to her, paid his respects, and sat in a suitable place. Thinking, "It is not proper to ask whether she is dissatisfied," he asked questions regarding the five aggregates and so forth. The Elder Nun Dhammadinnā answered every question he asked, as if cutting a lotus stalk with a sword.

The lay follower Visākha, recognizing the sharpness of Elder Nun Dhammadinnā’s wisdom, asked questions in every aspect regarding the three paths according to his own attainment, and then, based on what he had learned, he also asked about the path of Arahantship. Elder Nun Dhammadinnā, knowing that the lay follower Visākha’s range was only up to the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala), thought, "Now he is running beyond his own range," and wishing to stop him, she said: "Friend Visākha, you have overstepped the limit of questioning; you are unable to grasp the end of questions. For, friend Visākha, the holy life is rooted in Nibbāna, has Nibbāna as its destination, and has Nibbāna as its final goal. If you wish, friend Visākha, approach the Blessed One and ask him about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it."

The lay follower Visākha went to the Teacher and reported the entire conversation of questions and answers. The Teacher, hearing his words, said, "My daughter has no more craving for the aggregates of the past, future, and present," and spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"He for whom there is nothing in the past, the future, or the present;
him who is without possession and without attachment, I call a Brahmin."
280:
Then the Blessed One, having given his approval to Elder Nun Dhammadinnā, said to the lay follower Visākha: "Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is wise. Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has great wisdom. If you, Visākha, were to ask me about this matter, I would explain it in the same way as the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā has explained it. This is indeed its meaning, and you should remember it as such." Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana Monastery, as he was appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order, he took the occasion of this Cūḷavedalla Sutta and placed the Elder Nun Dhammadinnā in the foremost position among the bhikkhunīs who are speakers of Dhamma (dhammakathikā) in this Dispensation.

## The Story of Elder Nun Nandā

In the sixth discourse, with the words "Nandā is the foremost among those who meditate (jhāyīnaṃ)," he shows that Elder Nun Nandā is the foremost among the elder nuns who delight in jhāna. It is said that in the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she took rebirth in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Later, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appointing a bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who delight in jhāna. She performed meritorious deeds and aspired for that position. From then on, she wandered through the worlds of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and before our Teacher was born, she took rebirth in the womb of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. They named her Nandā. She was also called Rūpanandā. Later, because of her exceedingly beautiful appearance, she became famous as Janapadakalyāṇī (The Beauty of the Country).

When our Ten-Powered One attained Omniscience and eventually came to Kapilavatthu, he ordained Prince Nanda and Rāhula and then departed. When King Suddhodana passed away, she learned that "Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the mother of Rāhula have left the palace and ordained in the presence of the Teacher." She thought, "Since they have ordained, what business do I have left in this worldly life?" and went to Mahāpajāpatī to ordain. From the day she ordained, she thought, "The Teacher often criticizes physical beauty," and so she did not go to attend upon the Teacher. When it was her turn to receive instruction (ovāda), she would send someone else to bring the instruction. The Teacher, knowing that she was intoxicated with her own beauty, said, "Let them come to receive their own instruction themselves; no other bhikkhunī should be sent." Then Rūpanandā, seeing no other way, went for the instruction against her will.

The Teacher, according to her temperament, created the form of a woman by his psychic power, who appeared to be fanning him with a palm-leaf fan. When Rūpanandā saw that form, she thought: "I have been negligent and have not come for no reason at all; even women with such beauty as this [are in the presence of] the Teacher..."
281:
They move freely in the presence of the Blessed One. "My beauty is not worth even a sixteenth part of the beauty of these women; not knowing this, I have stayed away for so long." Taking that very beautiful image as her object, she stood watching. Because Rūpanandā was possessed of past merit, the Blessed One recited the verse in the Dhammapada beginning with "A city made of bones" (Dhp. 150), and spoke the Sutta verse:

"Whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down."

She, establishing the perception of rise and fall (decay) in that very form, attained Arahantship. In this context, this story is similar to the story of Khemā Therī mentioned below, so it is not elaborated further. From then on, Rūpanandā became the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who delight in meditation (jhāna). Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery, as he was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions, he appointed Nandā Therī to the foremost position among those who delight in meditation.

## The Story of Soṇā Therī

In the seventh discourse, with the words "āraddhavīriyānaṃ," the Blessed One shows that Soṇā is the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who possess aroused and perfected energy. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was reborn in a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Later, while listening to the Dhamma, she saw the Blessed One appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those of aroused energy. She performed acts of merit and aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was reborn in a noble family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. Later, living the household life, she had many sons and daughters and settled them all in their respective households. From then on, those children said, "What can this old woman do for us?" and did not even recognize her as "mother" when she came to them. Soṇā of Many Children, knowing their lack of respect for her, thought, "What is the use of living the household life?" and left to ordain. Then the bhikkhunīs, saying, "This woman does not know the duties; she does what is improper," imposed disciplinary tasks (daṇḍakamma) on her. When her children saw her performing those disciplinary tasks, they mocked her wherever they saw her, saying, "To this day, she does not even know the basic training." Hearing their words, she was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and thought, "It is proper to purify my own destiny." Thus, even while sitting...
282:
...and even while standing, she recited the thirty-two parts of the body. Just as she was previously known as "Soṇā Therī of Many Children" (Bahuputtikasoṇattherī), she later became famous as "Soṇā Therī of Aroused Energy" (Āraddhavīriyasoṇattherī).

Then one day, as the bhikkhunīs were going to the monastery, they said, "Soṇā, heat the water for the community of bhikkhunīs," and departed. Even before heating the water, she walked back and forth in the fire-room, reciting the thirty-two parts of the body and developing insight (vipassanā). The Blessed One, while sitting in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), uttered this verse of radiance:

"Though one should live a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma,
Better is a single day of life for one who sees the supreme Dhamma."

At the conclusion of the verse, she attained Arahantship and thought: "I have attained Arahantship. If the incoming bhikkhunīs, without investigating, should despise me and say something, they would produce much demerit. Therefore, it is proper to do something to make it known." She placed the water pot on the hearth but did not put fire beneath it. When the bhikkhunīs returned and looked at the hearth, they did not see any fire and said, "We told this old woman to boil water for the community of bhikkhunīs, but even now she has not put fire in the hearth." She said, "Sisters, what do you need fire for? If you wish to bathe with hot water, take the water from the pot and bathe." Thinking, "There must be a reason for this," they went and dipped their hands into the water, and knowing it was hot, they drew the water with a vessel. Wherever they drew water from, it became full again. Then, all of them, realizing her state of Arahantship, the younger bhikkhunīs first prostrated at her feet with the five-point prostration and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Sister, for so long we have harassed and spoken to you without investigating; please forgive us." The elder bhikkhunīs also sat crouching and asked for forgiveness, saying, "Sister, please forgive us." From then on, the virtue of the Therī became well-known: "Even though she ordained in her old age, through her aroused energy, she established herself in the highest fruit (Arahantship) before long." Later, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery, as he was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions, he appointed Soṇā Therī to the foremost position among those of aroused energy.
283:
## The Story of the Elder Nun Bakulā
In the eighth sutta, with the phrase "dibba-cakkhukānaṃ yadidaṃ bakulā," it is shown that among the nuns who possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), the Elder Nun Bakulā is the foremost. This future Elder Nun Bakulā was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. While listening to the Buddha's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain nun to the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye. She then performed a great act of merit and aspired for that position. She transmigrated among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and in the time of our Buddha, she was born into a noble family in the city of Sāvatthī. Later, upon hearing the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, she gained faith and ordained as a nun, attaining Arahatship before long. From that time on, she became one who had mastered the divine eye. Later, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery and appointing nuns to their respective foremost positions in order, he appointed this Elder Nun Bakulā to the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye.

## The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesā
In the ninth sutta, the term "khippābhiññānaṃ" shows that among the nuns with quick intuition (khippābhiññā), the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is the foremost. This future Elder Nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā was also born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. While listening to the Buddha's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Buddha appoint a certain nun to the foremost position among those with quick intuition. She performed a great act of merit and aspired for that position. She transmigrated among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, she was one of the seven sisters in the palace of King Kikī of Kāsi. For twenty thousand years, she observed the ten precepts and practiced the holy life of a maiden (komārikabrahmacariya), and she built and donated a residential compound for the Saṅgha. After transmigrating among devas and humans during the interval between two Buddhas, she was conceived into a merchant family in the city of Rājagaha during the time of our Buddha, and they named her Bhaddā Tissā.

On that very same day, a son was born to the royal chaplain (purohita) in that city. At the time of that child's birth, weapons throughout the entire city, starting from the royal palace, began to glow. Early in the morning, the chaplain went to the royal palace and asked the King if he had slept well. The King replied, "Teacher, how could I have slept well? All night today, I saw weapons glowing in the royal palace and was filled with fear." The chaplain said, "Great King, do not worry on that account. It was not only in your palace that the weapons glowed; it happened throughout the entire city." The King asked, "Teacher, for what reason?"
284:
"In our house, a boy was born under the thief constellation (coranakkhatta). This boy was born as an enemy to the entire city, and this glowing of weapons is the omen of his birth. There is no danger to Your Majesty. However, if you wish, we shall kill the child." The King replied, "If there is no harm to us, there is no reason to kill him." The chaplain, thinking, "My son has come bringing his own name," named the boy Sattuka (Enemy). In the merchant's house, the girl named Bhaddā grew up, and in the chaplain's house, Sattuka grew up. From the time Sattuka was able to run about and play on his own, he would take whatever items he found in the places he frequented and bring them back to fill his parents' house. Although his father tried to restrain him by giving a thousand reasons, he was unable to stop him.

Later, when the boy reached adulthood, the father realized that he could not be restrained by any means. He gave him two blue cloths, house-breaking tools, and a mechanical device (siṅghāṭakayantra), saying, "Live your life by this trade of theft," and let him go. From that day on, Sattuka would throw his mechanical device, climb up into the mansions of noble families, break through the walls, and take the property of others as if it were his own. There was hardly a house in the entire city that he had not robbed. One day, while the King was touring the city in his chariot, he asked the charioteer, "Why are only holes seen in various houses in this city?" The charioteer replied, "Your Majesty, a thief named Sattuka in this city breaks through walls and steals the property of noble families." The King summoned the city guard (nagaraguttika) and said, "I hear there is such a thief in this city. Why do you not catch him?" The guard replied, "Your Majesty, we are unable to find that thief with the stolen goods (sahoḍḍha)." The King commanded, "If you catch that thief today, you shall live. If you do not catch him, I will inflict the royal punishment upon you." Saying, "Very well, Your Majesty," the city guard ordered the people throughout the city to search. He caught Sattuka red-handed while he was breaking through a wall and stealing another's property, and presented him to the King. The King ordered, "Take this thief out through the south gate and execute him." The city guard obeyed the King's command and, having the thief beaten with a thousand lashes at every crossroads, led him toward the south gate.
285:
At that time, this merchant's daughter named Bhaddā, hearing the tumultuous noise of the crowd, opened the casement window and looked out. Seeing the thief named Sattuka being led away in that manner, she pressed both hands to her heart, went to her magnificent bed, and lay face down. As she was the only daughter of that merchant family, her relatives could not bear even a slight change in her facial expression. Then her mother, seeing her lying on the bed, asked, "Dear daughter, what are you doing?" She asked, "Mother, did you see that thief being led away to be executed?" The mother replied, "Yes, dear daughter, I saw him." She said, "If I get that man, I shall live; if I do not, I shall surely die." Although her relatives tried to persuade her in various ways, they were unable to do so, and thinking, "Life is better than death," they took it to heart.

Then her father went to the city guard, gave him a bribe of a thousand pieces, and said, "My daughter's heart is set on the thief; please release him by some means or other." The city guard agreed, saying "Very well" to the merchant. He took the thief and delayed the matter here and there until sunset. When the sun had set, he brought a man out from the prison, released Sattuka from his bonds, and sent Sattuka to the merchant's house. He then bound the other man with those same bonds, led him out through the south gate, and had him executed. The merchant's servants also took Sattuka and came to the merchant's residence. Upon seeing him, the merchant, thinking "I will fulfill my daughter's wish," had Sattuka bathed with scented water, adorned with all kinds of ornaments, and sent him to the upper palace. Bhaddā, thinking "My wish is fulfilled," adorned herself with many ornaments and attended to Sattuka.

After a few days had passed, Sattuka thought, "This woman's ornaments will be mine; it is proper to take these ornaments by some means." While sitting comfortably near her, he said to Bhaddā, "I have something to say to you." The merchant's daughter, with a joyful heart as if she had received a thousand pieces, said, "Lord, speak freely." He said, "You think, 'Because of me, this man has gained his life,' but while I was being captured, I made a vow to the deity dwelling on the Robbers' Cliff mountain, saying, 'If I gain my life, I will give you an offering.' Because of that deity, I have gained my life..."
286:
"...it has been gained; quickly prepare the offering." Bhaddā, thinking "I will fulfill his wish," prepared the offering, adorned herself with all her ornaments, mounted a single vehicle, and went with her husband to the Robbers' Cliff mountain. Intending to make the offering to the mountain deity, she began to ascend the mountain. The thief Sattuka thought, "If everyone ascends, I will not have the opportunity to take this woman's ornaments." So, he made Bhaddā herself carry the offering bowl and ascended the mountain.

When he spoke with Bhaddā, he did not speak endearing words. She understood his intention by his manner alone. Then he said to her, "Bhaddā, take off your outer robe and wrap the ornaments you are wearing in it." She asked, "Lord, what is my fault?" He replied, "You fool, do you think I have come for the sake of an offering? I will not pluck out my liver and give it to this mountain deity; rather, I have come here wishing to take your ornaments under the pretext of an offering." She said, "Lord, whose are the ornaments, and whose am I? We do not know such distinctions as 'this is yours' and 'this is mine.' Very well, lord, but please fulfill one wish of mine: let me embrace you from the front and from the back while I am still adorned." He agreed, saying "Very well."

Knowing that he had agreed, she embraced him from the front, and then, acting as if she were embracing him from the back, she pushed him off the mountain cliff. As he fell, he was dashed to pieces even in mid-air. Seeing the clever deed performed by Bhaddā, the deity dwelling on the mountain uttered these verses in praise of her virtues:

"That man is not a wise one in all circumstances;
A woman too is wise, being discerning here and there.
That man is not a wise one in all circumstances;
A woman too is wise, being able to think even in a moment."

Then Bhaddā thought, "It is no longer proper for me to return home in this state; I will go from here and go forth as a renunciant." She went to the park of the Nigaṇṭhas and requested ordination from them. Then they asked her, "In what manner shall the ordination be?" She said, "Whatever is the highest form in your ordination, perform that very one." They said "Very well" and plucked out her hair with a palmyra nut and ordained her. Her hair...
287:
Again, when her hair grew back, it grew in clusters, curling like earrings. For that very reason, she became known as Kundalakesā. Having learned all arts in the place where she was ordained, and realizing, "There is no further distinction in knowledge among these people," she wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Wherever there were wise men, she went there and learned all their knowledge. Then, because of her extensive training in many places, no one was able to offer a counter-argument to her. Finding no one capable of debating with her, whenever she entered a village or a market town, she would make a heap of sand at the gate and place a rose-apple branch upon it. She gave a sign to the children standing nearby, saying, "Whoever is able to refute my doctrine, let him trample this branch." Even after seven days, there was no one who would trample it. Then she would take the branch and depart.

At that time, our Blessed One had appeared in the world and was residing at the Jetavana monastery near Sāvatthī. Kundalakesā also eventually reached Sāvatthī and, upon entering the city, followed her old custom by placing the branch on a sand heap, giving the sign to the children, and then entering the city. At that time, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, entered the city alone after the assembly of monks had already entered. Seeing the rose-apple branch on the sand heap, he asked, "Why is this placed here?" The children explained the reason in full. "If that is so, children, take this branch and trample it," he said. Among those children, some did not dare to trample it upon hearing the Elder's words, but some trampled it immediately and crushed it to pieces. When Kundalakesā came out after finishing her meal and saw the trampled branch, she asked, "Whose work is this?" They told her that the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, had ordered it. She thought, "He would not have dared to order the trampling of this branch without knowing his own strength; surely he must be a great person. It would not be fitting for me to appear insignificant. It is proper to enter the village and give a sign to the public." Having thought so, she did accordingly. It should be understood that in the city where eighty thousand families resided, everyone—both those who agreed and those who disagreed—came to know of it.

The Elder, having finished his meal, sat at the foot of a certain tree. Then Kundalakesā, surrounded by a great crowd, went to the Elder, exchanged greetings, and stood at a respectful distance. She asked, "Venerable sir, did you order the trampling of the branch?" "Yes, I ordered it to be trampled," he replied. "If that is so, let there be a debate between us and your reverence,"
288:
"Venerable sir," she said. "Let it be so, sister," replied Venerable Sāriputta. "Who shall ask and who shall answer?" the wanderer asked. "Questions usually come to us, but you may ask whatever you know," the Elder said. With the Elder's permission, the wanderer named Bhaddā asked all the doctrines she knew, and the Elder answered them all. Having asked everything, she became silent.

Then the Elder said, "Sister, you have asked many questions; let us also ask one question." "Ask, venerable sir," she replied. "What is the one?" the Elder asked.
