Kundalakesā the wanderer replied, "I do not know, venerable sir." "If you do not even know this much, what else will you know?" the Elder said. The wanderer fell at the Elder's feet and said, "Venerable sir, I go to you for refuge." "There is no need to take refuge in me. In this world with its devas, the Supreme Person resides in the foremost monastery; go to Him for refuge," the Elder said.

The wanderer replied, "Venerable sir, I will do so." In the evening, at the time of the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, she went to the Teacher, prostrated with the fivefold touch, and stood at a respectful distance. To her, whose conditioned things were already contemplated, the Teacher, by the power of her temperament, spoke this verse from the Dhammapada:

"Though a thousand verses be composed of meaningless words,
Better is a single line of a verse,
Hearing which one becomes peaceful."

At the end of the verse, while still standing there, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights and requested ordination. The Teacher accepted her ordination. She went to the nunnery and was ordained. Later, a conversation arose among the fourfold assembly: "How great indeed is this Bhaddā Kundalakesā, who attained Arahantship at the end of a four-line verse!" The Teacher, making that matter the occasion, placed the Elder nun in the foremost position among those nuns of swift intuition (khippābhiññā).

## The Story of Bhaddā Kāpilānī Therī

In the tenth discourse, by the word "pubbenivāsaṃ," it is shown that Bhaddā Kāpilānī is foremost among those nuns who recollect the sequence of past aggregates. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a noble family in Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher place a certain nun in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives. She performed an act of merit and aspired to that position. For a hundred thousand aeons, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Before the current Buddha appeared, she took rebirth in a noble family in Bārāṇasī. While quarreling with her husband's sister, when the sister-in-law offered food to a Paccekabuddha, she thought, "This sister-in-law will make him follow her will by offering this food." She took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, threw away the food, filled it with mud, and offered it. People rebuked her, saying, "This woman is very foolish; what did the Paccekabuddha do to offend you that you act thus, rather than doing something to your sister-in-law with whom you quarrel?" Ashamed, the young woman took back the bowl, removed the mud, washed it, rubbed it with scented powder, filled it with the four sweet ingredients (catumadhu), poured ghee the color of a lotus heart on top, and placed the radiant food in the Paccekabuddha's hand, saying, "May this food result in a radiant complexion..."
289:
When offering alms-food, she thought, "By giving alms-food to this Paccekabuddha, I will be able to make him follow my will." She took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, threw away the food, filled it with mud, and offered it. The people censured her, saying, "This woman is foolish," and asked, "You did nothing to the ladle with which you quarreled, so how has the Paccekabuddha offended you?" Ashamed by their words, she took the bowl again, removed the mud, washed it, rubbed it with scented powder, filled it with the four sweet foods (catumadhura), and placed the radiant food—shining with ghee the color of a lotus womb poured on top—into the Paccekabuddha's hand. She made a wish: "Just as this alms-food is radiant, may my body also be radiant." This entire account should be understood in the same way as stated in the story of the Elder Mahākassapa.

The Elder Mahākassapa took the right-hand path and went to the foot of the Bahuputtaka Banyan tree, where the Blessed One was. This Bhaddā Kāpilānī, however, took the left-hand path and, because women were not yet allowed to ordain at that time, went to the park of the female wanderers. When Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī received the lower and higher ordinations, the Elder Bhaddā Kāpilānī also received them from her. Later, while practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she attained Arahantship and became one with mastery in the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana monastery, when appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order, He placed this Elder in the foremost position among those who recollect past lives.

## The Story of the Elder Bhaddā Kaccānā
In the eleventh discourse, with the words "Mahābhiññāppattānaṃ," the Teacher shows that among the bhikkhunīs who have attained great supernormal powers, the one named Bhaddā Kaccānā is the foremost. In the dispensation of a single Buddha, only four people possess great supernormal powers (mahābhiññā); the remaining disciples do not. Other disciples can only recollect up to a hundred thousand aeons (kappa), but not beyond that. However, those who have attained great supernormal powers can recollect an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) plus a hundred thousand aeons. In our Teacher's dispensation as well, these four—the two chief disciples, the Elder Bākula, and the Elder Bhaddā Kaccānā—were able to recollect this much, an incalculable period beyond a hundred thousand aeons. Therefore, this Elder became the foremost among the bhikkhunīs who attained great supernormal powers. The name of that young woman was Bhaddā Kaccānā. Because her body was like the color of fine gold, like the color of excellent gold, she was also known as Bhaddakañcanā. This name Bhaddakañcanā is indeed the name of Rāhula's mother.

The future Elder Bhaddā Kaccānā took conception in a family home in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who had attained great supernormal powers. She performed great meritorious deeds and aspired for that position. That future Elder wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and when our current Buddha appeared, she took conception in the house of Suppabuddha the Sakyan. They named that young woman Bhaddā Kaccānā.
290:
The body of that Bhaddā Kaccānā was like the color of excellent gold. Therefore, she received the name Bhaddakañcanā. Later, she came to be known simply as Kaccānā. This is a name for the mother of Rāhula.

Indeed, the future Elder Bhaddā Kaccānā took conception in a family home in Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Later, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who had attained great supernormal powers. She performed great meritorious deeds and aspired for that special position. She wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and when this Buddha appeared, she took conception in the house of Suppabuddha the Sakyan, and they named her Bhaddā Kaccānā.

When she reached the proper age, she went to the house of the Bodhisatta. Later, she gave birth to a son named Prince Rāhula. On the very day Prince Rāhula was born, the Bodhisatta went forth into homelessness, attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the Great Bodhi tree, and while benefiting the world, he eventually arrived at Kapilavatthu and provided assistance to his relatives. Later, when King Suddhodana passed away, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī went forth in the presence of the Teacher along with five hundred women. Both Rāhula's mother and Janapadakalyāṇī went to the Elder [Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī] and were ordained. From the time of her ordination, she was well-known as the Elder Bhaddā Kaccānā. Later, she developed insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship, and became one with mastery in the supernormal powers. Sitting in a single cross-legged posture, with a single advertence of mind, she could recollect an incalculable period plus a hundred thousand aeons. When that quality of the Elder became well-known, the Teacher, while residing at the Jetavana monastery and appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order, placed this Elder in the foremost position among those who have attained great supernormal powers.

## The Story of the Elder Kisāgotamī
12. With the words "Lūkhacīvaradharānaṃ," the Teacher shows that among the bhikkhunīs who wear refuse-rag robes (paṃsukūla) endowed with the three types of coarseness, Kisāgotamī is the foremost. Although her name was Gotamī, she was called Kisāgotamī because her body was somewhat thin (kisa). This future Elder also was born in a family home in Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes. She performed great meritorious deeds and aspired for that special position. For a hundred thousand aeons...
291:
After wandering through the realms of devas and humans, she was born into a poor family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. When she reached the age of maturity, she went to a certain family [to marry]. In that household, they looked down on her, saying, "She is the daughter of a poor family."

Later, she gave birth to a son; only then did they show her respect. When that child reached the age of running and playing about, he passed away, and intense grief (soka) arose within her. She thought, "In this very house, I was once deprived of gain and honor, and only since the birth of my son did I receive respect. These people might even try to throw my son away." Carrying her son on her hip, she went from door to door, asking, "Please give me medicine for my son." Wherever she was seen, people clapped their hands and mocked her, saying, "Where have you ever seen medicine for the dead?" She did not regain her senses through their words.

Then a wise man saw her and thought, "This woman must be mentally deranged due to grief for her son. No one else will know the medicine for her; only the Dasabala (the Buddha) will know." He said to her, "Mother, there is no one else who knows the medicine for your son. However, the Dasabala, the Supreme Person in the world including the devas, resides in the nearby monastery. Go to him and ask." She thought, "This man speaks the truth," and taking her son, she went to the Buddha while he was seated on the Buddha-seat. Standing at the edge of the assembly, she said, "Venerable Sir, please give me medicine for my son."

The Teacher, seeing her strong supporting condition (upanissaya) [for liberation], said, "Gotamī, you have done well to come here for medicine. Go, enter the city, and starting from the very first house, wander through the entire city. Bring a mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died." She, with a joyful heart, said, "Very well, Bhante," and entered the city. At the very first house, she said, "The Dasabala has sent me to get a mustard seed as medicine for my son. Please give me a mustard seed." They took some out and gave it to her, saying, "Here, Gotamī." She asked, "I cannot take it just like this. Has anyone ever died in this house?" They replied, "Gotamī, what are you saying? Who can count those who have died here?" She said, "In that case, I will not take it. The Dasabala told me to take it only from a house where no one has ever died." In this manner...
292:
She went to the third house and thought, "This must be the same pattern in the entire city. This must have been seen by the Buddha, who is compassionate for the welfare of beings." Gaining a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she went out from that house to the charnel ground. Taking her son in her arms, she said, "Dear son, I thought this death happened only to you. But this is not only for you; it is a nature common to all people." Having abandoned her son in the charnel ground, she recited this verse:

"It is not a law of the village, nor a law of the market town;
Nor is it a law for a single family alone.
For the entire world including the devas,
This is the law: namely, impermanence (aniccatā)."

Having said this, she went to the Teacher. Then the Teacher asked her, "Gotamī, did you obtain the mustard seed?" She replied, "Venerable Sir, the task with the mustard seed is finished. Please grant me a refuge." Then the Teacher recited this verse from the Dhammapada to her:

"The man whose mind is attached to children and cattle,
Whose heart is clinging to various objects—
Death seizes him and carries him away,
Like a great flood sweeping away a sleeping village."

At the end of the verse, Kisāgotamī, while standing right there, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and requested ordination. The Teacher permitted her ordination. She circumambulated the Teacher three times, paid homage, and went to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, where she received the novice and full ordination. Before long, applying herself with wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), she developed insight (vipassanā). Then the Teacher recited this verse of radiance to her:

"Though one should live a hundred years
Without seeing the Deathless State (Amata pada),
Better is a single day's life
For one who sees the Deathless State."

At the conclusion of the verse, Kisāgotamī attained Arahantship. She became extremely frugal in the use of requisites and went about wearing robes consisting of three coarse characteristics. Later, while the Teacher was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, as he was assigning the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions, he placed this elder nun in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes.
293:
## Story of the Elder Nun Siṅgālakamātā

In the thirteenth discourse, with the word "saddhādhimuttānaṃ," it is shown that Siṅgālakamātā is the foremost among those resolved through faith. This future elder nun was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, she saw the Buddha declare a certain nun as the foremost among those devoted through faith. She performed meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. She wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and in this Buddha's era, she was born into a merchant's family in the city of Rājagaha. Upon reaching a family of equal status, she gave birth to a son, whom they named Young Siṅgālaka. Because of her son, she also became known as Siṅgālakamātā (Mother of Siṅgālaka).

One day, after hearing the Buddha's Dhamma, she gained faith and went to the Buddha to be ordained. From the time of her ordination, she attained an extraordinary faculty of faith (saddhindriya). When she went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma, she would remain standing, merely gazing at the perfection of the Buddha's physical form. The Buddha, knowing her deep immersion in the quality of faith, taught her only the Dhamma that was suitable and inspiring. That elder nun, taking faith as her primary vehicle, attained Arahatship. Later, while the Buddha was residing at Jetavana Monastery and assigning various positions to the nuns in order, He declared this elder nun the foremost among those resolved through faith.

## 14. Etadagga Vagga
## (14) 6. Sixth Etadagga Vagga
## Story of Tapussa and Bhallika

In the first discourse of the Upāsaka Pali, with the phrase "paṭhamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchantānaṃ," it is shown that these two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, are the foremost among those who first took refuge. These two brothers were born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's Dhamma, they saw the Buddha declare two lay disciples as the foremost among those who first took refuge. They performed meritorious deeds and made an aspiration for that very position. They wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons...
294:
Long before our Bodhisatta attained Omniscient Wisdom, they were born into a householder's family in the city of Asitañjana. The elder brother was named Tapussa, and the younger brother was named Bhallika.

Later, while living as householders, they occasionally traveled for trade, yoking five hundred carts. At that time, our Bodhisatta attained Omniscience and, after staying at the Bodhi tree for seven weeks, sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree during the eighth week. At that moment, those merchants arrived at that place with about five hundred carts. Their mother from five lives ago had been reborn as a terrestrial deity in that region. She thought, "It is now appropriate for the Buddha to receive food. It is not possible to subsist without food beyond this day. These merchants, who are my sons, are traveling along this path; it is proper to have them offer alms-food to the Buddha today." Thus, she stopped the movement of the oxen yoked to the five hundred carts. The merchants looked for various omens, wondering, "What could this be?"

Then, the deity, knowing their weariness, possessed the body of a man and said, "Why are you weary? You are not being troubled by yakkhas, ghosts, or nāgas. I was your mother in your fifth previous life and have been reborn as a terrestrial deity in this place. This Buddha, the Ten-Powered One, is sitting at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Offer alms-food to Him before anyone else."

Hearing the deity's words, the merchants were filled with joy. They took rice cakes and honey balls in a golden bowl, went to the Buddha, and said, "Venerable Sir, please accept this food." The Buddha reflected on the practice of past Buddhas. Then, the Four Great Kings offered bowls made of stone. The Buddha, wishing that it might bring them great merit, resolved that the four bowls should become a single bowl. At that moment, the merchants placed the rice cakes and honey balls into the Buddha's bowl. After the Buddha had eaten and they had offered water, and the meal was finished, they paid homage to the Buddha and sat in a suitable place. Then the Buddha preached the Dhamma to them. At the end of the discourse, both of them were established in the two-word refuge (taking refuge in the Buddha and the Dhamma). They paid homage to the Buddha and returned to their city...
295:
Those merchants, wishing to return to their city, said, "Venerable Sir, please give us a memorial stupa for our worship." The Blessed One rubbed his head with his right hand and gave those two people eight hair-relics. Placing the hair-relics in golden caskets, they took them to their city and established a living hair-relic stupa at the gate of the city of Asitañjana. On Uposatha days, blue rays would emanate from that stupa. Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana monastery, as he was assigning lay disciples to various positions of rank, he placed these two merchant brothers in the foremost position among those who first took refuge.

## The Story of Anāthapiṇḍika the Merchant
In the second sutta, the phrase "among donors" (dāyakānaṃ) indicates that the householder Sudatta Anāthapiṇḍika is the foremost among donors who delight in giving. The future Anāthapiṇḍika was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appointing a lay disciple to the foremost position among donors, performed an extraordinary merit, and aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born in the house of Sumana the merchant in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha, and was named Sudatta.

Later, having established a household, he became a donor and a master of giving; because of this virtue, he became famous by the name "Anāthapiṇḍika" (provider for the destitute). Taking goods with five hundred carts, he went to the house of his dear friend, a merchant in Rājagaha, and there heard that the Buddha, the Blessed One, had appeared in the world. In the early dawn, through the power of a deity, he approached the Teacher through an opened gate, heard the Dhamma, and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). On the second day, having given a great offering to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he received a promise from the Teacher to come to Sāvatthī. Along the forty-five yojana journey, he spent hundreds of thousands to build a monastery at every yojana. He bought the Jetavana grove by covering the ground with crores of coins, purchasing it for eighteen crores, and spent another eighteen crores to construct the monastery buildings. When the monastery was completed, he held a dedication ceremony costing eighteen crores, giving whatever was desired to the four assemblies before and after meals. The dedication ceremony was completed in nine months...
296:
...reached completion. Other teachers say it was completed in five months. However, regarding the three months, there is no dispute among any of the teachers. Thus, having spent fifty-four crores of wealth, he constantly maintained such offerings in his house. Daily, there were five hundred portions of ticket-food (salākabhatta), five hundred portions of fortnightly food (pakkhikabhatta), five hundred portions of ticket-gruel (salākayāgu), five hundred portions of fortnightly gruel (pakkhikayāgu), five hundred portions of food offered at the front of the house (dhurabhatta), five hundred portions for guests (āgantukabhatta), five hundred portions for those departing on a journey (gamikabhatta), five hundred portions for the sick (gilānabhatta), five hundred portions for those attending the sick (gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta). Five hundred seats were also constantly prepared in his house. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana monastery, as he was assigning lay disciples to various positions of rank, he placed Anāthapiṇḍika in the foremost position among donors.

## The Story of Citta the Householder
In the third sutta, the word "among Dhamma-preachers" (dhammakathikānaṃ) indicates that the householder Citta is the foremost among lay disciples who preach the Dhamma. That householder Citta was born into a good family in Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to a Dhamma talk, he saw the Teacher appointing a lay disciple to the foremost position among Dhamma-preachers, performed an extraordinary merit, and aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born in a hunter's house during the time of Kassapa Buddha. Later, when he was old enough to work in the forest, one day while it was raining, he took a spear and went to the forest to kill animals. While looking for deer, he saw a monk sitting on a stone slab in an unrefined mountain cleft, covered with his rag-robe including his head. Thinking, "This venerable one must be sitting here practicing the Dhamma of a recluse alone," he quickly returned home and had meat obtained the previous day cooked on one stove and rice on another. Seeing two monks coming for alms, he took their bowls, seated them on prepared seats, offered alms-food, and instructed others, "Venerable sirs, please serve them." He put that food in a pot, tied the mouth of the pot with a leaf, and while carrying the pot, he picked various flowers along the way and put them in a leaf-basket. He went to the place where the elder was sitting, lowered the pot, and placed it in a suitable spot.
297:
“Venerable Sir, please show me favor,” he said, taking the Elder’s bowl, filling it with food, and placing it in the Elder’s hands. He then honored the Elder with those mixed flowers. Standing to one side, he made an aspiration: “Just as this offering of flowers along with this delicious food delights my heart, so too, in every place I am reborn, may a thousand gifts come to me, and may a rain of five-colored flowers fall.”

The Elder, seeing his strong supporting condition (upanissaya), taught him the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra). Having performed meritorious deeds throughout his life, he was reborn in the heavenly realm. In the place where he was born, a rain of divine flowers fell to the height of his knees. He himself was endowed with a beauty far superior to other deities. Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans for the interval between two Buddhas, he was reborn in a wealthy family in the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa in the kingdom of Magadha during the time of our Buddha. At the very moment of his birth, a rain of five-colored flowers fell throughout the entire city to the height of his knees. Then his parents, saying, “Our son has come bringing his own name; on the day of his birth, the whole city became beautiful with five-colored flowers,” named him Citta Kumāra.

Later, after establishing a household and upon his father’s death, he attained the position of a wealthy merchant (seṭṭhi) in that city. At that time, the Elder Mahānāma, one of the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya), arrived at the city of Macchikāsaṇḍa. Citta the householder, being inspired by the Elder’s deportment, took his bowl, invited him to his home, and served him with almsfood. After the meal was finished, he led the Elder to the garden named Ambāṭakārāma, built a dwelling for him there, and received a promise that the Elder would regularly accept alms at his house. The Elder, seeing his strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for attaining the paths and fruits, preached only the discourse on the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatana-vibhatti). Because Citta the householder had contemplated and practiced the formations (saṅkhāra) in previous lives, he soon attained the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmī-phala).

One day after that, the Elder Isidatta arrived and stayed in that city. After finishing a meal at the merchant’s house, the Venerable Mahānāma was unable to answer a question asked by the merchant and urged Isidatta to do so. When the Elder Isidatta answered the lay follower’s question, the merchant realized they had been friends in their previous lay lives. Thinking, “I should no longer stay here,” Isidatta departed at his convenience. On another day, the merchant Citta requested the Elder Mahānāma to perform a miracle. The Elder showed him a miracle based on the fire-element attainment (tejo-samāpatti) and, thinking, “It is no longer proper to stay here,” departed at his convenience. Then one day, the two Chief Disciples, accompanied by a thousand monks...
298:
(Citta the householder) requested (the Elder Mahānāma to perform a miracle). That Elder Mahānāma, having shown the householder Citta a miracle based on the fire-element attainment (tejo-kasiṇa-samāpatti), thought, “It is no longer proper to stay in this place,” and departed at his convenience.

Then one day, the two Chief Disciples, accompanied by a thousand monks, arrived at the Ambāṭakārāma monastery. The householder Citta prepared a grand offering for the Chief Disciples. The Elder Sudhamma, unable to tolerate this grand offering, insulted the merchant Citta with abusive words, calling him a “sesame-cake seller.” Because of this, he was expelled by the householder Citta. He went to the Buddha, received instruction, and following the Buddha’s advice, asked for Citta’s forgiveness. While staying at that same Ambāṭakārāma monastery, he developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship. At that time, the lay follower Citta thought, “I have let a long time pass without seeing the Buddha. It is not proper for one going to the Buddha to go empty-handed.” He took five hundred carts filled with oil, honey, molasses, and so on, and had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing, “Let those who wish to see the Buddha come with me.” Surrounded by two thousand people, he set out to see the Buddha. Along the thirty-league journey, deities provided gifts. When he reached the Buddha, he paid homage with the five-point prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita). At that moment, a rain of five-colored flowers fell from the sky.

The Buddha, according to Citta’s inclination, preached only the discourse on the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases (Saḷāyatana-vibhatti). Although he gave offerings to the Buddha for half a month, the rice, oil, honey, molasses, and other supplies he brought from home were not exhausted. The gifts sent by the citizens of Rājagaha were sufficient. After seeing the Buddha and returning to his city, he donated all the goods brought by the carts to the Saṅgha of monks. As soon as the carts became empty, deities filled them with the seven kinds of jewels. Among the people, a conversation arose: “How truly respected and honored is this householder Citta!” Hearing this, the Buddha uttered this verse in the Dhammapada:

“One who has faith, is endowed with virtue, and possesses fame and wealth, is honored wherever he goes.”

From then on, he traveled surrounded by five hundred lay followers who were noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka). Later, the Buddha (designated) the householder Citta (as the foremost) among lay followers...
299:
While the Buddha was assigning the lay disciples to their respective positions of distinction, he placed Citta the Householder in the foremost position among those who are preachers of the Dhamma, based on the Citta Saṃyutta.

## The Story of Hatthaka Āḷavaka
In the fourth discourse, he showed that Hatthaka Āḷavaka was the foremost among those who win over an assembly through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). This future Hatthaka Āḷavaka was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's teaching, he saw the Buddha placing a lay disciple, who was endowed with the four bases of sympathy, in a position of distinction. He performed a great meritorious deed and made a resolution for that same position. He wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand eons, and in this Buddha's era, he was conceived in the palace of King Āḷavaka in the city of Āḷavī, in the kingdom of Āḷavī. On the following day, he was to be sent to the yakkha Āḷavaka along with a pot of rice.

The sequential account of that story is as follows: One day, King Āḷavaka went to the forest to hunt. He pursued and killed a deer, cut it into pieces, hung them on the tip of his bow, and while returning, his body became exhausted from the wind and heat. He entered and sat at the foot of a banyan tree that provided cool shade. Then, after dispelling his weariness for a moment, as he was leaving, the deity residing in the tree grabbed his hand, saying, "Stop, stop! You are my food." Being firmly held and seeing no other means of escape, the king said, "I will send you a person and a pot of rice every day," and returned to the city. From then on, he sent a person from the prison along with a pot of rice. In this manner, when the people in the prison were exhausted, they said, "If elderly people are taken, the country will be in turmoil." So, without taking them, they began to seize young children. From that time on, mothers of children and pregnant women in the city fled to other countries.

At that time, the Buddha, surveying the world at the break of dawn, saw the powerful supporting condition (upanissaya) for Prince Āḷavaka to attain the three paths and fruits. Thinking, "This prince was one who made a resolution for a hundred thousand eons. Having passed away from the deva realm, he has been born in the palace of King Āḷavaka. Since they cannot find any other child, they will take this prince tomorrow along with a pot of rice." In the evening, he went to the mansion gate of the yakkha Āḷavaka in an incognito form and requested the gatekeeper yakkha named Gadabha for permission to enter the mansion. That yakkha said, "Venerable Sir, please enter. However, for me, it is not proper to remain without informing the yakkha Āḷavaka." He then went to the yakkha Āḷavaka, who had gone to an assembly of yakkhas in the Himālaya. The Buddha also entered that mansion and sat upon the jeweled throne of the yakkha Āḷavaka. At that time, while the yakkhas named Sātāgira and Hemavata were traveling through the sky above the mansion to the assembly...
300:
At that time, when the Buddha surveyed the world at the break of dawn, he saw the powerful supporting condition (upanissaya) for Prince Āḷavaka to attain the three paths and fruits. He thought, "This prince is one who made a resolution for a hundred thousand eons. Having passed away from the deva realm, he has been born in the palace of King Āḷavaka. Since they cannot find any other child, they will take this prince tomorrow along with a pot of rice." Thinking thus, in the evening, he went to the mansion gate of the yakkha Āḷavaka in an incognito form and requested the gatekeeper yakkha named Gadabha for permission to enter the mansion. That yakkha Gadabha said, "Venerable Sir, please enter. However, for me, it is not proper to remain without informing the yakkha Āḷavaka." That yakkha Gadabha went to the yakkha Āḷavaka, who had gone to an assembly of yakkhas in the Himālaya. The Buddha also entered that mansion and sat upon the jeweled throne of the yakkha Āḷavaka.

At that time, the yakkhas named Sātāgira and Hemavata, while traveling through the sky above the mansion of the yakkha Āḷavaka to the assembly of yakkhas, found their progress hindered. Reflecting, "What could be the reason?" they saw the Buddha sitting in the mansion of Āḷavaka. They went to the Buddha, paid their respects, and then proceeded to the assembly of yakkhas, where they spoke words of joy to the yakkha Āḷavaka: "Friend Āḷavaka, it is a great gain for you! The Supreme Person in the world, including the devas, is sitting in your mansion. Go and listen to the Dhamma from the Buddha." When the yakkha Āḷavaka heard their words, he thought, "These people are saying that a shaven-headed ascetic is sitting on my throne." Being displeased and overcome by anger, he said, "Today, I shall have a battle with this ascetic. In that battle, you all be my companions." He then lifted his right foot and stepped on a mountain peak sixty leagues in extent, and that mountain peak split into two. From this point, the battle with the yakkha Āḷavaka should be expanded upon. Although the yakkha Āḷavaka fought with the Tathāgata in various ways throughout the night, he was unable to do anything. He then approached the Buddha and asked eight questions, which the Buddha answered. At the end of the teaching, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). For those who wish to know the details, the commentary on the Āḷavaka Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā) should be consulted.

The next day at dawn, at the time for bringing the pot of rice, since no child suitable to be taken could be found in the whole city, they informed the king. The king asked, "Friends, is there a child in a place where it is improper to take one?" They replied, "Yes, Your Majesty. Today, a son was born in the royal family." The king said, "Friends, go. If we live, we can still have a son later. Send that child along with the pot of rice." While the queen was weeping and lamenting, those royal messengers took the child and, along with the pot of rice...
301:
"Send him," the King said. While the Queen was weeping and lamenting, those royal officials took the child along with a pot of rice and went to the entrance of the ogre Āḷavaka’s dwelling, saying, "Here, sir, receive your portion." When Āḷavaka heard their words, because he had become a Noble Disciple, he felt greatly ashamed and sat with his head bowed. Then the Blessed One said to him, "Āḷavaka, there is no need for you to be ashamed now; take the child and place him in my hands." The officials placed Prince Āḷavaka in Āḷavaka’s hands; Āḷavaka took the child and offered him into the hands of the Blessed One. The Teacher accepted him and then placed him back in Āḷavaka’s hands; Āḷavaka took him and placed him back in the hands of the officials. Because he had passed from hand to hand in this manner, they named the child "Hatthaka Āḷavaka."

Then the officials, with joyful hearts, took the child and went to the King. When the King saw the child, thinking, "Today he did not accept the pot of rice," he asked, "Friends, why have you returned like this (with the child)?" They replied, "Great King, there is joy and prosperity for the royal family. The Teacher sat in Āḷavaka’s dwelling, tamed him, established him as a lay follower, and has given this prince back to us." The Teacher then set out towards the city of Āḷavī, having Āḷavaka carry his bowl and robes. As he approached the city, the ogre Āḷavaka shrank back in shame. The Teacher looked at him and asked, "Āḷavaka, are you ashamed?" "Yes, Bhante. Because of me, the townspeople have suffered the deaths of mothers, fathers, children, and wives. If they see me, they will strike me with sticks and stones. That is why I am shrinking back, Bhante," he replied. "Āḷavaka, there is no danger for you while traveling with me; come along with confidence," the Teacher said, and he stopped in a forest grove not far from the city. King Āḷavaka also took the townspeople and went to welcome the Teacher. The Teacher taught the Dhamma to the assembled crowd, and at the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Deathless. The townspeople built a dwelling for Āḷavaka in that very forest grove and established an annual offering of food.

Āḷavaka, too, supported the townspeople by protecting them in accordance with the Dhamma. That Prince Āḷavaka, when he grew up, heard the Teacher’s Dhamma and realized the three paths and fruits. He always traveled surrounded by five hundred Noble Disciple lay followers. One day, he went to the Teacher with those lay followers, paid homage, and sat at a respectful distance. The Teacher, seeing that well-disciplined assembly...
302:
...said, "Prince Āḷavaka, your assembly is large; how do you win them over?" "Bhante, I win over those who are pleased by giving (dāna) through giving; I win over those who are pleased by pleasant speech (piyavācā) through pleasant speech; when matters arise, I win over those who are pleased by beneficial conduct (atthacariyā) through beneficial conduct; and I win over those who are pleased by impartiality (samānattatā) through impartiality," he replied. Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Teacher was residing at Jetavana Monastery, when appointing lay followers to various positions, he placed Prince Hatthaka Āḷavaka in the foremost position among those who win over an assembly through the four bases of sympathy.

## The Story of Mahānāma the Sakyan
In the fifth sutta, "paṇītadāyakānaṃ" means that among the donors who offer choice and delicious food, Mahānāma the Sakyan is the foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma, he saw the Teacher appoint a lay follower to the foremost position among those who offer choice and delicious food. Having performed great meritorious deeds, he aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into the Sakyan royal family in the city of Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha. Upon reaching adulthood, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) at his very first sight of the Blessed One.

Later, on one occasion, after the Teacher had spent the rains retreat in Verañjā, he traveled in stages to Kapilavatthu and resided at Nigrodhārāma Monastery. Mahānāma, hearing that "the Teacher has arrived," went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sitting at a respectful distance, addressed the Teacher thus: "Bhante, I have heard that the Saṅgha of monks was weary from wandering for alms in Verañjā. Please allow me to support the Saṅgha of monks for four months; I will infuse nutrition into the bodies of the Saṅgha of monks." The Teacher consented. Knowing the Teacher’s consent, from the next day onwards, Mahānāma supported the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with choice and delicious food, the four sweet substances (catumadhura), and so on. He then took a commitment for another four months, completing eight months, and again for another four months, supporting them for a full year. The Teacher did not consent beyond that one year. However, from then on, Mahānāma continued to provide hospitality in the same manner to the Saṅgha of monks who arrived from time to time. His reputation for this virtue became well-known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Thus, this story arose.
303:
Later, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher placed Mahānāma the Sakyan in the foremost position among those who give choice food.

## The Story of Ugga the Merchant

In the sixth sutta, with the words "manāpadāyakānaṃ", it is shown that Ugga the Merchant of Vesālī is the foremost among those who give agreeable food that is pleasing to the heart. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, he was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Later, while listening to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher placing a certain lay follower in the foremost position among those who give agreeable things. He performed an act of great merit and aspired to that position.

After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into a merchant family in the city of Vesālī during the time of this Buddha. At the time of his birth, his name was not yet fixed. However, later on, his physical form became lofty and perfect, shining brilliantly like a decorated archway or a raised variegated cloth. His virtues were also lofty. Because both his body and his virtues were lofty (ugga), he became known simply as "Ugga the Merchant".

Upon his very first meeting with the Ten-Powered One, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry, and later, he realized the three higher paths and fruits. When he was older, while sitting in a secluded place, he thought: "Whatever is dear and agreeable to me, that very thing I shall give to the Ten-Powered One. I have heard this in the presence of the Teacher: 'One who gives what is agreeable receives what is agreeable.'" Then the thought occurred to him: "It would be good if the Teacher, knowing my mind, would come to the door of my house."

The Teacher, knowing his mind, appeared at the door of the house surrounded by the community of monks. Hearing that the Teacher had arrived, he became extremely enthusiastic, went to the Ten-Powered One, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, took the Teacher’s bowl, and invited him into the house. Having seated the Teacher on the prepared noble Buddha-seat and the community of monks on the remaining seats, he served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with various exquisite flavors. At the conclusion of the meal, he sat to one side and said: "Venerable Sir, I have heard and received this in the presence of the Blessed One: 'One who gives what is agreeable receives what is agreeable.' Venerable Sir, whatever is agreeable to me, I have indeed given to the community of monks headed by the Buddha." Having informed the Teacher, from that time on, he gave whatever was agreeable to him to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. All of this will come in detail in the Ugga Sutta of the Pañcakanipāta. Thus, this story arose. Later, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher placed that lay follower Ugga in the foremost position among those who give agreeable things.
304:
All of those details will come extensively in the Ugga Sutta of the Pañcakanipāta. Thus, this story arose. Later, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher placed that lay follower in the foremost position among those who give agreeable things.

## The Story of Uggata the Householder

In the seventh sutta, "saṅghupaṭṭhākānaṃ" indicates that Uggata the Householder of Hatthigāma is the foremost among those who attend to the community of monks. He too was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, upon hearing the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching, he saw the Teacher placing a certain lay follower in the foremost position among those who attend to the Saṅgha. He performed an act of great merit and aspired to that special position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into a merchant family in Hatthigāma during the time of our Buddha, and they named him Uggata the Youth.

Later, while established in the life of a householder, he attained the position of a merchant upon his father's passing. At that time, the Teacher, wandering on a journey surrounded by the community of monks, reached Hatthigāma and stayed in the Nāgavana (Ironwood) Grove. Then, this Uggata the Merchant, having been intoxicated with liquor for seven days and surrounded by dancers, went to the Nāgavana Grove to enjoy himself. Upon seeing the Ten-Powered One, a powerful sense of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa) arose in him. Then, as he approached the Teacher, all his intoxication from the liquor vanished. He paid homage to the Teacher and sat to one side. Then the Teacher taught him the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, he penetrated the three paths and fruits.

From that time on, he dismissed the dancers, saying, "You may go as you please," and becoming one who delights in giving, he gave only offerings to the community of monks. Deities would come at the end of the first watch of the night and inform the merchant: "Householder, such a monk possesses the three knowledges; such a monk possesses the six direct knowledges; such a monk is virtuous; such a monk is immoral." Although he heard the words of those deities and knew the virtues of the monks as they truly were, he gave his gifts with an impartial mind. Even while sitting in the presence of the Teacher, he spoke only of the virtues of those monks. Later, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher placed that householder in the foremost position among those who attend to the community of monks.
305:
## The Story of Surambaṭṭha

In the eighth sutta, with the word 'aveccappasannānaṃ', it is shown that Surambaṭṭha is the foremost among lay followers who possess unwavering and unshakable devotion. This Surambaṭṭha, it is said, was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma discourse and seeing the Teacher appoint a certain lay follower to the foremost position among those with unwavering faith, he performed a great meritorious deed and aspired for that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into a merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī during the time of our Buddha's appearance, and they named him Surambaṭṭha.

Later, when he reached maturity, he established a household and lived as a supporter of those with outside views. At that time, the Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw the cause for his attainment of the path of Stream-entry and went to the door of his house at the time of the alms round. When Surambaṭṭha saw the One of Ten Powers, he thought: 'The ascetic Gotama is born of a noble family and is well-known in the world; therefore, it is not proper for me not to go to him.' He went to the Teacher, paid homage at his feet, took the bowl, invited him into the house, and seated him on a costly throne. After offering alms-food and when the meal was finished, he sat at a respectful distance. The Teacher taught the Dhamma according to his temperament. At the end of the discourse, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. The Teacher, having thus guided him, returned to the monastery.

Then Mara thought: 'This Surambaṭṭha belongs to me. But today the Teacher went to his house. I wonder if he has realized the path after hearing the Teacher's Dhamma. I will find out whether he has transcended my domain or not.' Using his power to assume any form he desired, he created a form resembling the One of Ten Powers, wearing the robes and holding the bowl exactly like the Buddha, and appearing with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he stood at the door of Surambaṭṭha's house. When Surambaṭṭha heard that the One of Ten Powers had come again, he thought: 'The Buddhas do not go anywhere without a reason. For what reason has he come?' Recognizing him as the One of Ten Powers, he went quickly to him, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance, saying: 'Venerable Sir, you have just finished your meal in this house and departed. For what reason have you come back again?' (Mara) said: 'Surambaṭṭha, while I was teaching the Dhamma, I spoke without careful consideration. I taught that all five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. But not all these aggregates are of such a nature. In truth, there are some aggregates that are stable, firm, and eternal (sassata).'

Then Surambaṭṭha reflected: 'This statement is very grave. Indeed, there is no such thing as Buddhas speaking without consideration.' He thought: 'I have heard that Mara is the opponent of the Buddha. Surely this must be Mara.' He asked: 'Are you Mara?' The words of the noble disciple were like being struck with an axe to Mara, so that he could no longer maintain his disguise and confessed: 'Surambaṭṭha, it is true, I am Mara.'
306:
'I spoke without careful consideration. Although I taught that the five aggregates are "all impermanent, suffering, and non-self," not all of them are like this. There are some aggregates that are permanent, stable, and eternal,' said Mara (in the guise of the Buddha).

Then Surambaṭṭha thought: 'This statement is extremely grave. The Buddhas never speak without careful consideration. Mara is known to be the adversary of the One of Ten Powers. Surely this must be Mara.' Having thought so, he asked: 'Are you Mara?' The words of Surambaṭṭha, the noble disciple, were like being struck with an axe to Mara, so that he could no longer remain in his assumed form and confessed: 'Surambaṭṭha, it is true; I am Mara.' Surambaṭṭha then said: 'Even if hundreds or thousands of Maras like you were to come, they could not shake my faith. The noble One of Ten Powers, born of the Gotama lineage, taught me while making me realize that "all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are impermanent." Do not stand at my door!' and he snapped his fingers. Hearing those words, Mara was unable to retaliate and vanished on the spot. In the evening, Surambaṭṭha went to the Teacher, reported Mara's actions, and said: 'Venerable Sir, in this way Mara attempted to shake my faith.' Based on this incident, the Teacher appointed Surambaṭṭha to the foremost position among the lay followers who have unwavering faith in this Dispensation.

## The Story of Jīvaka

In the ninth sutta, the phrase 'puggalappasannānaṃ' indicates that Jīvaka Komārabhacca is the foremost among lay followers who possess faith in individuals. He was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of the Buddha Padumuttara. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he saw the Teacher appoint a certain lay follower to the foremost position among those with faith in individuals. He performed an extraordinary meritorious deed and aspired for that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, when this Buddha appeared, he was born in the city of Rājagaha from the womb of a courtesan named Sālavatī, through Prince Abhaya. It is the nature of courtesans to discard a child if it is a son and to raise it if it is a daughter. Therefore, Sālavatī had the boy placed in an old winnowing basket and discarded on a dustheap. Then, Prince Abhaya, while on his way to serve the king, saw the child and sent people, saying: 'Friends, what is this that is surrounded by crows?'
307:
"O Prince, it is a boy," they reported. He asked, "Friends, does he live?" and upon hearing, "O Prince, he lives," he had the child raised within his palace. Because it was said of the child, "He lives" (jīvati), they gave him the name Jīvaka. Because he was caused to be raised by the prince (kumāra), they gave him the name Komārabhacca.

When he was about sixteen years of age, Jīvaka went to the city of Takkasilā and studied the art of medicine. After receiving honors from King Bimbisāra, he cured the illness of King Caṇḍapajjota. King Caṇḍapajjota sent Jīvaka five hundred wagons of rice, sixteen thousand kahāpaṇas, and a pair of priceless Siveyyaka cloths accompanied by a thousand other garments. At that time, the Blessed One was staying on the Gijjhakūṭa mountain near Rājagaha. While Jīvaka was treating the Blessed One by administering a purgative for the excess humors in his body, he thought, "May the four requisites be mine alone," and having the Blessed One stay in his own monastery, he treated him. He offered that pair of cloths, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One alone use this pair of cloths," and the thousand garments received along with that pair, he donated to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. This is a summary here; the details should be understood as they appear in the Khandhaka (Mahāvagga). Later, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Blessed One placed Jīvaka Komārabhacca in the foremost position among those who are devoted to individuals (puggala-ppasannānaṃ).

## The Story of Nakulapitā the Householder
In the tenth story, that of Nakulapitā the Householder, the phrase "vissāsakānaṃ" indicates that among the lay followers who are intimate in conversation, the householder Nakulapitā is the foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, this future householder Nakulapitā was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, he saw the Buddha appoint a certain lay follower to the foremost position among those who are intimate, and having performed an act of great merit, he aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, he was born into a merchant family in the city of Susumāragiri in the Bhagga country during the time of this Buddha. The Blessed One, wandering on a journey accompanied by the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, reached that city and stayed in the Bhesakaḷā forest. Then, the householder Nakulapitā went to the Blessed One together with the residents of Susumāragiri. Upon the very first sight, both he and his wife perceived the Ten-Powered One as "This is our son."
308:
Both Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā fell at the feet of the Blessed One and said, "Dear son, where have you been wandering, leaving us for so long?" This householder Nakulapitā had been the father of the Ten-Powered One for five hundred previous lives, his younger uncle for five hundred lives, his elder uncle for five hundred lives, and his maternal uncle for five hundred lives. Nakulamātā had also been his mother for five hundred lives, his younger aunt for five hundred lives, his elder aunt for five hundred lives, and his paternal aunt for five hundred lives. Thus, because of the affection that had followed them for a long time, they were unable to restrain themselves upon seeing the Ten-Powered One, perceiving him as "our son." The Blessed One did not say "Go away" as long as their hearts did not reach a state of calm. Then, when they regained their mindfulness and reached a state of equanimity, the Blessed One, knowing their inclination, preached the Dhamma. At the conclusion of the teaching, both were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Later, when they were advanced in age, the Blessed One visited that city again. Hearing that "The Blessed One has arrived," they went to him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and invited him for the next day. On the following day, after serving the Bhikkhu Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with various delicious foods in their home, they approached the Blessed One after his meal and sat at one side. Sitting at one side, the householder Nakulapitā said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, since the time the housewife Nakulamātā was brought to my home as a young girl when I was a youth, I do not recall ever transgressing against her even in thought, let alone in body. Venerable Sir, we wish to see each other in this very life and also to see each other in the life to come." The housewife Nakulamātā also said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, since the time I was brought to the home of the householder Nakulapitā as a young girl when he was a youth, I do not recall ever transgressing against him even in thought, let alone in body. Venerable Sir, we wish to see each other in this very life and also to see each other in the life to come." Later, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Blessed One, in appointing lay followers to various foremost positions in order, took the conversation of these two as the occasion and placed the householder Nakulapitā in the foremost position among those who are intimate (vissāsakānaṃ).

## Commentary on the Sixth Chapter.
## The Commentary on the Text on Lay Followers, adorned with ten suttas, is finished.
309:
## The Story of Sujātā
## (14) 7. The Seventh Etadagga Chapter
## 14. Etadagga Chapter

In the first sutta of the Upāsikā-pāḷi, by the phrase "pathamam saraṇam gacchantīnam," the Buddha shows that among the laywomen who were the very first to be established in the Triple Gem, the one named Sujātā, the daughter of the householder Seniya, is the foremost. This Sujātā was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Buddha's discourse, she saw the Buddha appoint a laywoman to the foremost position among those who first took refuge. Having performed great meritorious deeds, she made a resolution for that very position.

After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born in the house of the householder Seniya in the village of Senānigama in Uruvelā, even before our Buddha appeared. When she reached the age of maturity, she made a prayer at the foot of a banyan tree: "If I go to a house of equal status and obtain a son in my first pregnancy, I will make an annual offering." Her prayer was fulfilled.

On the full moon day of Kasone (Vesākha), when the Bodhisatta had completed six years of his great austerities (dukkara-cariyā), Sujātā thought, "I will make the offering early in the morning." She rose at dawn and had the cows milked. The calves did not come near the udders of the cows; as soon as the new vessels were brought under the udders, the streams of milk flowed out by their own nature. Seeing this miracle, Sujātā took the milk with her own hands, put it into a new pot, and started cooking it by lighting the fire herself. While the milk-rice (pāyāsa) was cooking, large bubbles rose and circled clockwise; not even a single drop spilled outside. Mahābrahmā held a white parasol, the four Great Kings stood guard with swords in hand, and Sakka gathered the firewood and lit the fire. Deities collected the essence (ojā) from the four great continents and put it into the pot of milk-rice.

Having seen these miracles in a single day, Sujātā called her servant named Puṇṇā and said, "Dear Puṇṇā, today our deity is very pleased. I have never seen such a miracle in all this time. Go quickly and clean the place of the deity's shrine."
"Very well, mistress," the servant replied, and she went hurriedly to the foot of the tree.
310:
The Bodhisatta, too, waiting for the time to go for alms, went early and sat at the foot of the banyan tree. Puṇṇā, the servant who had gone to clean the foot of the tree, returned and told Sujātā, "The deity is sitting at the foot of the tree." Sujātā said, "Hey girl, if you speak the truth, I will free you from servitude." She then adorned herself with all her ornaments, placed the milk-rice in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, covered it with another golden bowl, wrapped it in a white cloth, hung garlands of scents and flowers all around, and carried it on her head. Upon seeing the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), she felt intense joy. Starting from the place where she saw him, she approached with great humility, lowered the golden bowl from her head, opened it, and placed the milk-rice along with the bowl into the hands of the Great Being. She paid homage and said, "Just as my heart's desire has been fulfilled, may your heart's desire also be fulfilled," and then departed.

The Bodhisatta went to the bank of the Nerañjarā River, placed the golden bowl on the bank, bathed, and after coming out, he made forty-nine morsels and ate the milk-rice. After floating the golden bowl in the Nerañjarā River, he gradually ascended the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda) and attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). After spending seven weeks (Satta-sattāha) at the Bodhimanda, he turned the Noble Wheel of Dhamma at the Deer Park in Isipatana. Seeing the potential (upanissaya) for the attainment of the paths and fruits of Yasa, the son of Sujātā, he went and sat at the foot of a certain tree.

Yasa, the young man of noble birth, after the first watch of the night, saw his harem lying in disarray and was struck with agitation (saṃvega). Crying out, "Alas, it is distressed! Alas, it is oppressed!" he left his home and went to the Buddha outside the city. After hearing the Dhamma discourse, he realized the three paths and fruits. Then, Yasa's father followed his tracks, approached the Buddha, and asked about Yasa's whereabouts. The Buddha concealed Yasa and preached the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, the merchant householder was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), and Yasa attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Buddha called to the young man Yasa, "Come, monk (Ehi Bhikkhu)." At that very moment, his lay appearance disappeared, and he became a monk endowed with a psychic-made bowl and robes. Yasa's father then invited the Buddha. The Buddha, with Yasa as his attendant monk, went to that house, and after finishing the meal, he preached the Dhamma. At the end of the discourse, Yasa's mother, Sujātā, and his former wife were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. On that day, this Sujātā, along with her daughter-in-law, was established in the three-word refuge (te-vācika-saraṇa). This is the summary here.
311:
The account in this Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, is only a summary. In detail, this story has already appeared in the Mahāvagga Khandhaka. When the Blessed One later assigned the female lay disciples to their respective positions in order, He placed this lay disciple named Sujātā in the foremost position among those who first took refuge.

## The Story of Visākhā

In the second sutta, with the word "dāyikānaṃ", He shows that Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, is the foremost among the female lay disciples who delight in giving. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Later, while listening to the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching, she saw the Teacher placing a certain female lay disciple in the foremost position among donors. She performed an extraordinary meritorious deed and aspired for that position. Having wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born during the time of Kassapa Buddha as the youngest of seven sisters in the palace of King Kiki of Kāsi. At that time—

"Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā,
Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāsī"—

these seven sisters existed. They have now been born as—

"Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, Gotamī,
Dhammadinnā, Mahāmāyā, and the seventh, Visākhā."

Among those sisters, Saṅghadāsī wandered through the realms of devas and humans for the interval between two Buddhas. When our Gotama Buddha appeared, she was born in the city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Aṅga, in the womb of Sumanadevī, the chief consort of Treasurer Dhanañjaya, who was the son of Treasurer Meṇḍaka. They named her Visākhā. When she was seven years old, the Buddha, seeing the perfection of the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of Sela the Brahmin and other relatives who were capable of realizing the Dhamma, traveled on a walking tour surrounded by a great community of monks and arrived at that city of Bhaddiya in the kingdom of Aṅga.

At that time, the householder Meṇḍaka was the leader among the five people of great merit in that city and held the position of Great Treasurer. The five people of great merit were: Treasurer Meṇḍaka, his chief consort Candapadumā, their son named Dhanañjaya, his wife named Sumanadevī, and Treasurer Meṇḍaka's...
312:
...servant named Puṇṇa was also one of them. Not only was Treasurer Meṇḍaka the only one with immeasurable wealth within the jurisdiction of King Bimbisāra, but there were actually five such people of immeasurable wealth: Jotika, Jaṭila, Meṇḍaka, Puṇṇa, and Kākavaliya. Among these five treasurers, when Treasurer Meṇḍaka heard that the Buddha had arrived in his city, he called his granddaughter, the young girl Visākhā, daughter of Treasurer Dhanañjaya, and said: "Dear daughter, this is an auspicious occasion for you and for us. Taking five hundred chariots along with your five hundred attendant maidens, and surrounded by five hundred slave-women, go and welcome the Buddha." Having heard her grandfather's words, the young girl Visākhā did as he said. Being wise in discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate, she traveled by carriage as far as the ground permitted, then descended from the carriage and approached the Teacher on foot. After paying homage, she stood at a respectful distance. Then, the Teacher taught the Dhamma according to her temperament. At the conclusion of the teaching, she, along with the five hundred maidens, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Treasurer Meṇḍaka also went to the Teacher, paid homage, and stood at a respectful distance. Then, the Teacher taught the Dhamma according to his temperament as well. At the conclusion of the teaching, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. He invited the Teacher for the next day and, on the following day, served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with exquisite hard and soft food in his own home. In this manner, he gave a great alms-giving for half a month. The Teacher stayed in the city of Bhaddiya as long as He pleased and then departed.

From this point onward, setting aside other narratives, only the account of Visākhā's origins will be told. In the city of Sāvatthī, King Kosala sent a royal message to King Bimbisāra, saying: "In my jurisdiction, there is no family of immeasurable wealth. Please send a family of immeasurable wealth to us." King Bimbisāra consulted with his ministers. The ministers said, "It is not possible to send a great treasurer's family, but we will send a treasurer's son." They requested Dhanañjaya, the son of Treasurer Meṇḍaka. When the King heard the ministers' words, he sent Treasurer Dhanañjaya. Then, King Kosala gave him the position of treasurer in the city of Sāketa, seven yojanas away from Sāvatthī, and had him reside there.

In Sāvatthī, the youth named Puṇṇavaḍḍhana, son of Treasurer Migāra, had reached the age of maturity. Then his father, realizing "My son has reached maturity; it is time for him to lead a household life," said, "Look for a maiden in a family of the same caste as ours," and sent out men who were wise in discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate. Those men, not finding a maiden they liked in Sāvatthī...
313:
Knowing that "It is time to arrange a marriage for my son," [Migāra the merchant] sent men skilled in discerning what is appropriate and inappropriate, saying, "Seek a maiden from a family of equal status to ours." These men, not finding a maiden to their liking in Sāvatthī, went to Sāketa. On that very day, Visākhā, surrounded by five hundred maidens of her own age, went to a large village to celebrate a festival. Those men, having wandered through the city and not finding a maiden to their liking, stood outside the city gate. At that time, it began to rain. Then, the maidens who had come out with Visākhā, fearing they would get wet, ran quickly into a hall. Those men did not see a maiden to their liking among those girls either. However, Visākhā, coming last of all, entered the hall walking at a natural pace, getting wet without concern for the rain. Seeing her, those men thought, "A beautiful maiden should be just like this. But some people's beauty is like a decorated vessel; we will only know if she has sweet speech by making her speak." Then they said to her, "Mother, you walk like a very old woman."

"Fathers, what did you see that makes you say this?" [Visākhā asked]. "The other maidens, your playmates, fearing the rain, came quickly and entered the hall. But you come without exceeding a normal step, like an old woman, and you do not even care that your clothes are getting wet. If an elephant or a horse were to chase you, would you do the same?" [they said]. "Fathers, clothes are not hard to find; in my family, clothes are easily obtained. But women of marriageable age are like merchandise; if a woman becomes physically impaired with a broken hand or foot, people loathe her and spit as they go. Therefore, I came slowly," [she said].

Those men thought, "There is no woman like this in all of Jambudīpa; as she is in beauty, so she is in speech. She speaks knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate." They then threw a golden garland over her. Then Visākhā thought, "Previously I was unprotected, but now I am protected (betrothed)," and she sat on the ground with a graceful manner. Then they surrounded her right there with a curtain. Realizing she was now secluded, she returned home surrounded by her group of maidservants. Migāra the merchant's men also went with her to the presence of Dhanañjaya the merchant.
314:
When asked, "Friends, from which village do you come?" they replied, "We are the men of Migāra the merchant from the city of Sāvatthī." They then stated, "Our merchant sent us because he heard there is a maiden of marriageable age in your house." "Friends, very well. Although your merchant is not our equal in terms of wealth, he is our equal in terms of birth. One who is perfect in every aspect is hard to find. Go and tell the merchant that we have accepted," he said.

Hearing the merchant's words, they returned to Sāvatthī and reported the joy and prosperity to Migāra the merchant, saying, "Lord, we have found a maiden in the house of Dhanañjaya the merchant in the city of Sāketa." Hearing this, Migāra the merchant, with a joyful heart, thinking, "It is said we have found a maiden in a house of noble lineage," immediately sent a message to Dhanañjaya the merchant: "We shall bring the maiden now; please perform the necessary duties." Dhanañjaya the merchant sent back a reply: "This is not a burden for us; let the merchant perform his own necessary duties."

Migāra the merchant went to King Kosala and said, "Great King, I have a festive occasion to perform. I shall bring the maiden named Visākhā, daughter of Dhanañjaya the merchant, for your servant Puṇṇavaḍḍhana. Please grant me permission to go to Sāketa." "Great merchant, very well. Should we also come?" the King asked. "Great King, would it be possible to obtain the presence of someone like Your Majesty?" he replied. The King, wishing to honor a noble family, accepted, saying, "Very well, merchant, I shall come," and went to the city of Sāketa together with Migāra the merchant. Dhanañjaya the merchant, hearing that "Migāra the merchant is coming, bringing King Kosala with him," went out to welcome them and escorted the King to his own residence. Immediately, he prepared lodgings, flowers, perfumes, food, and all other necessities for the King, the royal army, and Migāra the merchant. He himself knew and arranged everything, thinking, "This is suitable for this person, that is suitable for that person." All those people thought, "The merchant is performing these honors especially for me."

Then one day, the King sent a message to Dhanañjaya the merchant: "Merchant, it is not possible for us to be supported and fed for a long time; let us know the time for the maiden's departure." The merchant also sent a message to the King: "Now the rainy season has arrived, and it is not possible to travel for four months. Whatever is needed for Your Majesty's army..."
315: “It is proper to receive it; all of this is my responsibility alone. May the Great King proceed only when I have sent word.” He sent this message. From that time on, the city of Sāketa became like a village in constant festival. In this way, three months passed. However, the Great Creeper Ornament (Mahālatā-pasādhana) for the daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya was not yet finished. Then, the supervisors of the work came and reported, “There is no lack of other materials, but there is not enough firewood to cook rice for the multitude of people.” He said, “Friends, go and dismantle the elephant and horse stables and cook the rice.” While they were cooking in this manner, half a month passed. Then they reported again, “Master, the firewood is no longer sufficient.” He said, “Friends, at this time it is not easy to obtain firewood. Open the storehouse of cloth, take the coarse cloths, make them into wicks, soak them in jars of oil, and cook the rice.” Cooking in this manner, four months were completed. Then, the merchant Dhanañjaya, knowing that his daughter's Great Creeper Ornament was finished, thought, “Tomorrow I shall send my daughter away.” He had his daughter sit near him and gave her advice, saying, “Dear daughter, a woman living in her husband's family should learn such and such conduct.” The merchant Migāra, sitting in an adjacent room, overheard the advice of the merchant Dhanañjaya. That merchant [Dhanañjaya] advised his daughter thus: “Dear daughter, a woman living in her father-in-law's house must not take the internal fire outside, and must not bring the external fire inside. One should give only to those who give; one should not give to those who do not give. One should give to both those who give and those who do not give. One should sit happily, eat happily, and sleep happily. The fire should be tended, and the internal deities should be honored.” Having given these ten admonitions, on the following day, he assembled all the guilds. In the midst of the King's army, he summoned eight householders to act as guarantors and said, “If any fault arises regarding my daughter in the place where she goes, you must clear it.” He had his daughter adorned with the Great Creeper Ornament worth ninety million. He gave wealth for the cost of bath powder to be carried by five thousand four hundred (5,400) carts, along with five hundred maidservants to constantly accompany his daughter, and five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses...
316: He gave a hundred of every kind of implement and building material. After seeing off King Kosala and the merchant Migāra, at the time of his daughter's departure, he summoned the men in charge of the cattle pens and instructed them: “Friends, in the place where my daughter arrives, there will be a need for cows for milk and bulls for yoking to vehicles. Therefore, open the gate of the cattle pen on the path my daughter travels, and let it be filled with a herd of cattle eight usabhas in width. There is a certain valley about three gāvutas away; when the front of the herd reaches that place, give a signal by beating a drum and close the gate of the pen.” They accepted the merchant's words, saying “Very well,” and did accordingly. When the gate of the pen was opened, only the most excellent cows came out. However, when the gate was closed, by the power of Visākhā's merit, strong cattle and young calves leaped out and followed along the road. Then, when Visākhā reached the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, she thought, “Should I enter sitting in a covered carriage or standing in a chariot?” Then it occurred to her, “If I enter in a covered carriage, the distinction of my Great Creeper Ornament will not be visible.” Showing herself to the people of the entire city, she entered the city standing in a chariot. The residents of Sāvatthī, seeing Visākhā's prosperity, said, “This Visākhā is indeed of such a nature, and this prosperity is truly suitable for this merchant's daughter.” Thus, with great prosperity and a large retinue, she entered the house of the merchant Migāra. On the day of her arrival, the people of the entire city thought, “When the merchant Dhanañjaya arrived at our city, he showed us great honor and hospitality,” and they sent gifts according to their means. Visākhā had all the gifts that were sent distributed among other families in that city. Then, in the early part of the night, one of her thoroughbred mares gave birth. Visākhā had her maidservants carry torches and went to that place. After bathing the mare with warm water and anointing her with oil, she returned to her own quarters. The merchant Migāra, while celebrating his son's wedding for seven days, did not pay mind to the Blessed One who was residing in the nearby monastery. On the seventh day, he filled the entire house and invited naked ascetics to sit. He then sent a message to Visākhā, saying, “Let my daughter-in-law come and pay homage to the Arahants.” Having heard the word “Arahants,” Visākhā, who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) and a noble disciple, was filled with joy and...
317:
Visākhā went to the place where those naked ascetics were sitting, and after looking at them, she thought, "Such persons as these are certainly not Arahants. Why did my father-in-law have me summoned to the presence of those who are devoid of shame and fear of wrongdoing?" Rebuking them with "Fie! Fie!", she returned to her own quarters. Upon seeing her, the naked ascetics all at once rebuked the Treasurer Migāra, saying, "Householder, could you not find another girl? Why did you bring this great wretch, a female disciple of the ascetic Gotama, into this house? Expel this wretch from this house immediately!"

Then the Treasurer thought, "I cannot expel this girl from the house just because of the words of these teachers; she is the daughter of a noble family." He then said, "Teachers, young people may act knowingly or unknowingly; please remain silent." Having dismissed the naked ascetics, he sat on a noble couch and, being served by Visākhā, began to eat sweet milk-rice prepared without water from a golden bowl, using a golden ladle.

At that time, an Elder wandering for alms arrived at the door of the Treasurer's house. Visākhā saw the Elder and thought, "It is not proper to tell my father-in-law." She stood aside in such a way that the Treasurer might see the Elder. However, that foolish man, though seeing the Elder, acted as if he did not see him and continued eating the milk-rice with his head bowed. Visākhā, realizing, "My father-in-law sees the Elder but pays no attention," approached the Elder and said, "Pass on, Bhante; my father-in-law is eating what is old (or: consuming old merit)."
