The Treasurer had endured while the naked ascetics were speaking, but the moment she said "eating what is old," he removed his hand and said, "Take this milk-rice away from here, and expel this girl from this house! For she makes me out to be an eater of filth in such an auspicious house as this." Now, all the servants and workers in that house belonged to Visākhā; who would dare to seize her by the hands or feet? There was no one even capable of speaking to her [reproachfully]. Then Visākhā, hearing her father-in-law's words, said, "Father, we do not leave because of such words. I was not brought by you from a watering place like a slave girl carrying a water pot. Daughters of living parents do not leave because of such words. For this very reason, on the day I came here, my father summoned eight householders and said, 'If any fault arises concerning my daughter...'
318:
...clear it (investigate it)," and he placed me in their hands. The Treasurer summoned those householders and said, "Please investigate whether I am at fault or not."

Then the Treasurer, thinking (sarcastically), "She speaks well," summoned the eight householders and said, "This girl, before even seven days have passed in this auspicious house, calls me an 'eater of filth' while I am sitting here." The householders asked, "Dear daughter, is it true that you said this?" She replied, "Fathers, my father-in-law might be one who wishes to eat filth, but I did not say it in the sense of him eating filth. Rather, while an Elder standing at the door was seeking alms, this Treasurer was eating sweet milk-rice and paid him no mind. For this reason, I said, 'Pass on, Bhante; my father-in-law is not making merit in this existence, he is only eating old merit.' That is all I said." The householders said, "Noble Treasurer, there is no fault in this. Our daughter spoke with reason. Why are you angry?" He said, "Sirs, let this fault pass for now. But this girl, on the very day she arrived, went to a place of her own choosing without informing my son." They asked, "Dear daughter, is this true?" She replied, "Fathers, I did not go to a place of my choosing. Rather, when a thoroughbred mare in this house was giving birth, I thought it improper to remain sitting without taking notice. So, having others carry torches and surrounded by slave girls, I went there and ensured the mare was cared for during the birth." The householders said, "Noble Treasurer, our daughter performed a task in your house that even slave girls could not do. What fault do you see in her going there?"

"Sirs, let this care for the mare be a merit then. But this girl's father, on the day she came to this house, gave her the advice: 'The indoor fire must not be taken outside.' How can we live without giving fire to our neighbors?" They asked, "Dear daughter, is this true?" She replied, "Fathers, my father did not mean ordinary fire. He meant that if there is any secret talk concerning the mother-in-law and others within the house, that talk should not be told to the male and female slaves. Such talk, when spread, leads to quarrels. My father said this with that intention, fathers."

"Sirs, let that be as it is. This girl's father said, 'The outdoor fire must not be brought inside.' How can we manage if the indoor fire goes out and we do not bring in fire from outside?" They asked, "Dear daughter, is this true?" She replied, "Fathers, my father did not mean ordinary fire. He meant that the fault-finding talk spoken by servants and workers should not be told to those inside the house..."
319:
The statement made by the merchant father, 'Give only to those who give,' was said with reference to the fact that one should give only to those who return borrowed articles after taking them.

The statement, 'Do not give to those who do not give,' was also said with reference to the fact that one should not give to those who do not return borrowed articles after taking them.

The statement, 'Give whether they give or not,' was said with reference to the fact that when poor relatives and friends arrive, it is proper to give to them regardless of whether they are able to return it or not.

The statement, 'One should sit happily,' was also said with reference to the fact that it is improper to remain sitting in a place where one should stand up upon seeing one's mother-in-law and father-in-law.

The statement, 'One should eat happily,' was said with reference to the fact that it is proper to eat only after serving one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband, and after knowing whether everyone has received food or not, without eating before them.

The statement, 'One should sleep happily,' was also said with reference to the fact that one should not go to bed and sleep before one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband; rather, it is proper to sleep only after performing the major and minor duties that ought to be done for them.

The statement, 'The fire should be tended,' was said with reference to the fact that it is proper to regard and look after one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband as if they were a great mass of fire or a king cobra.

Let these many virtues be for now. This maiden's father said, 'Let her worship the indoor deity.' What is the meaning of this? When they asked, 'Dear daughter, is this true?', she replied, 'Fathers, it is true. My father said this with reference to this: From the time of living in a separate household, upon seeing a monk who has arrived at the door of one's house, it is proper to eat only after giving to the monks whatever food or edibles are in the house.'

Then those householders said to the merchant Migāra, 'Great Merchant, it seems you prefer not giving when you see monks.' That merchant, finding no other reply, sat in silence with his head bowed.

Then the householders asked, 'Merchant, is there any other fault in our daughter?' 'Sirs, there is none,' he replied. 'If so, why did you, without cause, [expel] the faultless daughter...'
320:
...from the house?' At that moment, Visākhā said, 'Firstly, it is not yet proper for me to leave just by the word of my father-in-law. On the day I arrived, my father placed me in the hands of you householders to clear any faults or lack thereof. Only now is it appropriate for me to go.' She then ordered the male and female servants, 'Prepare the carriages and so forth.'

Then the merchant called those householders and said, 'Dear daughter, I spoke without knowing; please forgive me.' Visākhā replied, 'Father, I forgive what ought to be forgiven. However, I am the daughter of a family with unwavering confidence in the Buddha's Dispensation. We cannot live without the Saṅgha of monks. If I am allowed to look after the Saṅgha of monks according to my wish, I shall stay.' The merchant said, 'Dear daughter, look after your recluses as you wish.'

Then Visākhā had the Buddha invited, and on the following day, filling the house, she seated the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. The naked ascetics, hearing that the Buddha had gone to the house of the merchant Migāra, went there and sat surrounding the house. Visākhā, having offered the water of donation, sent a message: 'All the offerings have been prepared; let my father-in-law come and serve the Buddha.' Hearing the words of the Nigaṇṭhas, he said, 'Let my daughter herself serve the Buddha.'

Visākhā served the Buddha with various foods of excellent flavor, and when the meal was finished, she sent a message again: 'Let my father-in-law come and listen to the Dhamma of the Buddha.' Then the merchant thought, 'Now, not going would be truly groundless,' and as he was going with the desire to hear the Dhamma, the naked ascetics said, 'If you are going to listen to the Dhamma of the recluse Gotama, sit and listen from outside the curtain.' They had gone ahead and surrounded the area with a curtain. The merchant Migāra went and sat outside the curtain.

The Buddha said, 'Merchant, whether you sit outside the curtain, or on the other side of a wall, or on the other side of a mountain, or on the other side of the universe, I, the Buddha, am able to make you hear my voice.' He then preached the Dhamma as if shaking a mango tree with golden-colored fruits by the trunk. At the conclusion of the teaching, the merchant was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He lifted the curtain, prostrated at the Teacher's feet with the fivefold prostration, and in the presence of the Teacher himself, he placed Visākhā in the position of his mother, saying, 'Dear daughter, from today onwards, you are my mother.' From then on, Visākhā became known as Migāramātā.

One day, while a festival was taking place, she thought, 'There is no benefit in the inner city,' and surrounded by her maidservants, she went to listen to the Teacher's Dhamma. Thinking, 'It is not proper to go into the presence of the Buddhas in grand attire,' she removed the Mahālatā ornament, entrusted it to the hand of her maidservant, approached the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.
321:
Thinking, "It is inappropriate to approach the Buddhas in such a grand appearance," she removed the Mahālatā ornament and handed it to her servant. She then approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One delivered a Dhamma discourse. At the end of the discourse, Visākhā, the lay devotee, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed toward the city. The servant, without noticing where she had placed the ornament she was carrying, started to leave but then returned to retrieve it. Visākhā asked her, "Where did you leave it?" She replied, "Mistress, I left it within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi." Visākhā said, "Let it be, girl. Go and fetch it. However, it is not proper for us to take back something once it has been left within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi. Therefore, we shall relinquish that ornament and perform an act of merit. Leaving it there would cause concern (palibodha) for the venerable ones."

On the following day, the Blessed One, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, arrived at the door of Visākhā’s house. Seats had been permanently prepared in the house. Visākhā took the Blessed One’s bowl, invited Him inside, and had Him sit on the prepared seat. When the Blessed One had finished His meal, she brought the ornament, placed it at the Blessed One’s feet, and said, "Venerable Sir, I offer this ornament to You." The Blessed One rejected it, saying, "An ornament is not suitable for monks." She replied, "Venerable Sir, I know. However, I will have this ornament appraised and use the proceeds to build a Gandhakuṭi for You to reside in." Then the Blessed One accepted. Visākhā had the ornament appraised, received ninety million in wealth, and built a Gandhakuṭi for the Tathāgata to reside in at the Pubbārāma monastery, which was adorned with a thousand rooms. Visākhā’s house, in the morning, was always bright with the glow of saffron robes and filled with the breeze caused by the monks' robes and movements, just like the house of Anāthapiṇḍika. In her house, all kinds of food were always prepared. In the morning, she would support the Saṅgha of monks with material offerings, and in the afternoon, she would take medicines and the eight kinds of drinks to the monastery to offer to the Saṅgha. Afterward, she would listen to the Blessed One’s Dhamma discourse and return home. Later, when the Blessed One was assigning the female lay devotees to their respective positions, He appointed Visākhā Migāramātā to the foremost position (etadagga) among female donors.

## The Story of Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī

260-261. In the third and fourth verses, it means that among the female lay devotees who are learned, Khujjuttarā is the foremost; and among the female lay devotees who dwell in loving-kindness, Sāmāvatī is the foremost.
322:
It is shown that Sāmāvatī is the foremost among the female lay devotees who dwell in loving-kindness. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, both of them were reborn into noble families in the city of Haṃsavatī. Later, thinking, "We shall listen to the Dhamma of the Blessed One," they went to the monastery. There, Khujjuttarā saw the Blessed One appointing a female lay devotee to the foremost position among those of great learning. She performed an extraordinary act of merit and made a wish for that position. Sāmāvatī also saw the Blessed One appointing a female lay devotee to the foremost position among those who dwell in loving-kindness. She performed an extraordinary act of merit and made a wish for that position. Both of them performed wholesome deeds throughout their lives, were reborn in the deva realms, and wandered between the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand eons.

Then, even before the appearance of our Blessed One, a disease called the "snake-wind disease" (ahivātaka) broke out in the kingdom of Allakappa. In a single house, ten, twenty, or even thirty people would die at once. Only those who fled to other kingdoms survived. Knowing this, a certain man took his wife and son and departed from that kingdom, thinking, "I will go to another country." However, the provisions he had taken from his home were exhausted in the middle of a difficult forest journey before they could cross it. Their physical strength declined; sometimes the mother carried the son, and sometimes the father carried him. Then the father thought, "Our physical strength is failing. If we continue while carrying the son, we will not be able to cross this wilderness." Without letting the child's mother know, he pretended to stay behind for a call of nature, left the son sitting on the path, and proceeded alone.

Later, while his wife stood waiting for him on the path, she did not see the son in her husband's hands. She wept and ran to him, asking, "My lord, where is my son?" He said, "What use is a son to you? If we stay alive, we can have another son." The woman said, "This man is truly cruel!" and added, "You go on; I will not follow someone like you." The man said, "My dear, I have acted thoughtlessly; please forgive me for this fault," and he went back to bring the son.

They crossed that wilderness and arrived at a cowherd's house in the evening. On that day, the residents of the cowherd village had cooked thick milk-rice without adding water. Seeing them, the cowherds thought, "These people are extremely hungry," and they filled a large bowl with milk-rice, poured a ladleful of ghee over it, and offered it to them. When they ate the milk-rice, the woman ate with moderation, but the man ate excessively...
323:
After eating, being unable to digest the food, that man passed away during the first watch of the night. Upon passing away, due to his attachment to those cowherds, he took rebirth in the womb of a female dog in the cowherds' house. Before long, the female dog gave birth. Seeing that the puppy was handsome, the cowherd enticed it with lumps of rice, nurtured its affection for him, and they went about together.

Then one day, a Paccekabuddha arrived at the door of the cowherd's house during the time for alms-round. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, the cowherd offered alms-food and requested a promise from him to reside there depending on him. The Paccekabuddha took up residence in a forest grove not far from the cowherd's house. Whenever the cowherd went to the Paccekabuddha, he always took the dog with him. Along the way, in places where there were wild beasts, he would strike trees or stones to frighten the beasts away. The dog also noted the cowherd's actions. One day, while sitting near the Paccekabuddha, the cowherd said, "Venerable Sir, it is not possible for us to come all the time. This dog is clever; please come to our house door by taking the arrival of this dog as a sign." One day, the cowherd sent the dog, saying, "Go and bring the Paccekabuddha."

Listening to the cowherd's words, the dog went at the time for alms-round and lay down on its chest at the feet of the Paccekabuddha. Knowing that "this dog has come to me," the Paccekabuddha took his bowl and robes and set out on the path. To test the dog, the Paccekabuddha turned off and took another path. The dog stood in front of him and only moved aside when he returned to the path leading to the cowherd's house. At every place where the cowherd had struck a tree or a stone to frighten the wild beasts, the dog barked loudly upon reaching it. At that sound, the wild beasts fled. At the time of the meal, the Paccekabuddha gave the dog a large, choice lump of rice. Because of receiving the food, the dog developed an even greater affection for the Paccekabuddha.

After the Paccekabuddha had stayed for the three months of the rains, the cowherd offered him cloth sufficient for the three robes and said, "Venerable Sir, if it pleases you, please stay right here. If not, please go as you wish." The Paccekabuddha showed signs of departing. The cowherd followed the Paccekabuddha for a distance and then returned. Knowing that the Paccekabuddha was going elsewhere, the dog, due to its intense affection, was overcome by powerful grief; its heart broke, it died, and was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Of that deva son...
324:
Because he had made a loud sound to drive away wild beasts while traveling with the Paccekabuddha, when he spoke with the devas, his voice pervaded and filled the entire celestial city. For that very reason, he received his name and became known as the deva son Ghosaka. While that deva son was enjoying prosperity in that heaven, in the human realm, in the city of Kosambī, a king named Udena assumed the kingship. His story should be understood in the same manner as described in the commentary on the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsaka.

While that king was reigning, the deva son Ghosaka passed away and took rebirth in the womb of a certain courtesan in Kosambī. After ten months, she gave birth, and upon realizing it was a son, she had him discarded on a rubbish heap. At that moment, a laborer of the treasurer of Kosambī, while going early to the treasurer's house, wondered, "Why are crows swarming around this?" He went to look, saw the child, and thinking, "This child must be one of great merit," he sent him home in the hands of a man and then proceeded to the treasurer's house. The treasurer, while going to the royal palace to attend upon the king, saw the court chaplain on the way and asked, "What is the constellation today?" Standing right there, the chaplain calculated and said, "Today is such-and-such a constellation; a child born today under this constellation will obtain the position of treasurer in this city."

Hearing the chaplain's words, the treasurer quickly sent word to his house, saying, "The words of this chaplain are never double (they are always true). My wife is also heavily pregnant; go and see whether she has given birth or not." They went and found out, then said, "Master, she has not yet given birth." "In that case, go and search for a child born today in this city." While searching, they saw the child in the house of the treasurer's laborer and informed the treasurer. "Then go, my men, and summon that laborer." They summoned him. Then the treasurer asked the laborer, "Is there a child in your house?" "Yes, master." "Give that child to me." "I cannot give him, master." "Here, take a thousand [kahāpaṇas] and give him." The laborer thought, "Whether this child lives or dies is hard to know," so he took the thousand and gave him up.

Then the treasurer thought, "If my wife gives birth to a daughter, I will make this child my son. If she gives birth to a son, I will kill him." Having so thought, he nurtured him in the house. Then, after a few days, his wife gave birth to a son. Thereupon the treasurer thought, "In this way, the cattle will trample and kill him," and...
325:
“Lay this child at the gate of the cattle pen,” he said. They laid the child at that cattle pen gate. Then, the bull who was the leader of the herd, coming out first, saw the child and thought, “In this way, other cattle will not trample this child,” and stood over him, keeping him between his four legs. Then the cowherds saw the child and thought, “This child must be one of great merit; even animals recognize the virtue of such a child. We shall look after him,” and they took him to their home.

The treasurer, investigating the circumstances of the child's death, heard that the cowherds had taken him. He again gave a thousand [pieces of money] and ordered him to be cast away in a charnel ground. At that time, a goatherd was grazing his goats near the charnel ground, supported by the treasurer's house. Then a milch goat, through the power of the child's merit, left the path and went to give the child milk. Even when returning from that charnel ground, she did the same and gave him milk. The goatherd thought, “This goat left this spot even early this morning; what could this be?” He went to look and saw the child. He thought, “This child is of great merit; even animals recognize the virtue of this child. I will look after him,” and he took him and went home.

The next day, the treasurer had someone check, “Is the child dead or not?” Learning that the goatherd had taken him, he gave a thousand and ordered, “Tomorrow, a caravan leader's son will enter this city. Take this child and place him on the cart track. Thus, the cart wheel will pass over and crush him.” The oxen yoked to the first cart of the caravan leader saw the child placed on the track and stood still, planting their four legs like pillars. The caravan leader wondered, “What is this?” and looking for the reason the oxen stopped, he saw the child. He thought, “This child is of great merit; he should be looked after,” and he took him and went on.

The treasurer also had someone check whether he was dead or alive on the cart track. Learning that the caravan leader had taken him, he gave that caravan leader a thousand and ordered him to be thrown down a precipice at a place not far from the city. As the child fell down the precipice, he landed on a shed in the workplace of reed-makers. Through the power of his merit, that shed felt like the touch of a heap of cotton beaten a hundred times. Then the head reed-maker thought, “This child is meritorious; he should be looked after...”
326:
“...he should be looked after,” and taking him, he went home. The treasurer, searching to see if the child was dead or alive at the place where he fell from the precipice, learned that the head reed-maker had taken him. He gave him a thousand and gave an order.

Later, both the treasurer's own son and that boy reached the age of maturity. The treasurer, again plotting a way to kill the youth Ghosaka, went to his potter's house and said, “Friend, there is such a low-born boy in my house. It is proper to do something to kill that boy secretly.” The potter covered both his ears and said, “It is not proper to speak such a heavy word.” Then the treasurer thought, “This man will likely not do it for nothing,” and said, “Here, friend, take a thousand and accomplish this task.” A bribe can break even what is unbroken; therefore, the potter, having received the thousand, agreed and said, “My lord, on such and such a day, I will fire the kiln. At that time, send that boy at such and such an hour.”

The treasurer accepted the potter's words and, counting the days from then on, knew that the day mentioned by the potter had arrived. He summoned the youth Ghosaka and said, “Dear son, on such and such a day, we have need of many vessels. Go to our potter and say, ‘My father says he has told you of a certain task; accomplish that task today.’” The youth accepted his words, saying, “Very well,” and departed.

Then, on the way, he saw the treasurer's own son playing a game of marbles. The son ran to him and said, “Brother, I have lost this much playing with these boys. Play for me so that I may win it back.” The youth said, “I have no opportunity now; father has sent me to the potter on an urgent matter.” The other, the treasurer's son, said, “Brother, I will go there. You play with these boys and get back the stakes I lost.” Saying, “In that case, go,” Ghosaka told him the message he had been given and played with the boys. That treasurer's son went to the potter and delivered the message. The potter said, “Very well, dear son, I will accomplish it,” and he made the youth enter a room, cut him into pieces with a sharp axe, put them in a large jar, and [sealed] the mouth of the jar...
327:
Closing the mouth of the kiln and placing it among the pots, he started the fire for the raw pots. Young Ghosaka, having won many games of seeds, sat waiting for the arrival of his younger brother. Realizing that the boy was taking a long time and wondering, "Why is he so late?", he went quickly toward the potter's house. Not seeing him anywhere, he thought, "He must have gone home," and so he turned back and went home.

The treasurer, seeing Ghosaka coming from afar, thought, "What could be the reason? I sent this Ghosaka to the potter to be killed, yet now he is coming back here again." As he approached, he asked, "Dear son, did you not go to the potter?" "Father, I did not go," he replied. "Why not, dear son?" (the treasurer asked). Then young Ghosaka told him the reason for his return and the reason why his younger brother had gone to the potter's house. From the moment the treasurer heard those words, it was as if the great earth had fallen upon and crushed him. With a trembling heart, he cried, "Why do you say such a thing?" and rushed to the potter. In a manner that others could not hear, he said, "Wait, sir! Wait, sir!" "Lord Treasurer, why do you ask me to wait? The work is finished," the potter replied. The treasurer turned back from the potter's house and went home. From that time on, a mental affliction arose within him.

At that time, without eating with Ghosaka and suppressing his desire, he thought, "By some means or other, I must find an opportunity to kill my son's enemy, Ghosaka." He wrote a letter, called young Ghosaka, and instructed him: "Take this letter and go to my bailiff in such-and-such a village. Give him this letter and say, 'Carry out the instructions in this letter quickly.'" He also gave oral instructions: "On the way, there is a treasurer who is my friend living in a small village. Go to his house, have a meal, and then proceed." Young Ghosaka paid respects to the treasurer, took the letter, and departed. On the way, he went to the residence of the village treasurer. Having asked for the house, he saw the treasurer sitting outside the gatehouse having his beard trimmed. He paid respects and stood there. When asked, "Where do you come from, dear son?", he replied, "Father, I am the son of the Treasurer of Kosambī." The treasurer was delighted, thinking, "He is the son of my friend, the treasurer."
328:
At that moment, a maidservant of the treasurer's daughter was going to fetch flowers for her. Then the treasurer said to the maid, "My girl, set aside that task for a moment, wash young Ghosaka's feet, and prepare a bed for him." The maid did as she was told and then went to the market to fetch the flowers for the treasurer's daughter. When the treasurer's daughter saw her, she became angry, saying, "You have been outside for a very long time today!" and asked, "What were you doing all this time?" The maid replied, "My lady, do not say so. I have never seen anyone so handsome. A son of your father's friend, a treasurer, has arrived; his beauty is beyond description. The treasurer told me, as I was going for flowers, 'Wash that young man's feet and prepare a bed for him.' That is why I was delayed outside."

That treasurer's daughter had been his wife in their fourth previous existence. Therefore, from the moment she heard those words, she lost all awareness of whether she was standing or sitting. Taking that same maid with her, she went to where the young man was sleeping. While looking at the sleeping youth, she saw a letter tied to the hem of his garment. Thinking, "What letter is this?", she took the letter without waking him and read it. Realizing, "This young man is carrying his own death warrant," she tore up the letter. Then, while the youth was still asleep, she wrote a new letter: "I, the treasurer, have sent my son to you. My friend, the village treasurer, has a daughter of marriageable age. Take the wealth obtained from the area under our authority and, with full honors, marry my son to the village treasurer's daughter. When the wedding is completed, send word to me, saying, 'I have done according to your instructions.' I shall then arrange what needs to be done on this side." She sealed it and tied it back to the hem of his garment just as it had been tied before.

The young man stayed there that day, and on the following day, after taking leave of the treasurer, he went to the village where the bailiff was and delivered the letter. After reading the letter, the bailiff assembled the villagers and said, "You have been ignoring me, but my master has sent his eldest son to me to take a bride with full honors. Quickly collect the wealth produced in this place!" He prepared all the wedding festivities, sent word to the village treasurer, obtained his consent, and completed the marriage ceremony with full honors. Then he sent a letter to the Treasurer of Kosambī, saying, "I have performed such-and-such tasks according to the instructions in the letter sent by you."
329:
When the Treasurer of Kosambī heard that news, he felt as if he were being burned by fire. Thinking, "Now I am ruined," he fell ill with dysentery (lohitapakkhandika). He plotted, "By some means or other, I will summon him and make him no longer the owner of my property (disinherit him)." He sent a message, saying, "Since the wedding ceremony is over, why is my son still outside? Let him return quickly." Hearing the message, as the young man (Ghosaka) prepared to go, the Treasurer's daughter thought, "This fool does not know that he obtained this fortune because of me. I must find a way to prevent his departure." Then she said to him, "My lord, do not go in such great haste. One who goes to the village of his parents should go only after preparing his belongings and attendants."

The Treasurer of Kosambī, knowing that Ghosaka was taking a long time, sent another message: "Why is my son delaying? I am severely ill with dysentery. He should come and see me while I am still alive." At that time, the Treasurer's daughter told him the truth: "That man is not your father; you only mistakenly perceive him as your father. He once sent a letter to a foreman to have you killed. I removed that letter and wrote another, which is why you obtained this fortune. Now, too, he is calling you to disinherit you. Wait until his death." Thus, they did not go while the Treasurer was still alive, but went to the city of Kosambī only after hearing that he was extremely weak. Even from outside the city, the Treasurer's daughter warned him, "My lord, when you enter the house, do so only after placing guards throughout the entire house." She herself entered together with the Treasurer's son. Pretending to weep with both hands raised, she went to the great Treasurer who was lying in a dark place and struck his chest with her head. Because he was so weak, the great Treasurer passed away from the impact of that blow.

The young man, after performing the funeral rites for his father, gave bribes to the attendants and subordinates, saying, "You all must say that I am the biological son of the great Treasurer." Then, on the seventh day, the King said, "It is proper to find someone worthy of the position of Treasurer. Find out whether the great Treasurer has a son or grandson." The Treasurer's subordinates told the King that the Treasurer indeed had a son. The King, accepting this, said, "Very well," and...
330:
The King bestowed the position of Treasurer upon the young Ghosaka. He became known as the Treasurer Ghosaka (Ghosaka Seṭṭhi). Then his wife said to him, "My lord, you were born into a low condition, and I too was born into a poor family. However, through the power of past merit, we have obtained such fortune. Let us now perform meritorious deeds." The Treasurer accepted, saying, "Very well, dear lady," and began a daily distribution of alms, spending a thousand pieces of money.

At that time, Khujjuttarā, who was to serve those two, passed away from the celestial realm and took conception in the womb of a nurse in the house of the Treasurer Ghosaka. Because she was hunchbacked when she was born, they named her Khujjuttarā. Sāmāvatī also passed away from the celestial realm and took conception in the house of the Treasurer Bhaddavatiya in the city of Bhaddiya, in the kingdom of Bhaddavatiya. They named her Sāmā. Later, a famine arose in that city. Fearing the famine, people fled wherever they could. Then, this Treasurer Bhaddavatiya consulted with his wife, saying, "Dear lady, the end of this famine is not in sight. Let us go to our friend, the Treasurer Ghosaka, in the city of Kosambī. He will not neglect us when he sees us." It is said that this Treasurer was a friend of the Treasurer Ghosaka though they had never met; that is why he spoke thus. He sent back the rest of his people and, taking his wife and daughter, set out on the road to the city of Kosambī. The three of them experienced great suffering on the way and eventually reached Kosambī, where they took up residence in a rest house.

The Treasurer Ghosaka was having a great distribution of alms given at the door of his house to the destitute, travelers, wayfarers, and beggars. Then, the Treasurer Bhaddavatiya thought, "We should not show ourselves to our friend in this wretched state. When our bodies have returned to normal and we are well-clothed and groomed, then we shall go to see the Treasurer." Both parents sent their daughter to the alms-hall of the Treasurer Ghosaka. Carrying a vessel to bring back food for them, she went to the alms-hall and stood in a certain place with a bashful manner. Seeing her, the alms-manager thought, "The rest of the people are making a great noise and grabbing food like fishermen scrambling for fish, but this girl must be of noble birth; she is also endowed with a beautiful appearance."
331: After thinking thus, he said to the young woman, "Dear daughter, why do you not take the alms and leave like the rest of the people?" "Father, how can I enter such a crowded place?" she replied. "Dear daughter, how many of you are there?" he asked. "Father, there are three of us," she said. The man in charge of the alms gave her three portions of rice. The young woman gave that rice to her parents. Her father, having been hungry for a long time, overate and passed away. On the next day, she went and took only two portions of rice. On that very day, the merchant's wife passed away during the night due to exhaustion from hunger and grief over the death of the merchant, her husband. On the following day, the merchant's daughter took only one portion of rice. The man in charge of the alms, observing her behavior, asked, "Dear daughter, on the first day you took three portions, on the next day two, and today you take only one. What is the reason?" The young woman explained the reason for the deaths of her parents. When he asked, "Dear daughter, in which village do you live?" she told him everything without reserve. "Dear daughter, if that is the case, you are indeed our merchant's daughter. I have no other daughter; from this day forward, you shall be my daughter," he said, and he took the merchant's daughter as his own child. Whenever the young woman rose, she heard the loud noise in the alms-hall and asked, "Father, why is there such a great noise?" "Dear daughter, it is impossible to keep things quiet among a great multitude of people," he replied. "Father, I know a way for this," she said. "Dear daughter, what should be done?" he asked. "Father, build a fence all around and set up two gates. Place the rice vessels inside, and have people enter through one gate to take the rice and exit through the other gate," she said. "Very well, dear daughter," he said, and from the next day onward, he had it done that way. From then on, the alms-hall became as quiet as a lotus pond. Then, the merchant Ghosaka, not hearing the loud noise he was accustomed to hearing from the alms-hall, summoned the man in charge of the alms and asked, "Are you not giving alms today?" "Lord Merchant, I am giving them," he replied. "If so, why is no sound heard from the alms-hall?" he asked. "It is true, lord. I have a daughter. By following the method she suggested, I have made the alms-hall quiet," he said. "You have no daughter; from where did you get a daughter?" he asked. Being unable to lie, the man told the merchant the whole story of how the daughter had arrived. "My good man, why did you do such a serious thing? For all this time, you have kept my daughter with you and..."
332: The merchant Ghosaka said, "Why did you remain silent? Bring that young woman to our house immediately." Hearing the merchant's words, the man brought her, though unwillingly. From then on, the merchant placed the young woman in the position of a daughter and, thinking, "I shall pay honor to my daughter," he provided five hundred maidens of the same age and social class as her attendants. Then one day, while King Udena was wandering through the city, he saw Sāmāvatī playing, surrounded by those five hundred maidens. He asked, "Whose daughter is this young woman?" and upon hearing, "She is the daughter of the merchant Ghosaka," he inquired whether she had a husband. When he learned that she had no husband, he commanded, "Go and tell the merchant, 'The King desires your daughter.'" When the merchant heard those words, he replied, "We have no other daughter; we cannot give our only daughter to a place of rival wives." When the King heard this, he had the merchant and his wife removed from the house and had the entire house sealed. When Sāmāvatī returned from playing outside and saw her parents sitting outside the house, she asked, "Mother, Father, why are you sitting here?" Her parents told her the whole story. She said, "Mother, Father, why did you not know how to reply, 'My daughter cannot live alone in a place of enemies; if she is allowed to live with five hundred maiden attendants, then she will live there'? Now, have this message sent." Her parents said, "Very well, daughter, we did not know your wish," and they sent the message accordingly. The King was greatly pleased and said, "Even if there were a thousand, bring them all!" Then, at an auspicious astrological moment, they conducted Sāmāvatī to the palace along with her five hundred maiden attendants. The King made those five hundred maidens her attendants, consecrated her, and had her live in a separate palace. At that time, in the city of Kosambī, there were three men known as the merchant Ghosaka, the merchant Kukkuṭa, and the merchant Pavārika, who were friends with one another. These three men supported five hundred ascetics. The ascetics lived with the merchants for four months and in the Himālaya for eight months. Then one day, while the ascetics were returning from the Himālaya, they became thirsty and exhausted in a great wilderness. They reached a large banyan tree and sat down, hoping for favor from the deity dwelling in that tree. The deity [showed] a hand adorned with all kinds of ornaments...
333:
The deity extended his hand and offered water, drinks, and other refreshments to the ascetics, relieving their fatigue. Amazed by the deity's power, the ascetics asked, "O deity, what meritorious deed did you perform to obtain this celestial splendor?" The deity replied, "A Blessed One called the Buddha has appeared in the world; he is currently residing in Sāvatthī. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika attends to him. On Uposatha days, that treasurer gives his laborers their usual food and wages but has them observe the Uposatha. One day, I arrived at midday for my morning meal and, seeing no laborer working, I asked, 'Why are people not working today?' They told me about the Uposatha observance. Then I said, 'Half the day has already passed; is it possible to observe a half-day Uposatha?' After informing the treasurer, he said, 'It is possible.' So, I undertook the half-day Uposatha, died on that very day, and obtained this splendor."

Then those ascetics, filled with joy and exultation upon hearing that "the Buddha has appeared," wished to go from there to Sāvatthī. However, thinking, "The treasurers who support us are very helpful; we shall first inform them of this matter," they went to Kosambī. After receiving honor and respect from the treasurers, they said, "We shall go this very day." When asked, "Venerable sirs, why are you in such a hurry? Did you not previously stay for four or five months before leaving?" they informed them of the Buddha's appearance. When the treasurers said, "Venerable sirs, in that case, we shall go together," the ascetics replied, "We shall go ahead; you may come slowly." They went to Sāvatthī, were ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, and attained Arahantship.

Those three treasurers later went to Sāvatthī with an entourage of five hundred carts each. They set up camp in a place not far from the Jetavana monastery, went to the Blessed One, paid homage with the fivefold prostration, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to them according to their temperaments. At the conclusion of the teaching, all three treasurers were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). They invited the Buddha for the next day, and on the following day, they gave a great gift (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. In the same manner, inviting him for "today and tomorrow," they offered meals at their camp for half a month and then requested the Teacher to come to their city. The Teacher said, "Tathāgatas delight in empty places (secluded dwellings)." They replied, "We understand, Bhante. Please come when we send word."

Having paid homage to the Blessed One and circumambulated him three times, they returned to their own city. Those three treasurers then had monasteries built in their respective gardens. The monastery built by the treasurer Ghosaka was named Ghositārāma. The monastery built by the treasurer Kukkuṭa was named Kukkuṭārāma. The monastery built by the treasurer Pāvārika was named Pāvārikambavana (Pāvārika Mango Grove). When the monasteries were completed, they sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying, "May the Blessed One come to this city to show us favor." The Blessed One, intending to go to Kosambī, set out on a journey accompanied by a large company of monks. Along the way, he saw the powerful supporting condition (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship in the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya. Thus, he diverted his journey and went to the market town called Kammāsadamma in the Kuru country.
334:
(Those three treasurers) having addressed the Teacher, paid homage, and circumambulated him three times, returned to their own city. All three men had monasteries built in their respective gardens. The monastery built and offered by the treasurer Ghosaka became known as Ghositārāma; the one built and offered by the treasurer Kukkuṭa became known as Kukkuṭārāma; and the one built and offered by the treasurer Pāvārika became known as Pāvārikambavana. Having completed the construction of the monasteries, they sent a messenger to the Teacher, saying, "May the Teacher come to this city to show us favor." The Teacher said, "I shall go to Kosambī," and while setting out on a journey with a large entourage of monks, he saw the powerful supporting condition (upanissaya) for the fruit of Arahantship in the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya. Thus, he diverted his journey and went to the market town called Kammāsadamma in the Kuru country.

At that time, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, having tended the sacrificial fire outside the village all night, was entering the village early in the morning. The Blessed One also, while entering the village for alms the next day, showed himself to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya on the road. When the Brahmin saw the Blessed One, he thought, "For so long I have been wandering in search of a young man equal in beauty to my daughter. Although there are beautiful ones, I have desired only one who has taken such an ordination. This monk is extremely handsome and pleasing to look at; he is truly suitable for my daughter." Thinking thus, he went home quickly. It is said that the Brahmin had a lineage of renunciants in the past; therefore, his heart inclined toward the monk just by seeing him. He called the Brahmin woman and said, "Lady, I have never seen such a monk before. He has a noble complexion like the color of gold; he is truly suitable for my daughter. Dress our daughter quickly." While the Brahmin woman was dressing the daughter, the Blessed One left his footprints at the place where he had stood and entered the city.

Then the Brahmin, taking his daughter along with the Brahmin woman, came to that place. Since the Blessed One had already entered the village, the Brahmin looked here and there but did not see him. He scolded the Brahmin woman, saying, "There is no benefit from you! While you were delaying, that monk has already departed." She asked, "Brahmin, even if he has gone, in which direction did he go?" Saying, "He went in this direction," and looking toward the way the Teacher had gone, he saw the footprints and said, "Lady, these are the footprints of that man; he must have gone this way." Then the Brahmin woman, seeing the Teacher's footprints, thought, "This Brahmin is very foolish; he does not even know the meaning of the Vedic scriptures he has mastered."
335:
The Brahmin's wife thought, "This Brahmin is truly foolish; he does not even know the meaning of his own Vedic texts." Wanting to jest with the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, she said: "Brahmin, you are very foolish. You say you will give your daughter to such a man. The footprint of a man affected by lust, corrupted by hatred, or bewildered by delusion is not like this. Indeed, in this world, this is the footprint of the All-Knowing Buddha, who has drawn back the veil [of defilements]. Look, Brahmin:

'The footprint of one affected by lust is elevated at the heel.
The footprint of one corrupted by hatred is slightly dragged.
The footprint of one bewildered by delusion is suddenly pressed down.
The footprint of the one who has drawn back the veil is like this.'

Even though the Brahmin's wife spoke this much, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya did not listen and said, 'You are a harsh-tongued woman.' While the couple was arguing with each other, the Teacher, having finished his meal with the Saṅgha of monks after wandering for alms, came out within the Brahmin's sight. Seeing the Teacher approaching from afar, the Brahmin rebuked his wife and, with a very joyful mind, said, 'This is that man!' He stood before the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala) and said: 'O Ascetic, I have been searching for you since morning. In this Jambudīpa, just as there is no woman with a beauty equal to my daughter's, there is no man with a beauty equal to yours. I give my daughter to you to be cared for; take her.' Then the Teacher said: 'Brahmin, I did not desire even the daughters of deities, who dwell in the realm of sensual desire, possess supreme beauty, and speak various kinds of words, even when they came and stood near me to tempt me. Such being the case, why would I take this daughter of yours?' and he spoke this verse:

'Having seen Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāgā,
there was no desire even for sexual intercourse.
What is this body, full of urine and excrement?
I would not wish to touch it even with my foot.'

The maiden Māgaṇḍiyā thought: 'One who does not desire should simply say "I do not want it." But this ascetic says my body is full of urine and excrement and that he does not wish to touch it even with his foot. When I obtain some position of power, I shall seek an opportunity against this ascetic (to take revenge).' Thus she bore a grudge. Ignoring that grudge, the Teacher preached the Dhamma to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya according to his temperament. At the end of the discourse, both husband and wife were established in the Fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmiphala). Saying, 'Now there is no benefit for us in the life of householders,' they entrusted their daughter Māgaṇḍiyā to her paternal uncle, and both ordained and attained the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). After that, King Udena...
336:
(The Teacher) said, "I do not desire it." (Then Māgaṇḍiyā) bore a grudge, thinking, "If I obtain a position of power (authority), I shall seek an opportunity (fault) against this ascetic." Ignoring that grudge, the Teacher began the Dhamma teaching to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya according to his temperament. At the end of the teaching, both husband and wife were established in the Fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmiphala) and, saying, "Now there is no benefit for us in living in the house of householders," they entrusted their daughter Māgaṇḍiyā to her paternal uncle, and both ordained and reached the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). Then King Udena, after speaking with Cūḷamāgaṇḍiya, brought the maiden Māgaṇḍiyā to the palace with royal majesty, performed the consecration, and gave her a separate palace to reside in with five hundred female attendants.

The Teacher, wandering by stages, reached the city of Kosambī. The (three) treasurers, hearing of the Teacher's arrival, went out to welcome him, paid homage with the fivefold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita), and sat in a suitable place, saying to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, these three monasteries have been built dedicated to you. Venerable Sir, please accept these monasteries for the sake of supporting the Saṅgha from the four directions." The Blessed One accepted the monasteries. Those treasurers invited the Teacher for the next day, paid homage, and returned home.

Māgaṇḍiyā, hearing that the Teacher had arrived, summoned shameless drunkards, gave them bribes, and sent them off, saying, "You all abuse the Ascetic Gotama in various ways like this." When the Teacher entered the village for alms with his followers, they abused the Teacher with various kinds of insults. The Venerable Ānanda said to the Teacher: "Venerable Sir, let us not stay in such a place where there is abuse; let us go to another city." The Teacher said: "Ānanda, those who are Tathāgatas are not shaken by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). This sound of abuse will not last more than seven days; it will fall only upon the abusers. Do not worry." Those three city treasurers, having invited the Blessed One with great honor, offered a great alms-giving (Mahādāna). As they continued to give alms repeatedly, a month passed, and then they thought: "Buddhas arise out of compassion for all beings in the world; let us give others the opportunity to give alms as well." Then they gave the opportunity to the people of Kosambī, and from then on, the citizens also gave great alms-giving according to streets and groups.

Then one day, the Teacher sat in the house of the florist (Sumana) surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. At that moment, Khujjuttarā, a servant of Queen Sāmāvatī, took eight coins and went to that house to buy flowers. When the florist saw her, he said: "Dear Khujjuttarā, today there is no opportunity to give you flowers yet. I will serve the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. You also assist in the service. By doing so, you will be liberated from being one who performs the major and minor tasks of others in future lives." Then Khujjuttarā, after eating the food she received, performed the service in offering alms to the Buddhas. She learned and memorized all the Dhamma words preached by the Teacher to those sitting near him, and by hearing the Dhamma of appreciation (Anumodanā) again, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).
337:
One day, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, was staying at the house of the chief florist. At that moment, Khujjuttarā, an attendant of Queen Sāmāvatī, arrived at that house with eight kahāpaṇas to buy flowers. Seeing her, the chief florist said, 'Mother Uttarā, today I have no time to give you flowers. I am serving the community of monks headed by the Buddha. You too, be a helper in the serving. By helping in this way, you will be liberated from performing the service of others in the future.'

Then Khujjuttarā, after eating the food she received, performed the service of serving the Buddhas in the refectory. She learned and memorized the entire Dhamma spoken by the Teacher to those sitting nearby. After listening to the words of appreciation (anumodanā), she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

On other days, she used to take flowers after giving only four kahāpaṇas, but on that day, because she had realized the Truth, she did not allow a greedy thought for another's property to arise. She gave all eight kahāpaṇas, filled the basket, took the flowers, and went to Queen Sāmāvatī. Then the Queen asked her, 'Mother Uttarā, on other days you did not bring many flowers, but today there are many. Is the King more pleased with us than before?'

Because she had become incapable of telling a lie, she did not hide what she had done in the past and told everything. When asked, 'If so, why did you bring many flowers today?' she said, 'Today, having heard the Dhamma of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), I have realized the Deathless (Amata). Therefore, I will no longer deceive you, my ladies.'

Hearing this, all five hundred women stretched out their hands, saying, 'Mother Uttarā, give us too the Deathless Dhamma you have obtained.' 'My ladies, it is not possible to give it in this way. However, I will preach the Dhamma to you in the manner taught by the Teacher. If you have the supporting conditions (pāramī), you will obtain that Dhamma.' 'If so, Mother Uttarā, preach it,' they said. She said, 'It is not possible to preach in this way. Prepare a high seat for me, and you sit on low seats.'

Those five hundred women gave Khujjuttarā a high seat and sat down on low seats themselves. Khujjuttarā, established in the analytical knowledge (paṭisambhidā) of a trainee (sekha), preached the Dhamma to them. At the end of the preaching, with Queen Sāmāvatī at their head, all five hundred women were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. From that day on, they removed Khujjuttarā from her service as an attendant and said, 'Listen to the Dhamma talk from the Teacher and bring it back to preach to us.' From that day on, Khujjuttarā did accordingly.
338:
Why was this Khujjuttarā born as a servant? It is said that during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha, she made a novice nun perform her own chores. Because of that deed, she was born only as a servant of others for five hundred births.

Why was she hunchbacked? It is said that when a Buddha had not yet arisen, while living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, she saw a hunchbacked Paccekabuddha. Wanting to mock him in front of the women she lived with, she walked around imitating a hunchbacked form. Because of that, she was born hunchbacked.

By doing what good deed did she become wise? When a Buddha had not yet arisen, while living in the palace of the King of Bārāṇasī, she saw eight Paccekabuddhas coming from the palace carrying bowls filled with hot milk-rice. She said, 'Venerable sirs, please place the bowls on these (gold bracelets) and proceed,' and she took off eight gold bracelets and offered them. As a result of that deed, she was born wise.

Then, those five hundred women who were attendants of Sāmāvatī, although they had penetrated the Truth, were unable to go and see the Teacher at any time because of King Udena's lack of faith. Therefore, when the One of Ten Powers was walking on the street, and the windows were not enough, they made holes in their own rooms and watched through them.

One day, Māgaṇḍiyā, coming out from her palace and walking about, went to the place where those women lived. Seeing the holes in the rooms, she asked, 'What is this?' Those women, not knowing her malice toward the Teacher, said, 'When the Teacher comes to this city, we stand here to see and honor the Teacher.'

Māgaṇḍiyā thought, 'Now I know what must be done to this Buddha. These women are also his attendants; I know what must be done to these women too.' When she was in a private place with the King, she said, 'Great King, Sāmāvatī and the others have an outside connection. Within a few days, they will take your life. Sāmāvatī and her attendants have no affection or love for you. But to see the ascetic Gotama walking on the street, since the windows were not enough, they even broke through the rooms to make openings and watch him.'

The King did not believe her, saying, 'Those women would not do such a thing.' Even when she said it again, he still did not believe it. Then, when he did not believe even after she said it three times, she said, 'Great King, if you do not believe my words, go to the place where those women live and investigate.' The King went and saw the holes in the rooms. When he asked, 'What is this?' and was told the reason, he did not get angry with those women...
339: When the King was informed of that matter, he did not become angry with the five hundred queens led by Sāmāvatī. Without saying a single word, he had the openings closed. From that time on, King Udena had latticed windows with openings at the top made in the palace of those queens.  That Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, unable to make the King angry by that means, said, "Great King, let us find out whether these queens led by Sāmāvatī have love for you or not. Send eight chickens and have them cooked for you." Hearing her words, the King sent eight chickens to Queen Sāmāvatī, saying, "Let them cook these and send them back."  How could a noble disciple who is a Stream-enterer cook live chickens? Saying it was improper, she did not even wish to touch them with her hand.  Queen Māgaṇḍiyā then said, "Great King, let it be so. Send those same chickens to be cooked for the ascetic Gotama." The King did so. Māgaṇḍiyā had the chickens killed while they were on the way and sent them, saying, "Have these chickens cooked and given to the ascetic Gotama."  Because the chickens were dead and because they were intended for the Ten-Powered One, Sāmāvatī cooked them and sent them to the Ten-Powered One. Māgaṇḍiyā said, "Look, Great King," but even with this, she was unable to make the King angry.  This King Udena stayed for seven days at a time in the residence of each of those queens. Then, Māgaṇḍiyā had a young cobra placed inside a bamboo joint and kept it in her own residence.  Whenever the King went anywhere, he was accustomed to taking his elephant-charming lute with him. When the King came to her, Māgaṇḍiyā placed that young snake inside the lute and had the hole closed.  Then, when it was time for the King to go to Queen Sāmāvatī's residence, she said, "Great King, Sāmāvatī is a partisan of the ascetic Gotama; she does not respect you. She is planning some harm against you; be heedful."  After the King had spent seven days at Sāmāvatī's residence, on the seventh day, he went again to Māgaṇḍiyā's house. As soon as he arrived, Māgaṇḍiyā, as if asking, "Great King, is Sāmāvatī not seeking an opportunity against you?", took the lute from the King's hand, shook it, and said, "Great King, what is moving inside here?" She then provided an opening for the snake to come out and, crying, "Alas! There is a snake inside!", dropped the lute and ran away. At that time, King Udena, crackling with rage like a burning bamboo forest or like a furnace into which salt has been thrown...
340: ...said, "Quickly summon Sāmāvatī along with her attendants." The King's men went and summoned them.  Knowing the King's anger, Sāmāvatī gave an admonition to the other women: "The King summons you because he wishes to kill you. Throughout this day, radiate loving-kindness toward the King with a specific focus."  The King had those women summoned and made them all stand in a row. He took up his great bow, fitted a poison-tipped arrow, drew the bow to its full extent, and stood there. At that moment, all those women, led by Sāmāvatī, radiated focused loving-kindness. The King was unable to either shoot the arrow or lower it. Sweat poured from his limbs, his body trembled, saliva fell from his mouth, and he could not even see what he was supposed to be holding.  Then Sāmāvatī asked, "Great King, why are you weary?" "Yes, O Queen, I am weary. Be my refuge," he replied.  "Very well, Great King, point the arrow toward the great earth." The King did so.  She made a resolution: "May the arrow be released from the King's hand." At that moment, the arrow was released.  Immediately, the King bathed and, with wet hair and wet clothes, prostrated himself at Sāmāvatī's feet, saying, "Queen, forgive me. I have done this without investigating, based on the words of backbiters." "I forgive you, Great King," she said.  "Very well, Queen, thus I am forgiven by you. From this day forward, give alms to the Ten-Powered One as you wish. In the afternoon, go to the monastery and listen to the Dhamma. From today, I grant you protection."  She replied, "Great King, if that is so, from today, please request and bring a monk who will teach us the Dhamma." The King went to the Teacher and, upon making the request, obtained the Elder Ānanda. From then on, those five hundred women invited the Elder, paid him honor and respect, and after he had finished his meal, they learned the Dhamma in his presence.  One day, those women, being inspired by the Elder's talk of appreciation, offered him five hundred upper robes. It is said that in a previous life, when the Elder was a tailor, he had given a piece of cloth the size of a palm along with a needle to a Paccekabuddha. Due to the merit of giving the needle, he became one of great wisdom in this life. Due to the merit of giving the piece of cloth, in this same manner, he received robes five hundred times.
341:
Then, Queen Māgaṇḍiyā, seeing no other course of action, said, "Great King, let us go to the park." The King agreed, saying, "Very well, Queen." Knowing the King's consent, she sent for her uncle, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, and said: "When we go to the park, go to the palace where Sāmāvatī resides and lock Sāmāvatī and her attendants inside. Saying, 'It is the King's command,' close the doors, wrap the palace in straw, and set it on fire." Hearing the Queen's words, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya did as he was told. On that day, due to the power of obstructive karma (upapīḷaka-kamma) committed in a previous life, all those women, led by Sāmāvatī, were unable to enter the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (metta-jhāna-samāpatti) and were simultaneously consumed by fire like a handful of chaff. The guards of those queens went to the King and reported, "Great King, such a fire has occurred."

The King, investigating who had done it, realized it was caused by Queen Māgaṇḍiyā. He sent for her and said, "Lady, you have performed a good deed that I should have done. You have killed the women who were repeatedly striving to kill me. I am very pleased and will grant you prosperity; send for your relatives." Hearing the King's words, she sent for even those who were not her relatives, making them out to be so. Knowing that all had gathered, the King had them buried up to their necks in the palace courtyard and had their heads, which remained above ground, crushed by plowing them with great iron-tipped plows. He also had Queen Māgaṇḍiyā cut into pieces and fried in a frying pan.

Why were Sāmāvatī and her attendants burned by fire? It is said that in a life before a Buddha had arisen, she, along with those five hundred women, was playing in the Ganges River. When they came up to the bank, they felt cold and, seeing the leaf-hut of a Paccekabuddha nearby, they set fire to the outside to warm themselves, not knowing the Holy One was inside. Inside the leaf-hut, the Paccekabuddha was sitting in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). When the flames died down and they saw the Paccekabuddha, they thought, "What have we done? This Holy One is the King's personal teacher. If the King finds out, he will be angry with us. Let us now cremate this Holy One properly." So they piled on more wood and set it on fire again. When the fire died down once more, the Paccekabuddha emerged from his attainment and, while those women were watching, shook his robes and flew up into the air. Because of that evil karma...
342:
...having suffered in hell, they reached this destruction as a result of the remainder of that karma. However, among the fourfold assembly, the talk arose: "Khujjuttarā is indeed very learned; while remaining in the form of a woman, she preached the Dhamma to five hundred women and established them in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Sāmāvatī also, by pervading with loving-kindness, was able to ward off the arrow shot by the King." Thus, the multitude spoke of Sāmāvatī's virtues. In this way, this story arose. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana monastery, he used that very incident as the occasion to appoint Khujjuttarā to the foremost position among laywomen of great learning, and Sāmāvatī to the foremost position among laywomen who dwell in loving-kindness.

## The Story of Uttarā, Mother of Nanda

In the fifth sutta, "jhāyīnaṃ" means that among the laywomen who delight in meditation (jhāna), Uttarā, the mother of Nanda, is the foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher appoint a laywoman to the foremost position among those who delight in meditation. She performed meritorious deeds and made a resolution for that position. After wandering through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she took rebirth in the womb of the wife of a man named Puṇṇa, who lived under the patronage of the Treasurer Sumana in the city of Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha's appearance. They named her Uttarā.

Later, on a certain festival day, the Treasurer of Rājagaha sent for Puṇṇa and asked, "Dear Puṇṇa, what can a festival or an Uposatha day do for a poor man? Nevertheless, tell me: will you take provisions and enjoy the festival, or will you take the strong oxen and the plow and plow the field?" Puṇṇa replied, "Master, let me consult with my wife first." He then told his wife about the matter. His wife said, "Master, the Treasurer is our lord; it is fitting for him to speak with you. Do not give up your work of plowing." He followed his wife's advice, took his plowing equipment, and went to plow the field.

On that very day, the Venerable Sāriputta emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and reflected, "Whom should I favor today?" Seeing the strong potential (upanissaya) of this man Puṇṇa, he took his bowl and robes at the time for alms-round and went to the place where Puṇṇa was plowing, making himself visible nearby. Puṇṇa, seeing the Elder, [stopped] his plowing...
343:
Punna stopped plowing and went to the Elder, prostrating with the fivefold touch. The Elder looked at him and asked about a source of water. Punna thought, "The Venerable One must wish to wash his face." Then, he went quickly, brought a tooth-stick, prepared it properly, and offered it to the Elder. While the Elder was using the tooth-stick, Punna took out the water-filter along with the bowl, filled it with water, and brought it back. After the Elder washed his face, he set out on the path for alms-round. Punna thought, "The Elder does not usually come this way on other days; today he must have come to favor me. Oh, if only my wife would offer the food she is bringing for me into the Elder's bowl, how wonderful it would be!"

At that time, his wife, thinking, "Today is a festival day," prepared whatever food and snacks she could obtain early in the morning and set out for the place where her husband was plowing. On the way, she saw the Elder and thought, "On other days, when I see the Elder, I have no gift to offer; when I have a gift, I do not see the Venerable One. Today, however, both the recipient and the gift have come together. I will prepare food for my husband again later; for now, I will offer this food to the Elder." With the threefold volition, she placed the food into the bowl of the Elder Sāriputta and said, "By virtue of this offering, may I be released from such a miserable life of poverty." The Elder said, "May your wish be fulfilled," and after giving the blessing (anumodanā), he turned back and went to the monastery.

The laywoman then returned home, prepared food for her husband again, and went to the plowing field. Fearing her husband's anger, she said, "My lord, please keep your mind calm for just this one day." When asked "Why?", she explained, "While I was bringing food today, I saw the Elder on the way and offered your portion of rice into his bowl. Then I went back home, cooked fresh food, and brought it here." Punna replied, "Dear, you have done a delightful thing. I too, early this morning, offered a tooth-stick and water for washing to the Elder. Today is a truly auspicious dawn for us. Everything offered to the Elder has become our own property." Thus, the minds of the couple were in perfect harmony. Then, after Punna finished his meal, he rested his head on his wife's lap and slept for a moment. He fell into a deep sleep. After sleeping for a while, when he woke up...
344:
Punna looked at the area he had plowed, and everywhere he looked, it appeared as if it were covered with large Mahākosātakī flowers. He said to his wife, "Dear, what is the meaning of this? Today, this plowed field appears to have the color of gold." His wife replied, "My lord, perhaps your eyes are spinning because you have been exhausted all day." Punna said, "Dear, if you do not believe my words, look for yourself." Then the wife looked and said, "My lord, you speak the truth; it is indeed so."

Punna stood up, took a piece of gold, and struck it against the head of the plow; it stuck to the plow-head like a lump of molasses. Punna called his wife and said, "Dear, the seeds sown by others usually bear fruit in three or four months. For us, however, the seed of faith sown in the Venerable Elder Sāriputta has surely borne fruit this very day. In this area of about one karīsa, there is not even a clod of earth the size of a myrobalan fruit that has not turned into gold." The wife asked, "My lord, what shall we do now?" Punna said, "Dear, it is not proper to steal and consume such a vast amount of gold." Leaving his wife there, he filled the bowl she had brought the rice in with gold, went to the King, and had it announced, "A man is standing here holding a bowl of gold."

The King summoned him and asked, "Friend, where did you get this gold?" Punna replied, "Great King, my entire plowed field has turned into gold. Please send people to collect it." The King asked, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Punna, Great King." The King commanded, "Friends, go, yoke the carts, and bring the gold from Punna's plowed field."

The King's men who went with the carts said, "This is due to the King's merit," and tried to take the gold nuggets, but every piece they picked up turned back into mere clods of earth. They returned and reported this to the King. The King then said, "Friends, if that is the case, go and take them saying, 'This is due to Punna's merit'." Then, every piece they picked up remained as gold. They brought all that gold and piled it in the royal courtyard. The pile was about the height of a palm tree. The King summoned the merchants and asked, "In whose house is there this much gold?" They replied, "Great King, there is none in anyone's house." When asked, "What should be done for the owner of such wealth?", they replied, "Great King, he should be appointed as a Dhana-Seṭṭhi (Wealthy Treasurer)." The King said, "In that case, appoint Punna as the Dhana-Seṭṭhi in this city." He gave all that gold to Punna and conferred the title of Seṭṭhi upon him that very day. That Dhana-Seṭṭhi...
345:
## 
When performing the naming ceremony, he gave a great alms-offering for seven days to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. On the seventh day, at the end of the Buddha's discourse of appreciation for the meal, the Treasurer Punna, his wife, and his daughter all became established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

Later, the Treasurer of Rājagaha heard that "the Treasurer Punna has a daughter who has reached marriageable age," and sent a message to his house for the sake of his son. Upon hearing the message, Punna sent back a reply: "I will not give my daughter."

The Treasurer Sumana sent again: "You lived depending on my house and now that you have suddenly become wealthy, do you refuse to give me your daughter?" Then Punna said: "First, you speak only of this treasurer-nature of yours; one should not consider that a man is always of such a nature. Indeed, now I am able to take such men as slaves, but I do not wish to destroy your lineage. However, my daughter is a Stream-enterer, a noble female disciple; she performs worship daily with flowers worth a kahāpaṇa. I cannot send her to the house of those with wrong view like you."

Knowing Punna's refusal, the Treasurer of Rājagaha sent a message again: "Do not break our old friendship; I will arrange flowers worth two kahāpaṇas daily for my daughter-in-law." He accepted, saying "Very well," and sent his daughter to that treasurer's house.

Then one day, Uttara, the daughter of the Treasurer Punna, said to her husband: "While I was in my parents' house, I constantly observed the Uposatha for eight days a month. Now, if you permit, I would like to undertake the Uposatha precepts." The treasurer's son said, "It is not possible," and did not consent. Being unable to convince him, she remained silent. Again, during the Rains Retreat, she asked for permission saying, "I will observe the Uposatha," but still did not receive it. When two and a half months of the Rains Retreat had passed and only half a month remained, she sent a message to her parents: "It is as if you have thrown me into a prison; for all this time, I have not received the opportunity to undertake the Uposatha precepts for even a single day. Please send me fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas." Her parents, upon hearing their daughter's message...
346:
(The parents) upon hearing that message, sent (the money) without even asking "For what reason?" Uttara took those kahāpaṇas and, as there was a courtesan named Sirimā in that city of Rājagaha, she had Sirimā summoned and said: "Lady Sirimā, I shall undertake the Uposatha precepts for this half-month. You take these fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas and attend to the treasurer's son for this half-month." Sirimā accepted, saying, "Very well, noble lady." From then on, the treasurer's son, thinking "I shall enjoy myself with Sirimā," consented to Uttara's observance of the Uposatha for the half-month.

Knowing that the treasurer's son had consented, Uttara, surrounded by her group of maidservants, prepared hard and soft food with her own hands for the Teacher every morning. When the Teacher had finished his meal and departed for the monastery, she would undertake the Uposatha precepts, ascend to the magnificent palace, and sit reflecting on her own virtues. Having passed the half-month in this way, on the day of concluding the Uposatha, she was moving about early in the morning preparing gruel, snacks, and so on. At that time, the treasurer's son, being in the magnificent palace with Sirimā, opened the latticed window and stood looking into the courtyard. Uttara also looked up through the window opening. Seeing Uttara, the treasurer's son smiled, thinking: "This treasurer's daughter is truly like a denizen of hell; having abandoned such luxury, she moves about for no reason among the maidservants, smeared with soot from the cooking pots." Uttara, knowing the treasurer's son's state of negligence, also smiled, thinking: "This fool likely thinks his own wealth and prosperity will be permanent forever."

Then Sirimā, becoming angry, thought: "This servant girl is smiling at my husband in this way while I am right here!" and she quickly descended. Uttara, just by seeing Sirimā's manner of approach, knew: "This foolish woman, having lived in this house for only half a month, has come to think of this house as her own." At that very moment, she entered into a meditative state of loving-kindness and stood there. Sirimā, pushing through the maidservants, took a ladle, filled it with boiling oil from the place where cakes were being fried, and poured it over Uttara's head. Due to the power of the meditative state of loving-kindness, the boiling oil poured over Uttara's head rolled off like water droplets on a lotus leaf.

At that moment, the maidservants standing near Sirimā looked at her and said: "Hey, you wicked woman! You came here having taken payment from our mistress's hand..."
347:
"Are you striving to be like our mistress while living in this house?" they rebuked her to her face. At that moment, Sirimā realized that she was merely a guest. She went from there, prostrated at Uttarā's feet, and said, "Mistress, I have acted thoughtlessly; please forgive my fault." "Sister Sirimā, I cannot forgive you here yet. I am a daughter who has a father. Only when the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) forgives will I forgive."

The Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, arrived and sat on the prepared seat in Uttarā's house. Sirimā went, prostrated at the Teacher's feet, and said, "Venerable Sir, I have committed a fault against the mistress Uttarā. She says she will forgive only if you forgive. Exalted One, please forgive me." "Sirimā, I forgive you," the Teacher said. Then Sirimā went and asked Uttarā for forgiveness. On that very day, Sirimā, having heard the Teacher's discourse of appreciation for the meal—

"Conquer anger with non-anger,
Conquer the wicked with goodness,
Conquer the stingy with giving,
Conquer the liar with truth."

At the end of the verse, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). She invited the Buddha and offered a great donation (mahādāna) the next day. Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana monastery, when assigning laywomen to various positions, he placed Uttarā (also known as Nandamātā) in the foremost position among those who practice meditation (jhāyīnaṃ).

## The Story of Suppavāsā (Suppavāsā-vatthu)

In the sixth sutta, 'paṇīta-dāyikānaṃ' means that among the laywomen who give choice and delicious food, the Koliya princess Suppavāsā is the foremost. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher appoint a laywoman to the foremost position among those who give choice gifts. She performed meritorious deeds and aspired for that position. For a hundred thousand aeons, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans. In this Buddha's era, she was born into the royal family of the Koliya country and was named Suppavāsā. When she reached marriageable age, she went to the house of a Sakyan prince. Upon first seeing the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma discourse...
