348:
Suppavāsā arrived at the house of the Sakyan prince. Upon first seeing the Teacher and hearing the Dhamma discourse, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Later, she gave birth to a son named Sīvali. His story is detailed below.

On one occasion, she offered various kinds of delicious and choice food to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. When the Teacher had finished his meal, he gave a discourse of appreciation to Suppavāsā: "Suppavāsā, a noble female disciple who gives food gives five things to the recipients. She gives life, she gives beauty, she gives happiness, she gives strength, and she gives intelligence. By giving life, she becomes a partaker of long life, whether divine or human... By giving intelligence, she becomes a partaker of great intelligence, whether divine or human." Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Teacher was staying at the Jetavana monastery, when assigning laywomen to various positions, he placed the Koliya princess Suppavāsā in the foremost position among those who give choice gifts.

## The Story of Suppiyā (Suppiyā-vatthu)

In the seventh sutta, by the term "gilānupaṭṭhākīnaṃ," it is shown that among the laywomen who attend to the sick, the laywoman Suppiyā is the foremost. Let me elaborate on this. This Suppiyā was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Later, while listening to the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Teacher appoint a laywoman to the foremost position among those who attend to the sick. She performed extraordinary meritorious deeds and aspired for that position. Having wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born into a good family in the city of Vārāṇasī when our Buddha appeared. She was named Suppiyā. Later, the Teacher, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Vārāṇasī. Upon first seeing the Teacher, she heard the Dhamma and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Then one day, she went to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. While walking around the monastery, she saw a sick monk. She paid homage, greeted him kindly, and asked, "Venerable Sir, what would be suitable for you to receive?" "Laywoman, it would be suitable to have meat broth (rasa)," he replied. "Very well, Venerable Sir, I shall send it," she said. She paid homage to the elder and returned to the city. The next morning, she sent her maid to the market to get meat from a fresh kill (pavaṭṭa-maṃsa). The maid could not find such meat in the entire city and reported the failure. The laywoman thought, "I have told the venerable one that I would send meat broth. If I do not send it, the venerable one will not get it from elsewhere and will suffer. It would be good if I could perform some act to send it."

Having thought thus, she entered her room, cut a piece of flesh from her own thigh, and gave it to the maid, saying, "Take this meat, prepare it with spices to make it delicious, and take it to the monastery to offer to the venerable one. If he asks about me, say that I am unwell." The maid did exactly as Suppiyā had instructed.

The Teacher, knowing of this matter, went to Suppiyā's house the next day at mealtime, surrounded by the community of monks. Suppiyā's husband heard that the Teacher had arrived. Suppiyā said to her husband, "My lord, I am unable to go to the Teacher. Please go, invite the Teacher into the house, and offer him a seat." The husband did as his wife said. The Teacher asked, "Where is Suppiyā?" "Venerable Sir, she is unwell," he replied.
349:
Suppiyā thought, 'If I do not send it, the venerable one will not obtain it from elsewhere and will suffer. It is proper to do something and send it.' She entered her room, cut flesh from her thigh, and gave it to her maid, saying, 'Take this meat, prepare it with spices, make a broth, take it to the monastery, and offer it to the venerable one. If he asks about me, say I am ill.' The maid did as she was told.

The Buddha, knowing the matter, went to the laywoman's house the next day during the alms-round, accompanied by the Saṅgha. Suppiyā's husband, hearing of the Buddha's arrival, was told by Suppiyā: 'My lord, I am unable to go to the Buddha. You go, invite the Buddha inside, and have him sit.' He did so. The Buddha asked, 'Where is Suppiyā?' 'Venerable Sir, she is ill,' he replied. 'Call her,' the Buddha said. They went and said, 'The Buddha calls you.' Suppiyā thought, 'The Buddha, who is compassionate and seeks the welfare of the whole world, would not call me without seeing this reason.' She immediately rose from her couch. By the Buddha's power, her wound healed instantly, and her skin became beautiful, even more radiant than the rest of her body. At that moment, the laywoman smiled, paid homage to the Buddha with the fivefold prostration, and sat to one side. The Buddha asked, 'Why was this laywoman unwell?' She told him everything. After finishing his meal, the Buddha returned to the monastery, convened the Saṅgha, rebuked that monk in many ways, and prescribed a training rule (Mahāvagga 280). Thus this story arose. Later, while staying at Jetavana, the Buddha placed Suppiyā in the foremost position among laywomen who attend to the sick.

## Kātiyānīvatthu
In the eighth discourse, 'aveccappasannānaṃ' refers to laywomen endowed with unwavering confidence gained through the attainment of the Path. Kātiyānī is the foremost among them. In the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a family in Haṃsavatī. Seeing the Buddha place a laywoman in the foremost position among those with unwavering confidence, she performed great meritorious deeds and aspired to that position. For a hundred thousand aeons, she wandered among gods and humans...
350:
Having wandered in saṃsāra, she was born in the city of Kuraraghara during the time of this Buddha. They named her Kātiyānī.

Later, when she reached maturity, she became a firm friend and companion of a laywoman named Kāḷī who lived in Kuraraghara. When the Elder Kuṭikaṇṇa Soṇa was requested by his mother, 'Please preach the Dhamma to me just as it was taught by the Buddha,' he sat on a decorated Dhamma-seat inside the city at night and began the Dhamma teaching, using his mother as the witness. At that time, the laywoman Kātiyānī went with Kāḷī and stood at the edge of the assembly listening to the Dhamma.

At that time, about five hundred thieves, following a mark made during the day, dug a tunnel starting from the house at the edge of the city and reached Kātiyānī's house. The leader of the thieves did not enter the house with them but went to the place where the Elder Soṇa was preaching to investigate why the crowd had gathered. He stood at the edge of the assembly, right behind Kātiyānī.

Then Kātiyānī called her maid and said, 'Girl, go into the house and bring oil for the lamps. We shall light the lamps and listen to the Dhamma.' The maid went to the house, saw the thieves in the tunnel, and returned without taking the oil. She told her mistress, 'Mistress, thieves are digging a tunnel in the house.' Hearing this, the thief leader thought, 'If this woman listens to her maid and goes back home, I will cut her in two with my sword right here. But if she continues to listen to the Dhamma despite what she knows, I will have the thieves return the goods they have taken.' Kātiyānī, hearing the maid's words, said, 'Dear, do not make a sound. Thieves will take only the wealth they see. As for me, today I am listening to the Dhamma which is difficult to hear. Do not create an obstacle to my listening to the Dhamma.' Hearing her words, the thief leader thought, 'We who are stealing the property in the house of such a woman with such an intention should sink into the earth.' He immediately went and made the thieves discard the stolen goods, then returned with them to listen to the Dhamma...
351:
(The bandit leader) stood at the edge of the assembly. The female lay disciple Kātiyānī also, at the end of the Elder's sermon, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry.

Then, at dawn, the bandit leader went and prostrated at the feet of the female lay disciple, saying, "Lady, please forgive us all." When she asked, "What have you done to me?" the bandit leader informed her of all the wrongs he had committed. "Dear ones, if that is so, I forgive you," she said. "Lady, it is not enough for us to be merely forgiven in this way. Please have us all ordained as monks in the presence of your son, the Elder," they requested. The female lay disciple took all of them and had them ordained in the presence of Elder Kuṭikaṇṇasoṇa. Those bandits, having been ordained in the presence of the Elder, all attained the fruit of Arahantship. Thus, this story arose. Later, while the Blessed One was residing at Jetavana Monastery, in appointing female lay disciples to various positions, he placed the female lay disciple Kātiyānī in the foremost position among those with unwavering faith.

## The Story of Nakulamātā
In the ninth sutta, with the word "vissāsikānaṃ," he shows that the householder Nakula's mother is the foremost among female lay disciples who are intimate in conversation. Everything that should be said in this sutta is exactly as already stated below in the Upāsaka Pāḷi. It should be understood that here, Nakulamātā is simply made the primary subject.

## The Story of Kāḷī of Kuraraghara
In the tenth sutta, with the word "anussavappasannānaṃ," he shows that the female lay disciple Kāḷī of Kuraraghara is the foremost among female lay disciples who are possessed of faith arisen merely through hearsay. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born in the city of Kuraraghara in the kingdom of Haṃsavatī. While listening to the Blessed One's Dhamma discourse, she saw the Blessed One appointing a female lay disciple to the foremost position among those with faith through hearsay. Having performed a great meritorious deed, she aspired to that position. After wandering through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born into a noble family in the city of Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha, and they named her "Kāḷī."
352:
When that Kāḷī reached the age of maturity, she went to her husband's family in the city of Kuraraghara. At that time, she conceived a child through their union. When her pregnancy was full-term, she thought, "It is not appropriate to give birth in another's house," and returned to her own family's city. Just after the first watch of the night, while staying in the upper part of her mansion, she heard the conversation of the yakkhas Sātāgira and Hemavata, who were standing in the sky and praising the virtues of the Triple Gem. Having developed faith through hearsay, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) even without seeing the Teacher. Later, her delivery took place. All this story has been detailed below. Later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks at Jetavana Monastery, when appointing laywomen to various positions, He placed this laywoman in the foremost position among those who gain faith through hearsay.

## The commentary on the Upāsikā-pāḷi, which is ten suttas in length, is finished.

## Thus, in the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

## the entire commentary on the Etadagga-pāḷi is finished.

## 15. Aṭṭhāna-pāḷi

## (15) 1. Commentary on the First Chapter of the Aṭṭhāna-pāḷi

In the Aṭṭhāna-pāḷi, "aṭṭhānaṃ" means the rejection of the basis for a result. "Anavakāso" means the rejection of a supporting cause. By both terms, only the cause is rejected. For a cause is called "ṭhāna" (basis) and "avakāsa" (opportunity) for its own result because it occurs depending on that cause. "Yaṃ" means "by which cause." "Diṭṭhisampanno" refers to a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) who is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) endowed with the Right View of the Path. For that noble disciple, there are many names such as: one endowed with right view (diṭṭhisampanno), one endowed with vision (dassanasampanno), one who has come to this True Dhamma, one who sees this True Dhamma, one endowed with the knowledge of a trainee (sekkha-ñāṇa), one endowed with the higher knowledge of a trainee (sekkha-vijjā), one who has entered the stream of Dhamma (dhammasota-samāpanno), a noble one with penetrative wisdom (ariya nibbedhika-pañña), and one who stands knocking at the door of the Deathless (amata-dvāraṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati).

"Kañci saṅkhāraṃ" means even a single formation among the conditioned formations (saṅkhata-saṅkhāra) in the four planes of existence (cannot be taken as permanent). "Niccato upagaccheyya" means to hold the view that it is permanent. "Netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati" means the cause for such a view does not exist and cannot be found. "Yaṃ puthujjano" means "by which cause a worldling (can hold such a view)." "Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati" means the cause for this exists. It means that a worldling, through the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), can take any formation among the conditioned formations in the three planes of existence as permanent.
353:
The formations (saṅkhāras) belonging to the fourth plane (the supramundane), however, do not become objects for wrong view or other unwholesome states, just as a red-hot iron ball that has been heated all day does not serve as a resting place for flies. In this manner, the meaning of the passages beginning with "approaching any formation as pleasure" should also be understood.

"Approaching as pleasure" refers to the grasping of pleasure through the power of the view of self, such as: "After death, the self is exclusively happy and free from disease" (D. i. 76, 79; M. ii. 21, 22). However, with a mind dissociated from wrong view, a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka), being oppressed by the fever of defilements, might approach a certain formation with the perception of pleasure for the sake of calming that fever, just as a clean brahmin, terrified by a rogue elephant, might approach a cesspit.

In the section on self (attavāra), the word "dhamma" (any phenomenon) is used instead of "saṅkhāra" (formation) in order to include designations such as the kasiṇas. Here too, the delimitation for a noble disciple should be understood by way of the four planes, while for a worldling (puthujjana), it is by way of the three planes. Alternatively, in all sections, it is appropriate to delimit even for the noble disciple by way of the three planes only. For whatever a worldling grasps, from that very thing the noble disciple unties the knot of grasping. Whatever a worldling grasps as permanent, pleasant, and self, the noble disciple grasps as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, thereby untying that grasping. Thus, in these three suttas, only the untying of the worldling's grasping of self is discussed.

In the passages beginning with "mother," the mother who is the progenitor, the father who is the progenitor, and the Arahant who is a human being and whose taints are exhausted are intended. Would a noble disciple deprive another of life? This is impossible. Even if a noble disciple who has gone to another life and does not know his own status as a noble disciple were told by someone, "Kill this ant and take the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch over the entire universe," he would not deprive that ant of life. Furthermore, if they were to say to him, "If you do not kill this person, we will cut off your head," he would rather have his own head cut off than kill that person. However, this is stated to show the great fault of the state of being a worldling and to demonstrate the powerful strength of the noble disciple. The intention here is this: the state of being a worldling is blameworthy, for a worldling might even commit the heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) such as matricide. But the noble disciple is very powerful, for he does not commit these deeds.
354:
Even if someone were to say, "If you do not kill this person, we will cut off your head," and then cut off the head of that disciple of the Buddha, that disciple would not kill another. The Buddha taught the words beginning with "a worldling might kill his mother" to show the grave fault of being a worldling and the great strength of the noble disciple's faith and other virtues. The state of being a worldling is extremely blameworthy because a worldling is capable of committing even the heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) such as matricide. The noble disciple, however, is powerful and does not commit those heinous crimes.

"With a corrupt mind" (paduṭṭhacitto) means having a mind corrupted by the intent to kill. "Should shed blood" (lohitam uppādeyya) means causing blood to flow (causing a bruise or internal bleeding) on the person of the living Buddha, even in an amount as small as what a tiny fly might drink.

"Should split the Saṅgha" (saṅghaṃ bhindeyya) means causing a schism in a Saṅgha that shares the same communion and stays within the same boundary, by way of five causes. This has also been stated: "Upāli, the Saṅgha is split by five means: by a legal act (kamma), by a recitation (uddesa), by speaking (voharantā), by proclamation (anussāvana), and by taking voting tickets (salākaggāha)" (Parivāra, 458).

Among those five, "by a legal act" means by any one of the four legal acts, such as an act of leave-taking (apalokana). "By a recitation" means by any one of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha. "By speaking" means explaining the eighteen grounds for schism, such as declaring "what is not Dhamma as Dhamma," through various pretexts. "By proclamation" means speaking words that cause division close to the ear in this manner: "Do you not know that I am one who has gone forth from a high family and am very learned? It is not proper for you even to think that one like me would cause people to take up what is not Dhamma and not Vinaya as the Teacher's Dispensation. Is the Avīci hell as cool as a forest of blue lotuses for me? Do I not fear the danger of the states of woe?" "By taking voting tickets" means, after proclaiming thus and strengthening the minds of those monks to the point of no return, saying, "Take this voting ticket."

In this context, only the legal act (kamma) or the recitation (uddesa) is the actual measure of the split; speaking, proclamation, and taking voting tickets are merely the preliminary stages. For even if one who speaks by way of explaining the eighteen grounds proclaims into their ears to generate interest and they take the voting tickets, the Saṅgha is not yet split. But when four or more monks take the voting tickets and perform a separate legal act or recitation, only then is the Saṅgha said to be split. Thus, it is impossible for a person possessed of right view (a sotāpanna) to split the Saṅgha. By this much, the five heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) such as matricide, which worldlings commit but noble disciples do not, have been shown. To clarify those heinous crimes:

"The decision should be understood by way of action (kamma), door (dvāra), duration of the aeon (kappaṭṭhiti), and commonality of result, etc."
355:
Among these five decisions, first, it should be understood by way of classifying the ānantarika-kamma (actions with immediate result). To explain in detail: here, if a person, being a human, deprives of life their mother or father who is also a human—even if their gender has changed—that person’s action is an ānantarika-kamma. Even if one were to fill the entire world-system with golden stupas the size of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya) thinking, 'I will prevent the result of that ānantarika-kamma,' or give a great offering (mahādāna) to the Saṅgha of monks sitting and filling the entire world-system, or walk along without letting go of the corner of the Blessed One’s robe, upon the dissolution of the body, one will certainly be reborn in hell.

If a human kills a parent who has become an animal, or if an animal kills a parent who is a human, or if an animal kills an animal parent, that action does not constitute an ānantarika-kamma. However, that action is very grave and stands as equivalent to an ānantarika-kamma. This problem is taught only with respect to those of human birth.

In this context, the sheep-tetrad, the battle-tetrad, and the thief-tetrad should be discussed. For even if one intends to kill a sheep, but kills a human mother or father who is standing in the place of the sheep, one incurs the ānantarika-kamma. If one kills a sheep while perceiving it as a sheep or perceiving it as a parent, one does not incur the ānantarika-kamma. But if one kills a parent with the intention of killing a parent, one certainly incurs it. This same method should be understood for the other two tetrads. As it is understood regarding parents, so should these tetrads be understood regarding Arahants. Only by killing a human Arahant does one incur the ānantarika-kamma, not by killing one who is a yakkha. However, that action is grave, just like an ānantarika-kamma. Even if a weapon-strike or poison is given to a human Arahant while they were still a worldling (puthujjana), if they attain Arahantship and die because of that very injury, the perpetrator is indeed a killer of an Arahant. However, if a gift given during the worldling stage is consumed after attaining Arahantship, that gift is considered given to a worldling. For one who kills other noble persons (ariya-puggala), there is no ānantarika-kamma, but the action is very grave, just like an ānantarika-kamma.

Regarding the action of wounding a Tathāgata (lohituppāda): because the body of the Tathāgata is of an unbreakable nature, there is no such thing as causing blood to flow by cutting the skin through the effort of another. Rather, blood merely collects in one place within the body. The splinter that broke off from the rock hurled by Devadatta struck the edge of the Tathāgata’s foot; the foot became bruised with internal blood as if struck by an axe. For one who acts in such a way, it is an ānantarika-kamma. Jīvaka, however, for the Tathāgata...
356:
Jīvaka, according to the Blessed One’s wish, cut the skin with a small knife, removed the stagnant blood from that spot, and made Him comfortable. For one who acts in such a way, it is only a meritorious action.

Now, if it is asked: 'What happens to those who, after the Tathāgata has attained Parinibbāna, destroy a stupa, cut the Bodhi tree, or attempt to destroy a relic?' It is a grave action, equivalent to an ānantarika-kamma. However, it is allowable to cut a Bodhi branch that is harming a stupa containing relics or an image. Even if birds nesting there drop excrement on the stupa, it is certainly allowable to cut it. For a bodily relic stupa (sarīra-cetiya) is greater than a cetiya of use (paribhoga-cetiya). It is also allowable to cut and remove a Bodhi root that is breaking the foundation of a stupa. However, one is not permitted to cut a Bodhi branch that is harming a Bodhi-house (bodhighara) for the sake of protecting the house. For the house is for the sake of the Bodhi tree, not the Bodhi tree for the sake of the house. The same method applies to an altar-house (āsanaghara). But if relics are enshrined in that house, it is allowable to cut a Bodhi branch to protect that house. It is certainly allowable to cut a branch that is absorbing nutrients or a decayed branch for the sake of tending to the Bodhi tree; this results in merit, just like tending to the living body of the Blessed One.

Regarding the schism of the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda): for one who, before the Saṅgha within the boundary has assembled, gathers a separate group and makes them hear the proclamation for schism, makes them take the voting sticks, or performs an apalokana act, or recites the Pātimokkha—there is both a split in the Saṅgha and the incurrence of an ānantarika-kamma. However, for one who does so with the perception that the Saṅgha is united, or with the perception that 'this is allowable,' there is only a split in the Saṅgha, not an ānantarika-kamma. The same applies to a group of fewer than nine. At the minimum limit, whoever splits the Saṅgha among nine persons incurs the ānantarika-kamma. For the followers of that schismatic who speak what is not Dhamma, there are actions of great fault. For those who speak what is Dhamma, there is no fault.

Regarding those nine persons in a schism of the Saṅgha, there is this Sutta passage: 'Upāli, on one side there are four; on the other side there are four; the ninth person makes them hear the proclamation and makes them take the voting sticks, saying: "This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction; take this, approve of this." In this way, Upāli, there is both a crack in the Saṅgha (saṅgharāji) and a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda). With nine, Upāli, or with more than nine, there is both a crack in the Saṅgha and a schism in the Saṅgha.' Among these five ānantarika-kamma, the act of splitting the Saṅgha is a verbal action (vaci-kamma), while the remaining four are physical actions (kāya-kamma). Thus should the decision be understood by way of action.
357:
The decision should be understood by way of doors (dvāra). All these heinous crimes (ānantariya kamma) arise from both the body-door (kāyadvāra) and the speech-door (vacīdvāra). Among those five, the first four deeds (such as matricide, etc.) arise from the speech-door through the effort of command (āṇattika) and knowledge (vijjāmaya), yet they fulfill only the body-door. The crime of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabhedaka kamma) arises from the body-door for one who causes the schism by making hand gestures, yet it fulfills only the speech-door. Thus, in these heinous crimes, the decision should also be understood by way of doors.

The decision should be understood by way of duration in an aeon (kappatthitiya). Among these heinous crimes, only the causing of a schism in the Saṅgha is a deed that lasts for an entire aeon. This is because, whether the schism is caused while the aeon is being established or in the middle of an aeon, one is released from that kamma only when the aeon is destroyed. Even if one causes a schism in the Saṅgha today, thinking "The world will be destroyed tomorrow," one is released tomorrow, having suffered in hell for only one day. However, such an occurrence does not happen. The remaining four deeds are merely heinous crimes (ānantariya); they are not deeds that last for an entire aeon. Thus, in these heinous crimes, the decision should also be understood by way of duration in an aeon.

The decision should be understood by way of fruition (pāka). If a person has committed all five of these heinous crimes, for that person, only the crime of causing a schism in the Saṅgha yields the result of rebirth (paṭisandhi). The remaining deeds fall into the category of "lapsed kamma" (ahosi kamma), where it is said, "The kamma existed, but the result of the kamma did not exist." If there is no crime of causing a schism in the Saṅgha, the deed of wounding a Buddha (lohituppāda) yields the result. If that deed is absent, the deed of killing an Arahant (arahantaghāta) yields the result. If that deed is absent, if the father is virtuous and the mother is immoral, or if the mother is not virtuous in that way, the deed of killing the father (pitughāta) yields the result of rebirth. If the mother is virtuous, the deed of killing the mother (mātughāta) yields the result. If both are equal in virtue or immorality, only the deed of killing the mother yields the result of rebirth. This is because a mother is one who does what is difficult to do for her children and is of great benefit to them. Thus, in these heinous crimes, the decision should also be understood by way of fruition.

The decision should be understood by way of commonality (sādhāraṇa) and so forth. The first four deeds are common to all, both laypeople and monastics. However, regarding the causing of a schism in the Saṅgha, according to the words of the Blessed One: "Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not divide the Saṅgha, a female trainee (sikkhamānā) does not, a novice (sāmaṇera) does not, a female novice (sāmaṇerī) does not, a male lay follower (upāsaka) does not, a female lay follower (upāsikā) does not divide the Saṅgha. Upāli, it is a bhikkhu who is of regular standing (pakatatta), of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka), and staying within the same boundary (samānasīmā) who divides the Saṅgha" (Cūḷavagga 351). Thus, it applies only to a bhikkhu of the described type and not to anyone else. Therefore, the crime of causing a schism in the Saṅgha is an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) deed. By the word "ādi" (etc.), it should be understood that all these heinous crimes are accompanied by painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) and are associated with hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha). Thus, in these heinous crimes, the decision should also be understood by way of commonality and so forth.
358:
Another teacher (aññaṃ satthāraṃ) means taking another sect-founder (titthakara) even in another life, thinking, "This teacher of mine is unable to perform the duties of a teacher; this [other] person is my teacher." Such a taking is impossible (netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati).

In a single world system (ekissā lokadhātuyā) means in a ten-thousandfold world system. Indeed, there are three fields: the field of birth (jātikhetta), the field of authority (āṇākhetta), and the field of scope (visayakhetta). Therein, the field of birth is the ten-thousandfold world system. It trembles at the time of the Tathāgata’s descent into his mother’s womb, at the time of his birth, at the time of his enlightenment, at the time of the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the time of the relinquishing of the life-formation, and at the time of his final parinibbāna. The hundred thousand million universes are called the field of authority. The authority of the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta, Mora Paritta, Dhajagga Paritta, Ratana Paritta, etc., prevails here. As for the field of scope, there is no limit to its extent. For the Buddhas, according to the statement: "As far as the knowledge extends, so far extends the knowable; as far as the knowable extends, so far extends the knowledge; the knowable has knowledge as its limit, and knowledge has the knowable as its limit," there is nothing that is not within their scope.

Among these three fields, excluding this universe, there is no sutta (text) stating that Buddhas arise in another universe; however, there are texts stating that they do not arise. There are three Pitakas: the Vinaya Pitaka, the Suttanta Pitaka, and the Abhidhamma Pitaka. There are three councils: the council of Elder Mahākassapa, the council of Elder Yasa, and the council of Elder Moggaliputtatissa. In the Word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) contained in the Tipitaka as established in these three councils, there is no sutta stating that Buddhas arise elsewhere, excluding this universe; rather, there are suttas stating that they do not arise.

"Neither before nor after" (apubbaṃ acarimaṃ) means they do not arise simultaneously, neither earlier nor later [together]. It means they arise either before or after [each other]. Therein, from the time of sitting on the Throne of Enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka) with the thought, "I shall not rise until I attain enlightenment," until the taking of conception in the mother's womb [of the next Buddha], it should not be understood as "before". For at the moment of the Bodhisatta’s conception, the field is already occupied by the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world system, and within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is already prevented. From the time of the final parinibbāna as long as even a mustard-seed-sized relic remains, it should not be understood as "after". For as long as the relics remain, the Buddhas are considered to be still present. Therefore, within this interval, the arising of another Buddha is already prevented. However, when the parinibbāna of the relics (dhātu-parinibbāna) has occurred, the arising of another Buddha is no longer prevented.
359:
Why do they not arise simultaneously (neither before nor after)? It is because it would not be extraordinary. For Buddhas are extraordinary human beings. As the Blessed One said: "Monks, when one person arises in the world, he arises as an extraordinary human being. Who is that one person? It is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One." (A. Ni. 1.172). If two, four, eight, or sixteen Buddhas were to arise at the same time, they would not be extraordinary. Just as in a single monastery, if there are two stupas, the offerings and honor do not become grand; and just as monks, by being numerous, do not seem extraordinary, so it would be for the Buddhas. Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously.

It is also because there would be no distinction in the teaching. Whatever Dhamma, such as the Satipaṭṭhāna and so on, that one Buddha teaches, even if another were to arise, that same Dhamma would have to be taught. In that case, it would not be extraordinary. Only when a single Buddha teaches the Dhamma does the teaching itself become extraordinary.

It is also because of the possibility of dispute. If many Buddhas were to arise, the disciples of various teachers, like those of different masters, might dispute, saying, "Our Buddha is more inspiring, our Buddha has a more melodious voice, is more successful, and has greater merit." For this reason also, they do not arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, this reason was explained in detail by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda. It is stated in that Milindapañhā (Mil. Pa. 5.1.1):

"Venerable Nāgasena, it has been said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise simultaneously in a single world system; this cannot happen.' Yet, Venerable Nāgasena, when all the Tathāgatas teach, they teach only the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma); when they speak, they speak only of the Four Noble Truths; when they train others, they train them only in the Three Trainings; and when they admonish, they admonish only in the practice of heedfulness (Appamāda). Venerable Nāgasena, if the instruction, the discourse, the training, and the admonition of all Tathāgatas are the same, for what reason do two Tathāgatas not arise at the same moment? This world is already illuminated by the arising of just one Buddha; if there were a second Buddha, would this world not become even more brilliantly illuminated by the radiance of the two? And if two Tathāgatas were to give advice, they could do so comfortably; if they were to admonish..."
360:
...they could admonish comfortably. Please teach me the reason for this, so that I may be free from doubt."

"Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it can support the virtues of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake, tremble, bend, sag, tilt, break apart, scatter, and perish; it would not remain stable.

"Great King, suppose there were a boat that could carry only one man. When one man boards it, that boat remains level with the water. Then, a second man, equal to the first in age, complexion, years, stature, and build, comes and boards that boat. Great King, would that boat be able to carry both men?" "No, venerable sir. It would shake, tremble, bend, sag, tilt, break apart, scatter, and perish; it would not remain stable and would sink into the water."

"Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha; it can support the virtues of only one Tathāgata. If a second Buddha were to arise, this ten-thousandfold world system could not support him; it would shake... (as before) ...it would not remain stable.

"Or again, Great King, suppose a man were to eat as much food as he desired, filling himself up to the throat. When that man is satiated, full, and stuffed so that he is as stiff as a rod and cannot bend, he then eats the same amount of food again. Great King, would that man be at ease?" "No, venerable sir. He would die from that single meal."

"Even so, Great King, this ten-thousandfold world system can support only one Buddha... (as before) ...it would not remain stable."

"Venerable Nāgasena, does the earth shake because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma?" "Great King, suppose there were two carts filled with jewels up to the brim. If one were to take the jewels from one cart and pour them into the other, Great King, would that cart be able to carry the jewels of both carts?" "No, venerable sir. Its hub would split, its spokes would break, its rims would fall off, and its axle would break." "Great King, does the cart break because of the excessive weight of the jewels?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Even so, Great King, the earth shakes because of the excessive weight of the Dhamma."
361: Great King, this reason is set forth to demonstrate the power of the Buddhas. Hear also another suitable reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same moment. Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same moment, a dispute would arise among their followers, saying, 'Your Buddha, our Buddha,' and they would become divided into two factions. Great King, just as a dispute arises among the followers of two powerful ministers, saying, 'Your minister, our minister,' and they become divided into two factions, even so, Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same moment, a dispute would arise among their followers, saying, 'Your Buddha, our Buddha,' and they would become divided into two factions. Hear this first reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same moment. Great King, hear also another further reason why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same moment. Great King, if two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas were to arise at the same moment, the statement that 'the Buddha is the foremost' would be false. The statements that 'the Buddha is the eldest, the most excellent, the most distinguished, the highest, the best, the peerless, the equal of the unequaled, the incomparable, the matchless, the unique person' would be false. Great King, accept this reason also according to its true meaning, why two Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas do not arise at the same moment. Moreover, Great King, it is the natural characteristic of the Blessed Buddhas that only one Buddha arises in the world. Why is that? Because of the greatness of the qualities of the Omniscient Buddha. Great King, other things that are great are also unique. Great King, the earth is great, and it is only one. The ocean is great, and it is only one. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, is great, and it is only one. Space is great, and it is only one. Sakka is great, and he is only one. Brahmā is great, and he is only one. The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha is great, and he is only one. Where they arise, there is no room for others. Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha arises as the only one in the world. "Venerable Nāgasena, the question has been well answered with similes and reasons," he said.
362:
"Ekissā lokadhātuyā" means in a single universe (cakkavāḷa). By this very term, ten thousand universes are included, and those ten thousand universes are also delimited by a single universe. For the Buddhas, when they arise, they arise only in this universe; when the place of arising is restricted, it is already excluded that they arise in universes other than this one.

## The Commentary on the First Chapter is finished.

## 15. Aṭṭhānapāḷi

## (15) 2. Aṭṭhānapāḷi - Commentary on the Second Chapter

In the phrase "apubbaṃ acarimaṃ," "pubba" refers to the time before the appearance of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana), and "carima" refers to the time after the disappearance of that same wheel-treasure. There are two ways the wheel-treasure disappears: either by the death of the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) or by his renunciation. Regarding the disappearance, that wheel-treasure disappears on the seventh day from either the death or the renunciation; after that, the appearance of another Universal Monarch is not prohibited.

Why do two Universal Monarchs not arise simultaneously in a single universe? It is to prevent dispute, for the sake of wonder, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure. Indeed, if two were to arise, a dispute might arise: "Our king is greater, our king is greater." Also, if it were said, "There is one Universal Monarch on each island," it would not be wonderful. Furthermore, the great power of the wheel-treasure, which is capable of granting sovereignty over the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands, would diminish. Thus, to prevent dispute, for the sake of wonder, and because of the great power of the wheel-treasure, two Universal Monarchs do not arise simultaneously in a single universe.

Regarding the statement "A woman could be an Arahat, a Fully Enlightened Buddha"—let alone the state of Buddhahood, which is capable of delivering the world from the round of rebirths by bringing forth all the qualities of omniscience—even the mere aspiration (paṇidhāna) is not fulfilled by a woman.

"Being human, being of the male sex,
(having the potential for Magga and Phala) having the sufficient cause, the sight of the Teacher,
renunciation, the attainment of virtues (such as jhāna and abhiññā),
extreme dedication (even at the cost of life), and strong desire—
when these eight factors come together, the resolution (abhinīhāra) succeeds."
363:
These eight factors are the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration for Buddhahood. For a woman who is unable to fulfill even this aspiration, how could the state of Buddhahood be possible? Therefore, it is said: "It is impossible, bhikkhus, there is no occasion for a woman to be an Arahat, a Fully Enlightened Buddha." Since merit that is complete in all aspects produces a physical form that is complete in all aspects, only a man becomes an Arahat, a Fully Enlightened Buddha, not a woman.

In the phrases beginning with "He could be a Universal Monarch," because a woman lacks the marks such as the male organ being ensheathed, the marks are not complete. Because of the absence of the woman-treasure (itthi-ratana), the possession of the seven treasures is not achieved. Also, she does not possess a physical form superior to all humans. Therefore, it is said: "It is impossible, bhikkhus, there is no occasion for a woman to be a Universal Monarch."

Since the three positions such as being Sakka are noble, and the female gender is inferior, those positions such as being Sakka are also prohibited for her.

Is it not the case that just as there is no female gender in the Brahma realm, there is also no male gender? Therefore, should it not also be said that "It is possible for a man to exercise the state of a Brahma"? It is not that it should not be said (it should indeed be said). Why? Because a man from here is reborn there. By "the state of a Brahma," the state of Mahābrahmā is intended. A woman, having developed jhāna here, when she passes away, reaches the company of the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas, but not the state of Mahābrahmā. It cannot be said that a man is not born in that Mahābrahmā realm. Although both genders are absent there, the Brahmas have only the male form, not the female form. Therefore, this statement is well-said.

In the phrases beginning with "of bodily misconduct," just as the seeds of neem or bitter gourd do not produce sweet fruit but produce only unpleasant and non-sweet fruit, so bodily misconduct and so on do not produce sweet results but produce only non-sweet results. And just as the seeds of sugarcane or hill rice produce only sweet and delicious fruit and not unpleasant or bitter fruit, so bodily good conduct and so on produce only sweet results and not non-sweet results. It is also said:
"According to the seed that is sown,
So is the fruit that is reaped.
The doer of good reaps good,
And the doer of evil reaps evil."
364:
Therefore, it is said: "It is impossible, bhikkhus, it cannot happen, that for one who has practiced bodily misconduct..." and so on.

290-295. In the phrases such as "one possessed of bodily misconduct" (kāyaduccarita-samangī), there are five kinds of possession (samangitā): possession of accumulation (āyūhana-samangitā), possession of volition (cetanā-samangitā), possession of kamma (kamma-samangitā), possession of result (vipāka-samangitā), and possession of manifestation (upatthāna-samangitā). Among these, at the moment of striving for wholesome or unwholesome kamma, it is called "possession of accumulation." Likewise, it is called "possession of volition."

As long as beings have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, all beings are called "possessed of volition" because they are endowed with the volition accumulated in the past. This is possession of volition. As long as they have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, all beings are called "possessed of kamma" with reference to the kamma accumulated in the past that is capable of yielding results. This is possession of kamma. Possession of result should be understood only at the moment of yielding results.

As long as beings have not reached the fruit of Arahantship, for those who pass away from various existences and are to be reborn in hell, hell appears through manifestations such as flames and iron cauldrons. For those to be reborn in a womb, the mother's womb appears. For those to be reborn in the deva world, the deva world appears through manifestations such as wish-fulfilling trees and celestial mansions. Thus, the sign that is the cause of rebirth (upapatti-nimitta) appears. The state of not being free from the appearance of this rebirth-sign for those beings is called "possession of manifestation." This possession of manifestation is changeable, while the remaining four are unchangeable. Even after hell has appeared, the deva world can appear; even after the deva world has appeared, hell can appear. Even after the human world has appeared, the animal realm can appear; and even after the animal realm has appeared, the human world can appear.

In this regard, there is this story: At the Acela Monastery at the foot of Mount Soṇa (Soṇagiri), there was a Dhamma-preacher monk named Elder Soṇa. His father was a hunter who used dogs. Although the Elder tried to restrain him, he could not establish him in restraint. Thinking, "Let this poor man not perish," he ordained him against his will in his old age. While that father-monk was lying on his sickbed, the sign of hell appeared. Large dogs came from the foot of Mount Soṇa and surrounded him as if wanting to bite and eat him. Terrified by this great danger, he cried out, "Dear Soṇa, stop them! Dear Soṇa, stop them!" When asked, "What is it, Great Elder?", he replied, "Dear son, don't you see?" and told him what was happening. Elder Soṇa thought, "How could the father of one like me [be reborn] in hell..."
365:
Thinking, "Will [my father, being the father of a monk like me,] be reborn in hell? I will provide a support for him," he had the novices bring various flowers and made offerings by spreading them on the ground of the stupa courtyard and the Bodhi tree courtyard, as well as offering seats. He then carried his father on a couch to the stupa courtyard, sat him on the couch, and said, "Great Elder, this offering is made for your sake. Say, 'Blessed One, this is a poor man's gift,' and pay homage to the Blessed One to gladden your heart." Seeing the offering, the Great Elder did so and gladdened his heart. At that very moment, the deva world appeared to him. It was as if the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Missaka Grove, Phārusaka Grove, celestial mansions, and divine dancers were standing there surrounding him. He said to the monk, "Move away, Soṇa! Move away, Soṇa!" When asked, "Great Elder, what is this?" he replied, "Dear son, those mothers of yours are coming." The monk thought, "The deva world has appeared to the Great Elder." It should be understood that this attainment of manifestation (upaṭṭhāna-samangitā) is active. Among these attainments, in this context, "one possessed of bodily misconduct" (kāyaduccarita-samangī) and so on are spoken of by way of the attainment of volitional karma (āyūhana-cetanā-kamma-samangitā).

In that passage [regarding one possessed of bodily misconduct, etc.], some teachers say, "At the very moment one exerts karma, at that moment heaven is barred for him." Others say, "Exerted karma may or may not have the opportunity to ripen. Between these two, only when the karma gets the opportunity to ripen is heaven barred for him." The remaining words have clear meanings everywhere.

## The Commentary on the Aṭṭhāna Pāḷi is finished.

## 16. Ekadhamma Pāḷi

## (16) 1. Commentary on the First Chapter of the Ekadhamma Pāḷi

In the Ekadhamma Pāḷi, 'a single thing' (ekadhamma) means a single nature. 'For absolute disenchantment' (ekantanibbidāya) means for the sake of being weary or disgusted with the round of rebirths. 'For the fading of lust' (virāgāya) means for the sake of the fading of lust for the round, or for the fading and disappearance of defilements such as lust. 'For cessation' (nirodhāya) means for the sake of the cessation and non-occurrence of defilements such as lust, or for the cessation of the round of rebirths itself. 'For calming' (upasamāya) means for the sake of calming the defilements. 'For direct knowledge' (abhiññāya) means for the sake of knowing distinctly by applying the three characteristics such as impermanence. 'For awakening' (sambodhāya) means for the sake of awakening to the Four Truths. 'Awakening' (bodhi) refers to [the knowledge] in the four paths.
366:
'Knowledge' (ñāṇa) means for the sake of penetrating the four path-knowledges as thus spoken. 'For Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) means for the sake of realizing the unconditioned Nibbāna.

Thus, the Blessed One praised the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-kammaṭṭhāna) with these seven terms. Why? It is to inspire the people, just as a molasses merchant praises his goods. A 'poison-thorn merchant' (visakaṇṭaka-vāṇija) refers to a molasses merchant. It is said that he took molasses, syrup, sugar, and so on by cart to a remote village and cried out, "Take poisonous thorns! Take poisonous thorns!" Hearing this, the villagers thought, "Poison is harsh and terrible. Whoever eats it dies. A thorn also pierces and kills. Both are severe. What benefit is there here?" They closed their doors and made their children run away. Seeing this, the merchant thought, "These villagers are not skilled in terminology. Now I will make them take it by a stratagem." He then cried out, "Take something very sweet! Take something very delicious! Molasses, syrup, and sugar can be obtained for a low price; they can even be obtained for base beans or base coins!" Hearing this, the villagers were delighted and went in groups, paying a high price to buy them.

In this analogy, the Blessed One's teaching of the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha should be understood as the merchant's cry, "Take poisonous thorns!" Just as the merchant inspired the people to take the molasses by praising its qualities, the Blessed One inspired the people by praising the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha with these seven terms.

The question "What is the single thing?" is a question asked with the desire to explain (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). 'Recollection of the Buddha' (Buddhānussati) is the repeated recollection that arises in reference to the Buddha; it is a name for mindfulness that has the qualities of the Buddha as its object. This meditation on the recollection of the Buddha is of two kinds: for the purpose of gladdening the heart and for the purpose of insight. How? When the mind of a monk who is developing one of the objects of foulness (asubha) becomes weary, bored, and joyless, it does not follow the path of meditation but runs here and there like a rogue ox. At that moment, he leaves his primary meditation and recollects the mundane and supramundane qualities of the Tathāgata in the manner beginning with "Itipi so bhagavā..." As he thus recollects the Buddha, his mind becomes clear and free from hindrances...
367: (The hindrances are removed). That meditating monk, having thus disciplined the mind repeatedly, again applies his mind only to the original meditation subject. How does he apply his mind? Just as a strong man, while cutting a large tree for the pinnacle of a peaked house, might find his axe-edge ruined merely by cutting the branches and foliage, and though unable to cut the large tree, he does not give up but goes to a smithy, has a sharp axe made, and then cuts that large tree again. In this same way, the fulfillment of this simile should be understood. That meditating monk, having repeatedly disciplined the mind by the power of the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), again applies his mind to the original meditation subject, brings forth the first jhāna with the foulness (asubha) meditation subject as its object, reviews the jhāna factors, and enters the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi). Thus, it is first for the purpose of gladdening the mind. Furthermore, when this meditating person repeatedly recollects the Buddha and investigates with wisdom: "Who is this person who recollects in the manner beginning with 'Itipi so bhagavā'? Is it a woman? Is it a man? Is it one among the deities, humans, Māra, or Brahmās?"—he sees that, apart from ultimate reality, it is no one else other than the mind associated with mindfulness that repeatedly recollects. He sees that: "That mind, by way of aggregate, is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakhandha); the feeling associated with that aggregate of consciousness is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākhandha); the perception associated with it is the aggregate of perception (saññākhandha); the states such as contact (phassa) arising together with it are the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakhandha)." Thus, having defined these four mental aggregates (nāmakhandha) as having arisen, and searching for the basis of that mentality, he sees the heart-base (hadayavatthu). He then grasps the four great elements (mahābhūta) which are the basis of that heart-base, and the remaining derived materiality (upādārūpa) that exists depending on those great elements. Defining that "all this materiality is the aggregate of materiality (rūpakhandha)," he defines mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa) in brief as "this materiality and the previously mentioned mentality," and in detail as the five aggregates. Again, defining the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) in brief as "these five aggregates are the Truth of Suffering," he defines the four Truths in the preceding stage thus: "The craving that produces that Truth of Suffering is the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca); the cessation of that Truth of the Origin is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca); the practice that knows Nibbāna in detail is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca)." Having thus defined the four Truths, he enters the plane of the Noble Ones in due order. At that time, for that meditating person, this meditation subject is said to have the benefit of insight (vipassanā). The section on attainment (appanāvāra) beginning with "Ayaṃ kho" should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In the recollections of the Dhamma (dhammānussati) and so forth, the method is the same. Herein, the word-definition is: Recollection arising in connection with the Dhamma is dhammānussati; this is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-expounded (svākkhātatā), as its object. Recollection arising in connection with the Saṅgha is saṅghānussati; this is a designation for mindfulness having the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its good conduct (suppaṭipannatā), as its object.
368:
This name (is the name of the mindfulness that takes the virtues of the Saṅgha as its object). Repeated recollection that arises by taking virtue (sīla) as the object is called Sīlānussati. This name Sīlānussati is given to the mindfulness that takes the virtues of virtue, such as being unbroken and untorn, as its object. Repeated recollection that arises by taking generosity (cāga) as the object is called Cāgānussati. This name Cāgānussati is given to the mindfulness that takes the virtue of generosity, such as being open-handed, as its object. Repeated recollection that arises by taking deities (devatā) as the object is called Devatānussati. This name Devatānussati is given to the mindfulness that takes one's own virtues, such as faith, as the object, while placing the deities in the position of witnesses. Mindfulness that arises by taking inhalation and exhalation as the object is called Āနာပါနဿတိ (Ānāpānassati). This name Ānāpānassati is given to the mindfulness that takes the sign of inhalation and exhalation as its object. Mindfulness that arises by taking death as the object is called Maraṇassati. This name Maraṇassati is given to the mindfulness that takes the cessation of the life-faculty as its object. It is called Kāyagatā because it reaches (by way of object) the physical body consisting of various parts such as hair, or because it occurs in that body. That mindfulness is both "kāyagatā" (gone to the body) and "sati" (mindfulness), thus it is called Kāyagatāsati. In the Pali text, it is mentioned as "Kāyagatāsatī" without shortening the vowel. This name Kāyagatāsati is given to the mindfulness that takes the sign of the body parts, such as hair, as its object. Repeated recollection that arises by taking peace (Nibbāna) as the object is called Upasamānussati. This name Upasamānussati is given to the mindfulness that takes the pacification of all suffering (Nibbāna) as its object.

Alternatively, peace (upasama) is of two kinds: absolute peace (accantūpasama) and peace through destruction (khayūpasama). Among these, absolute peace is Nibbāna, and peace through destruction is the Path (magga). The mindfulness that arises in one who repeatedly recollects these two kinds of peace is called Upasamānussati; this is the meaning here. Thus, among these ten meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), these three—Ānāpānassati, Maraṇassati, and Kāyagatāsati—are solely for the purpose of insight (vipassanā). The remaining seven also serve the purpose of gladdening the mind (as well as the purpose of insight).

## Commentary on the First Chapter.

## 16. Ekadhamma-pāḷi

## (16) 2. Commentary on the Second Chapter of the Ekadhamma-pāḷi

In the second chapter, "micchā-diṭṭhi" (wrong view) is the name for the sixty-two types of wrong views. "Micchādiṭṭhikassa" refers to one who is endowed with that view.

"Sammā-diṭṭhi" (right view) is the name for the five types of right views. "Sammādiṭṭhikassa" refers to one who is endowed with that view.

"Ayoniso manasikāra" (improper attention) is attention by an improper means (anupāya-manasikāra).
369:
Yoniso manasikāra means wise attention (upāya-manasikāra). Between these two types of attention, for one who attends unwisely (ayoniso), wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) that has not yet arisen arises, and wrong view that has already arisen increases until it enters the fixed course of wrongness (micchā-niyāma). Once it has entered the fixed course, it is said to have increased. For one who attends wisely (yoniso), right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) that has not yet arisen arises, and right view that has already arisen increases until the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). When the fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) is reached, it is said to have increased.

In this statement, "Monks, beings who are possessed of wrong view," some wrong views both obstruct heaven and obstruct the path. Some obstruct only the path but not heaven. Some obstruct neither heaven nor the path. Among those wrong views, these three views—the view of non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi), the view of the non-doing of actions (akiriya-diṭṭhi), and the nihilistic view (natthika-diṭṭhi)—obstruct both heaven and the path. The wrong view of limited scope (antaggāhika-micchā-diṭṭhi) with ten bases obstructs only the path but not heaven. Identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) with twenty bases obstructs neither heaven nor the path. However, setting aside this classification, because it is said in this sutta, "Monks, those possessed of wrong view," it is stated that starting from identity view with twenty bases at the very least, no wrong view is capable of leading to heaven; indeed, it causes one to sink only into hell. Just as stones or pebbles the size of mung beans or black grams, when thrown into water, never float to the top but certainly sink to the bottom, even so, identity view at the very least is not capable of leading to heaven; indeed, it causes one to sink only into the planes of misery (apāya).

In this phrase, "possessed of right view," there are five kinds of right view: right view of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā-sammā-diṭṭhi), right view of absorption (jhāna-sammā-diṭṭhi), right view of insight (vipassanā-sammā-diṭṭhi), right view of the path (magga-sammā-diṭṭhi), and right view of fruition (phala-sammā-diṭṭhi). Among these five, right view of the ownership of kamma draws one toward a prosperous existence in a happy destination. Right view of absorption gives rebirth in the fine-material or immaterial realms. Right view of the path destroys the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). Right view of fruition prevents further existence. If it is asked, "What does right view of insight do?", that too does not draw one toward rebirth. However, the Elder Cūḷābhaya, the master of the Tipitaka, said, "If the developed right view of insight is able to lead to Arahantship in this very life, that is good. If it is not able to do so, friends, it gives seven more existences." Thus, this mundane and supramundane right view is explained. However, in this context, only the mundane right view that produces existence in a happy destination should be understood.
371: Just as in the place of origin, in this sutta as well, kaṭuka should be understood as a bitter taste. Asātattāya means because of being unsweet. In this Bījūpama Sutta, the ancient elders said, "By the word diṭṭhi, fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is taken." Rejecting that statement, it is said, "All sixty-two types of wrong views are indeed taken." In the Anantara Sutta, by the method starting with "For one who abstains from taking life, for one who abstains from taking what is not given, for one who abstains from sexual misconduct, there is no merit arising from that [abstinence]," bodily actions etc. established in wrong view should be understood by comparison. In this sutta, however, only the stability of mind associated with right view should be understood as patthanā (aspiration). In this sutta, right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is spoken of as both mundane and supramundane. The remaining words have meanings that are already clear in all suttas. ## Commentary on the Second Group. ## 16. Ekadhamma Pāḷi. ## (16) 3. Commentary on the Third Group of the Ekadhamma Pāḷi. In the first sutta of the third group, micchādiṭṭhiko means one who has an incorrect view. Viparītadassano means one who has a perverted vision through that very wrong view. Saddhammā vuṭṭhāpetvā means causing one to depart from the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha). Asaddhamme patiṭṭhāpeti means causing one to be established in the asaddhamma (false Dhamma) known as the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakamma-patha). In this term ekapuggala, the six (great wrong-view) teachers, along with Devadatta and others of such nature, should be understood. In the second sutta, sammādiṭṭhiko means one who has a correct view. Aviparītadassano means one who has an unperverted vision through that very right view. Asaddhammā means from the ten courses of unwholesome action. Saddhamme means in the saddhamma (true Dhamma) known as the ten courses of wholesome action. In this term ekapuggala, before the arising of a Buddha, persons such as the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and the Omniscient Bodhisatta are obtained. When a Buddha has arisen, the Buddha himself and the Buddha's disciples are obtained. In the third sutta, micchādiṭṭhiparamāni means those in which wrong view is the most extreme, because among those faults, wrong view has the most excessive fault. The five ānantariya karmas are called "having great blame." The meaning is that wrong view itself has even greater blame than those ānantariya karmas. Why? Because there is a limit (to the result) of those ānantariya karmas. It is said that the four ānantariya karmas cause rebirth in hell...
372:
...Among the five heinous crimes, even the act of causing a schism in the Sangha (saṅghabheda) lasts for only one aeon (kappa) in hell. Thus, there is a limit to the results of those heinous crimes; an end can be known. However, there is no limit to the results of fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). For that [wrong view] is the root of the round of suffering (vaṭṭa); for one possessed of that view, there is no emergence from existence. It leads those who think his words should be heard into the wrong path. For one possessed of that view, there is neither a path to heaven nor a path to the fruition of the Path (magga). Even when the world is destroyed and most people are reborn in the Brahma realm, one with fixed wrong view is not reborn there but is reborn in the space outside the world-system (piṭṭhicakkavāḷa). If one asks, "Does that outer world-system not burn?" [The answer is] it does burn. The teachers say that even while it is burning, this person continues to suffer the pains of hell in a certain location in the open space.

In the fourth sutta, 'Makkhali' is a teacher of a sect who received this name based on the words "Do not slip (mā khali)". 'Nadīmukha' is the meeting place of two rivers. This is just a teaching [by way of example]; it refers to the meeting place of two ravines, two currents of water, the ocean and a salt-water creek, the ocean and a river, or any such place where water meets. 'Khipa' means casting a net (a fishing tool). 'Uḍḍeyya' means setting it up. People make a trap out of reeds, sugarcane, bamboo, or bamboo splints, large enough to hold one, two, or three pots, tie the rim with a rope, take it to the river mouth, drive stakes into both sides, and tie it there with ropes. This was said in reference to that. Even small fish that enter that trap have no way of escape. 'Anayāya' means for non-growth (misfortune). 'Byasanāya' means for ruin. 'Makkhali moghapuriso' means this Makkhali Gosāla is a hollow man. 'Manussakhippam maññe loke uppanno' means he has appeared in the world like a man-trap to catch people and block their path to heaven and Nibbāna.

In the fifth sutta and others, 'durakkhāte, bhikkhave, dhammavinaye' refers to a doctrine outside the Dispensation. In that [doctrine], the teacher is also one who is not all-knowing (asabbaññū), the Dhamma is also badly expounded, and the group [of disciples] is also practicing wrongly. 'Yo ca samādapeṭi' refers to the teacher who encourages [others] to undertake [the practice]. 'Yañca samādapeṭi' refers to the disciple who is encouraged to undertake [the practice]. 'Yo ca samādapito tathattāya paṭipajjati' refers to the disciple who, being encouraged by the teacher, practices accordingly and [follows] the teacher's words...
373:
He practices so that it becomes as the teacher instructed. 'They produce much demerit' means that when an instigator encourages many beings in killing (pāṇātipāta) and so forth, he obtains demerit equal to the unwholesome deeds of all those beings. Therefore, it is said: 'All of them produce much demerit.'

Svākkhāte means well-expounded, well-taught. In such a Dhamma-Vinaya, the Teacher is the Omniscient One (Sabbaññū), the Dhamma is well-expounded, and the assembly of disciples is practicing rightly. 'All of them produce much merit' means that when an instigator, seeing monks entering for alms, encourages people to offer rice porridge (yāgu), almsfood (bhatta), and so forth, he obtains merit equal to the wholesome deeds of all the donors. Therefore, it is said: 'They produce much merit.'

'The donor should know the measure' means the donor person must know the limit; they should give according to the measure, and should not give in excess after fulfilling [the need]. It does not directly say 'do not give,' but says one should give only a little according to the measure. Why? Because even if one gives in excess after fulfilling the need, there is no excessive human prosperity, celestial prosperity, or the prosperity of Nibbāna. 'Not for the recipient' means there is no requirement for the recipient to know the measure and receive. Why? Because for that recipient, there is no practice of fewness of wishes (appiccha-paṭipadā) based on knowing the measure and fulfilling it. Whatever he receives, he should take. Taking in excess would be for the purpose of supporting a wife and children.

'The recipient should know the measure' means the recipient person must know the measure. How? He must know the capacity of the donor, the capacity of the gift, and his own strength. If the gift is abundant but the donor wishes to give only a little, he should take only a little according to the donor's wish. If the gift is small but the donor wishes to give much, he should take only a little according to the capacity of the gift. If the gift is abundant and the donor also wishes to give much, he should know his own strength and take only according to the measure. One who receives knowing the measure in this way fulfills the practice of fewness of wishes. Gains not yet arisen will arise, and gains already arisen will become stable. Those not yet confident will become confident, and those already confident will become more so; he becomes like an eye for the great multitude and makes the Sāsana endure for a long time.
374:
Regarding this fewness of wishes, there are these stories: In the Rohaṇa district, at the Kuṭimbiya Monastery (Kumbhandhariya in Myanmar), during a time of famine, a young monk used to receive one spoonful of rice for eating at the house of a laborer in that village and one spoonful for the journey. One day, seeing a guest monk at that house, he took only one spoonful. When asked, 'For what reason?' he explained the matter, and that gentleman, being inspired, said, 'Please be our regular visitor (kulūpaka); the Venerable is indeed possessed of such virtue,' and he told his friends and ministers at the palace gate. All of them, being inspired by the monk's virtue of fewness of wishes, established sixty regular alms-meals in a single day. Thus, one who has fewness of wishes brings about gains not yet arisen.

King Saddhātissa, wishing to test his young attendant Minister Tissa, had a partridge cooked and brought to him. Then, at the time of consumption, thinking, 'I will consume it after giving the best portion,' he offered the partridge meat to a novice (sāmaṇera) who was the storekeeper of the Great Elder in the Aṭṭhakasāla precinct. When that novice took only a little, the King, inspired by the novice's virtue of fewness of wishes, said, 'Dear novice, I am very inspired; I grant you eight regular alms-meals.' The novice replied, 'Great King, I give them to my preceptor (upajjhāya).' 'I give another eight,' the King said. 'I give them to my teacher (ācariya),' the novice replied. 'I give another eight,' the King said. 'I give them to my fellow-monks (samānupajjhāya),' the novice replied. 'I give another eight,' the King said. 'I give them to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha,' the novice replied. 'I give another eight,' the King said. The novice then accepted. Thus, the gains that arose for him became stable.

Regarding the phrase 'Those not yet confident become confident'—it is said that Dīgha-Brāhmaṇa, while feeding brahmins, could not satisfy them even by giving five bowls of rice each. One day, hearing that 'recluses are said to have fewness of wishes,' he had food brought to test them. Going to the monastery at the time of the Saṅgha's meal, he saw about thirty monks eating in the refectory. He took one bowl of rice and approached the Elder of the Saṅgha. The Elder moved his finger and took only a little. In this manner, that single bowl of rice reached all the monks. Then the brahmin, thinking, 'The virtue of these recluses is indeed true,' was inspired by their fewness of wishes. He spent a thousand [coins] and built a cetiya in that very monastery. Thus, those not yet confident become confident.
375:
Regarding the statement, "Those who are already confident become even more confident," there is no need for a specific illustrative story. Indeed, when those who are already confident see a monk with fewness of wishes (appiccha), their confidence increases even further. When the multitude sees one with fewness of wishes, such as the Elder Majjhantika Tissa, they think of becoming ones with fewness of wishes themselves; thus, a monk with fewness of wishes is like an eye for the multitude. According to the words, "Monks, fewness of wishes (appicchatā) leads to the stability, non-disappearance, and non-vanishing of the True Dhamma," a monk with fewness of wishes is said to make the Dispensation endure for a long time.

"Not because of the donor" (no dāyakena) means that in the well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya, there is no need to limit the act of giving by considering the status of the donor. One should give by offering whatever gift is available without reservation. Because of giving without reservation, that person obtains increasingly sublime and noble attainments, surpassing human bliss, divine bliss, and the bliss of Nibbāna.

"One who exerts effort lives painfully" refers to one who practices the five-fold heat, jumping from cliffs or mountain peaks, enduring the sun's heat, or practicing in a squatting position; such a person lives painfully in the present life. Due to the result of such ascetic practices undertaken in external sects, they are reborn in hell and thus live painfully in the future life as well.

"The lazy person lives painfully" means this person also lives painfully in both the present and future lives. How? From the time of ordination, they lack wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), do not learn the Buddha's words, do not perform duties toward their teacher and preceptor, and do not perform duties at the shrine terrace or the Bodhi tree terrace. Instead, they consume the offerings given in faith by the people without reflection, indulging all day in the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of reclining, and when awake, they think of the three types of [unwholesome] thoughts. Such a person falls away from monkhood within a few days. Thus, they live painfully in the present life. Furthermore, because they do not properly practice the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) despite being ordained:

"Just as kusa grass, wrongly grasped, cuts the hand,
So the ascetic life, wrongly handled, drags one to hell."

According to these words, they are reborn only in the states of deprivation (apāya), and thus live painfully in the future life as well.
376:
"The lazy person lives happily" means that by performing only a tiny bit of the aforementioned ascetic practices from time to time, and at other times wearing white clothes, wearing garlands and perfumes, eating sweet food, and sleeping on soft beds, they live happily in both the present and future lives. Because they did not grasp those ascetic practices too tightly, they do not experience excessive suffering in hell. Therefore, they are said to live happily in the future life.

"One who exerts effort lives happily" means that the one who exerts effort, from the time of ordination, fulfills the major and minor duties, learns the Buddha's words, and acts with wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Then, as they reflect on the fulfillment of duties, the learned words of the Buddha, and the practice of the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), their mind becomes clear and peaceful. Thus, they live happily in the present life. If they are unable to reach Arahantship in the present life, they become ones with swift direct knowledge (khippābhiññā) in a future existence; thus, they are said to live happily in the future life as well.

"Monks, just as excrement, even in a small amount, is foul-smelling"—this discourse was spoken due to a particular occasion. What was that occasion? It was the occasion for the arising of the Sattuppāda Sutta in the Navaka Nipāta. While the Tathāgata was teaching that matter, he said, "Nine types of persons are freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, and freed from the realm of ghosts." Then it occurred to him: "If my sons (the monks), having heard this teaching, think, 'We are completely freed from hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, and the states of deprivation, suffering, and ruin,' and do not think of striving for the higher paths and fruits, I shall arouse a sense of urgency (saṃvega) in them." To arouse that sense of urgency, he began this discourse: "Monks, for example..."

In that context, "a small amount" (appamattako) means a tiny quantity, even as much as can be picked up on the tip of a blade of kusa grass and smelled; it is still foul-smelling. "I do not praise even a small amount of existence" means I do not praise being reborn in existence even for a small amount of time. Now, to show the simile, he said, "even for the duration of a finger-snap." By the ultimate limit, this means the time it takes to snap two fingers together. The remaining words have a clear meaning in all places.

## Commentary on the Third Chapter.
377:
## (16) 4. Ekadhammapāḷi-catutthavaggavaṇṇanā
## 16. Ekadhammapāḷi
In the first sutta of the fourth group, the term 'Jambudīpe' refers to the island that is well-known and famous for its rose-apple tree (Jambū); thus, it is called Jambudīpa. It is heard that there is a great rose-apple tree named Mahājambū, which is the symbol of this island, standing one hundred yojanas high, with branches spreading fifty yojanas, and a trunk circumference of fifteen yojanas. It grows in the Himavantā mountains and lasts as long as the aeon (kappa). Because of this great rose-apple tree, this island is called Jambudīpa. Just as the rose-apple tree in this island lasts as long as the aeon, so too do the Kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna island, the Wishing tree (Kapparuakkha) in Uttarakuru island, the Sirīsa tree in Pubbavideha island, the ornate Pāṭali tree of the Asuras, the Simbalī (silk-cotton) tree of the Garuḍas, and the Pāricchattaka (coral) tree of the Devas last as long as the aeon.

It is said: 'The Pāṭalī, Simbalī, Jambū, the Devas' Pāricchattaka, the Kadamba, the Kapparuakkha, and the Sirīsa is the seventh.'

'Ārāmarāmaṇeyyaka' refers to the delightfulness of parks, such as flower gardens and fruit orchards, similar to Veḷuvana, Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, Jetavana, and the Pubbārāma monastery. The meaning is that such delightful parks are very few and limited in this island of Jambudīpa; they are not many. The same method applies to the remaining terms. Here, 'vanarāmaṇeyyaka' (delightfulness of forests) should be understood as the wild forests in places like Mount Vaṅka and the slopes of the Himavantā, similar to groves of Nāga (ironwood), Sāla, and Campaka (jasmine).
