For this reason, it is said: "The Blessed One taught Right View first because it is of great benefit to the practitioner who is practicing for the attainment of Nibbāna."

Right Intention is of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, it was taught immediately after Right View. For example, just as a money-changer, turning a coin over and over in his hand and looking at it with his eyes, knows, "This is a counterfeit, this is genuine," even so, the practitioner in the preliminary stage, thinking over and over with initial application (vitakka) and looking with the wisdom of insight, knows, "These states belong to the sense sphere, these states belong to the fine-material sphere," and so on. Or, just as a woodworker (carpenter) takes a large tree given to him by a man who has held and turned it at the end, and by hewing it with an adze, brings it into use for work; even so, the practitioner, having demarcated the states given by thinking over and over with initial application through wisdom in the manner of "These states belong to the sense sphere, these states belong to the fine-material sphere," brings them into use for work. For this reason, it is said: "Right Intention is of great benefit to that Right View; therefore, it was taught immediately after it."
405:
Just as that Right Intention is helpful to Right View, so too is it helpful to Right Speech. As the Buddha taught: "Householder, having first thought and pondered, one afterwards breaks into speech." Therefore, Right Speech was taught immediately after Right Intention.

Since people in the world first arrange with speech, saying, "I will do this, I will do that," and then engage in activities, speech is helpful to bodily action. Therefore, Right Action (Sammā-kammanta) was taught immediately after Right Speech.

Only for one who abandons the four types of verbal misconduct and the three types of bodily misconduct and fulfills the two types of good conduct is the morality with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) perfected, and not for any other. Therefore, Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva) was taught immediately after those two (Right Speech and Right Action).

One who has such pure livelihood should not be content with just this, thinking, "My livelihood is pure," and live in negligence and sleep. Rather, to show that this effort should be exerted in all postures, Right Effort (Sammā-vāyāma) was taught immediately after Right Livelihood.

To show that one who has thus exerted effort should well establish mindfulness in the four objects such as the body, Right Mindfulness (Sammā-sati) was taught immediately after Right Effort.

Since mindfulness thus well-established is able to investigate the tendencies of states that are helpful or unhelpful to concentration and to fix the mind on a single object, it should be understood that Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi) was taught immediately after Right Mindfulness. Thus, this Eightfold Path is also taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

In the passages such as "Perceiving forms internally" (ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī), one is called "perceiving forms internally" by virtue of the preliminary work (parikamma) on the forms within one's own continuity. Indeed, one who performs the preliminary work on the blue (nīla) internally does so on the hair, or the bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on the yellow (pīta) does so on the fat, or the skin, or the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on the red (lohita) does so on the flesh, or the blood, or the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who performs the preliminary work on the white (odāta) does so on the bones, or the teeth, or the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. However, that internal kasina is not perfectly blue, perfectly yellow, perfectly red, or perfectly white; it is only impure.
406:
In the phrases beginning with "one who is percipient of forms internally," the meaning should be understood as follows. By virtue of the preliminary practice (parikamma) on the kasiṇa-form existing within oneself, one is called "one who has the preliminary perception of the kasiṇa-form internally." Indeed, a person practicing the blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa) on the kasiṇa-form within oneself does so on the hair, bile, or eyes. One practicing the yellow kasiṇa (pīta-kasiṇa) does so on the fat, skin, palms, soles, or the yellow part of the eyes. One practicing the red kasiṇa (lohita-kasiṇa) does so on the flesh, blood, tongue, or the red part of the eyes. One practicing the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa) does so on the bones, teeth, nails, or the white part of the eyes. These internal blue, yellow, red, and white kasiṇas are not intensely blue, intensely yellow, intensely red, or intensely white; they are merely impure.

"Alone, he sees forms externally" means that for such a person, the preliminary practice (parikamma) arises internally in the manner described, but the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arises externally. Such a person is said to be "percipient of forms internally, and alone he sees forms externally" by virtue of the preliminary practice internally and the attainment (appanā) externally.

"Parittāni" refers to objects that have not been expanded. "Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni" means they are either beautiful or ugly in color. This sphere of mastery (abhibhāyatana) should be understood as being spoken of only by way of limited objects. Regarding the phrase "having transcended those forms" (abhibhuyya): for example, when a man with a strong digestive fire receives only a spoonful of rice, he thinks, "What is there to eat here?" and gathering it all up, makes it into a single mouthful. In the same way, a person of superior and clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to attain in this limited object? This is not my burden," and having transcended those kasiṇa-forms, he enters into attainment. This means he reaches attainment (appanā) simultaneously with the arising of the counterpart sign in this limited object.

By the words "he knows, he sees," his reflection (ābhoga) is described. This reflection occurs only for one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment itself. "He is thus percipient" means he is percipient through the perception of reflection as well as the perception of jhāna. The perception of transcending exists for him even within the attainment, but the perception of reflection occurs only for one who has emerged from the attainment.

"Appamāṇāni" means objects of expanded measure, meaning they are great. Regarding the word "transcending" (abhibhuyya) here: for example, when a man who eats a great deal receives a single serving of rice, he says, "Let there be another serving; what can this one do for me?" and does not see it as being much. In the same way, a person of superior and clear knowledge thinks, "What is there to attain here? This is not immeasurable; it is no burden for me to achieve one-pointedness of mind," and having transcended those immeasurable objects, he enters into attainment. This means he reaches attainment (appanā) simultaneously with the arising of the sign in this immeasurable object.

"One who is not percipient of forms internally" refers to one who is devoid of the preliminary perception (parikamma-saññā) of the kasiṇa-form within oneself, either because of not obtaining it or because of not desiring it. "He sees forms externally" means that for such a monk, both the preliminary practice (parikamma) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) arise only externally. Such a person is said to be "not percipient of forms internally, and alone he sees forms externally" by virtue of the preliminary practice externally and the attainment (appanā). The remaining meaning in this fourth sphere of mastery (abhibhāyatana) is the same as the method already described. Among these four spheres of mastery, the limited (paritta) is brought by way of one of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita). The immeasurable (appamāṇa) is brought by way of one of deluded temperament (mohacarita). The beautiful (suvaṇṇā) is brought by way of one of hateful temperament (dosacarita). The ugly (dubbaṇṇā)...
407:
By way of one with a lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*). These [kasinas] are suitable for such persons; the details of this suitability are stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the *Cariyāniddesa* (Description of Temperaments).

In the fifth *Abhibhāyatana* and so on, the word '*nīlāni*' (blue) is stated by way of encompassing all shades of blue. '*Nīlavaṇṇāni*' refers to the color. '*Nīlanidassanāni*' refers to the appearance; it means they appear as a solid mass of blue, with no visible gaps and unmixed colors. '*Nīlanibhāsāni*' is said by way of radiance; it means having a blue radiance or endowed with blue light. By this, the extreme purity of these [kasinas] is shown. These four *Abhibhāyatanas* are stated solely by way of pure color. Regarding the statement, 'One taking the blue kasina takes the sign in a flower, or a cloth, or a color-element,' the entire procedure for making the kasina, the preliminary work (*parikamma*), and the method of absorption (*appanā*) are stated in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*. These eight *Abhibhāyatana* jhanas pertain to the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*), serve as a basis for the round, serve as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*), are for dwelling happily in the present life, serve as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), and serve as a basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*). However, it should be understood that they are only mundane (*lokiya*) and not supramundane (*lokuttara*).

In the phrase '*rūpī rūpāni passati*' (possessing form, one sees forms), the fine-material jhana (*rūpajjhāna*) produced by way of the blue kasina etc. in internal things like hair is called '*rūpa*'; because one has that jhana, one is called '*rūpī*'. '*Bahiddhā rūpāni passati*' (externally one sees forms) means one sees external kasina-forms like the blue kasina with the eye of jhana. By this, the four fine-material jhanas of a person who has produced jhana in kasinas based on internal and external objects are shown. '*Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī*' (internally perceiving no form) means not having the perception of form internally; the meaning is a person who has not produced fine-material jhana in their own hair and so on. By this, the fine-material jhanas of a person who has produced jhana only externally after performing the preliminary work externally are shown.

By the phrase '*subhanteva adhimutto hoti*' (one is intent only on the beautiful), the jhanas in the extremely pure color kasinas like blue are shown. Therein, although there is no such advertence as 'it is beautiful' within the absorption itself, because one dwells having made a pure and beautiful kasina-object, one is worthy of being called 'one intent on the beautiful'; thus this teaching was given. In the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* Pali, however, it is said: 'How is the liberation of being intent only on the beautiful? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... because of the development of loving-kindness, beings are not harassed (they are beautiful). He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity... because of the development of equanimity, beings are not harassed. Thus is the liberation of being intent only on the beautiful.' Regarding all the words stated in '*sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ*' and so on...
408:
beings are not repulsive. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion... with altruistic joy... with equanimity... etc... because of the development of equanimity, beings are not repulsive. Thus is the liberation of being intent only on the beautiful,' as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. All that should be said regarding the phrases 'sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ' and so on has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

In the phrase 'pathavīkasiṇaṃ bhāveti' (he develops the earth kasiṇa), it is called 'kasiṇa' because of its sense of entirety/wholeness; the earth itself is the kasiṇa, thus 'earth kasiṇa' (pathavīkasiṇa). This term 'earth kasiṇa' is used for the preliminary earth, the learning sign (uggahanimitta), the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta), and the absorption that arises making that sign its object. In this context, however, the absorption having the earth kasiṇa as its object is intended. Indeed, he develops that absorption. The same method applies to the water kasiṇa (āpokasiṇa) and others.

A person who wishes to develop these kasiṇas should first purify their virtue (sīla). Established in pure virtue, they should cut off any of the ten impediments (palibodha) they may have, approach a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta) who gives meditation subjects, and take up a subject that is suitable (sappāya) according to their temperament. Then, abandoning a dwelling that is unsuitable for kasiṇa meditation and living in a suitable one, they should cut off minor impediments and develop the meditation without neglecting any part of the meditative procedure. This is the summary here; the details are stated in the Visuddhimagga. Specifically, the consciousness kasiṇa (viññāṇakasiṇa) does not appear separately there; in essence, that consciousness kasiṇa is the consciousness occurring in the space kasiṇa (ākāsakasiṇa). And that is stated by way of the object, not by way of the attainment. For when one develops the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-samāpatti) by taking 'consciousness is infinite' as the object, he is said to be 'developing the consciousness kasiṇa.' These ten kasiṇas also belong to the round of rebirth, serve as the basis for the round of rebirth, the basis for insight, the basis for a pleasant dwelling in this very life, the basis for direct knowledge, and the basis for the attainment of cessation. They are mundane only, not supramundane.

In the phrase 'asubhasaññāṃ bhāveti' (he develops the perception of foulness), 'perception of foulness' (asubhasaññā) refers to the perception associated with the first absorption (pathamajjhāna) that arises in the ten objects such as a bloated corpse (uddhūmātaka). He develops it, increases it, expands it; the meaning is that he produces what has not yet arisen and protects what has arisen. The entire method of developing the ten kinds of foulness has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.
409:
The details have already been explained. In the phrase "develops the perception of death," it means one develops the perception that arises by taking as an object the three types of death: conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa), momentary death (khaṇika-maraṇa), and death by cutting off (samuccheda-maraṇa); one brings into being the perception of death that has not yet arisen, and protects the perception of death that has already arisen. Alternatively, the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) with the characteristics mentioned below is called "perception of death" (maraṇasaññā) here; it means one develops it, brings it into being, and increases it. The method of developing this perception of death has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Develops the perception of the repulsiveness of food" means one develops, brings into being, and increases the perception that arises in one who contemplates the nine kinds of repulsiveness, such as the repulsiveness of going [for food], in the nutriment consisting of edible balls of food (kabaḷīkāra āhāra), which is divided into what is eaten, drunk, and so forth. The method of developing the perception of the repulsiveness of food has also been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

"Develops the perception of non-delight in the whole world" means one develops the perception of non-delight, the perception of weariness, in the entire world of the three planes.

"Develops the perception of impermanence" means one develops the perception that arises as "impermanent" regarding the five aggregates, which grasps the arising, falling away, and change of the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha).

"Develops the perception of suffering in the impermanent" means one develops the perception that arises as "suffering" in the five aggregates which are impermanent, grasping the characteristic of suffering known as constant oppression.

"Develops the perception of non-self in suffering" means one develops the perception that arises as "not-self" in the five aggregates which are suffering due to the sense of oppression, grasping the characteristic of non-self known as the state of not being under one's control.

"Develops the perception of abandonment" means one develops the perception that arises by taking as an object the five kinds of abandonment (pahāna).

"Develops the perception of dispassion" means one develops the perception that arises by taking as an object the five kinds of dispassion (virāga).

"Develops the perception of cessation" means one develops the perception that arises by taking as an object the cessation of conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Some also say it is the perception that arises by taking Nibbāna as an object.

In this context, powerful insight (vipassanā) is taught through these three perceptions: the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of suffering in the impermanent. Furthermore, the beginning of the practice of insight is taught through the ten perceptions starting with "develops the perception of impermanence."

Terms such as "mindfulness of the Buddha" (buddhānussati) have the meanings already stated.

"Accompanied by the first jhāna" (paṭhamajjhāna-sahagata) means occurring together with the first jhāna; it means associated with the first jhāna. "Develops the faculty of faith" (saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti) means one develops, augments, and increases the faculty of faith by making it accompanied by the first jhāna. This method should be understood in all cases.

## Commentary on the other Accharāsaṅghāta Vagga.
410:
## 19. Commentary on the Kāyagatāsati Vagga

In the phrase "pervaded by the mind" (cetasa phuṭo), there are two kinds of pervasion: pervasion by the water element (āpo-pharaṇa) and pervasion by the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-pharaṇa). Among these, pervasion by water through attaining the water kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa) is called āpo-pharaṇa. In the great ocean thus pervaded, all the small rivers that flow into the ocean become as if they are contained within it. Developing light and seeing the entire ocean with the divine eye is called dibba-cakkhu-pharaṇa. In the great ocean thus pervaded, all the small rivers that flow into the great ocean become as if they are contained within it. "Contained within him" (antogadhā tassa) means they are contained within that monk's meditation.

In the phrase "conducive to knowledge" (vijjābhāgiya), it is called vijjābhāgiya because it associates with knowledge (vijjā) by way of association (sampayoga); or it is called vijjābhāgiya because it exists in the category of knowledge (vijjā-koṭṭhāsa). In this context, the eight kinds of knowledge—insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), mind-made power (manomayiddhi), and the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā)—are called "knowledge." According to the first meaning, the states associated with these eight kinds of knowledge are also called vijjābhāgiya. According to the latter meaning, any one of those eight kinds of knowledge is "knowledge," and the remaining kinds of knowledge are vijjābhāgiya. Thus, both knowledge and the states associated with knowledge should be understood as vijjābhāgiya.

"For great spiritual urgency" (mahato saṃvegāya) means for the sake of great spiritual urgency (saṃvega). This same method applies to the two subsequent phrases. Here, "great spiritual urgency" refers to insight (vipassanā), "great benefit" (mahā-attha) refers to the four paths (magga), and "great security from bondage" (mahā-yogakkhema) refers to the four fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). Alternatively, "great spiritual urgency" refers to the path together with insight, "great benefit" refers to the four fruits of recluseship, and "great security from bondage" refers to Nibbāna. "For mindfulness and clear comprehension" (satisampajaññāya) means for the sake of mindfulness and knowledge. "For the attainment of knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya) means for the sake of attaining the divine eye knowledge. "For a pleasant dwelling in this life" (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya) means for the sake of dwelling happily in this very present existence. "For the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation" (vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāya) means for the sake of reviewing the fruit which is the result of knowledge and liberation. In this context, "knowledge" (vijjā) refers to the wisdom of the path (magga-paññā), and "liberation" (vimutti) refers to the remaining states associated with that path. Their fruit is the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala); "for the realization of that" is the meaning.

"The body also becomes tranquil" (kāyo pi passambhati) means both the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (karajakāya) become tranquil; the distress (daratha) is stilled. "Thought and examination also" (vitakkavicārā pi)—these states are said to be stilled by the second jhāna; however, here it is said with reference to the stilling of gross (oḷārika) thought and examination.
411:
"Kevalā" means entire, all, or without remainder. "Vijjābhāgiyā" means the constituents of knowledge, and these have been shown separately below.

"Avijjā pahīyati" means the abandoning of ignorance (aññāṇa), which is the root of the round of rebirth in eight instances and is like a thick mass of darkness. "Vijjā uppajjati" means the arising of the knowledge (vijjā) associated with the path of Arahantship. "Asmimāno pahīyati" means the abandoning of the ninefold conceit called "I am." "Anusayā" means the seven latent tendencies. "Saṃyojanāni" means the ten fetters.

"Paññāpabhedāya" means for the sake of reaching the distinction of wisdom. "Anupādāparinibbānāya" means for the sake of realizing Nibbāna, which is peaceful and free from clinging.

"Anekadhātupaṭivedho hoti" means the penetration of the characteristics of the eighteen elements. "Nānādhātupaṭivedho hoti" means the penetration of the characteristics of those same eighteen elements through their diverse aspects. By the phrase "Anekadhātupaṭisambhidā hotī," the knowledge of the distinction of elements is taught. Knowledge of the distinction of elements (dhātupabhedañāṇa) is the wisdom that knows, "When this element is abundant, such a benefit arises." This knowledge does not occur in everyone; it occurs without remainder only in the Buddhas. The Blessed One did not teach that knowledge in its entirety. Why? Because even if it were taught, there would be no special benefit.

The sixteen terms beginning with "Paññāpaṭilābhāya" have been expanded in the Paṭisambhidāmagga by setting out the matrix (mātikā) thus: "Monks, these four things, when developed and frequently practiced, lead to the acquisition of wisdom... (p)... lead to the state of having wisdom that penetrates [defilements]: associating with good people, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma." It is taught as follows:

In the phrase "Paññāpaṭilābhāya saṃvattanti," what is the "acquisition of wisdom" (paññāpaṭilābha)? It is the obtaining, re-obtaining, reaching, well-reaching, touching, realizing, and accomplishing of the four path knowledges, the four fruit knowledges, the four analytical knowledges, the six higher knowledges, the seventy-three knowledges, and the seventy-seven knowledges. This is the acquisition of wisdom that leads to the acquisition of wisdom.
412:
In the phrase "lead to the growth of wisdom," what is the "growth of wisdom"? The wisdom of the seven types of trainees (sekhas) and of the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) is currently growing. The wisdom of the Arahant is growth that has already grown. This phrase "lead to the growth of wisdom" is called the growth of wisdom.

In the phrase "lead to the abundance of wisdom," what is the "abundance of wisdom"? The wisdom of the seven types of trainees and of the virtuous worldling is currently reaching abundance. The wisdom of the Arahant has already reached abundance. This phrase "lead to the abundance of wisdom" is called the abundance of wisdom.

In the phrase "lead to the state of great wisdom," what is "great wisdom"? It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great meanings. It is called great wisdom because it comprehends great dhammas... (p)... great linguistics (nirutti), great inspirations (paṭibhāna), great aggregates of virtue, great aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation, great right and wrong causes (ṭhānāṭhāna), great dwelling attainments (vihārasamāpatti), great Noble Truths, great foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, great faculties, great powers, great factors of enlightenment, great noble paths, great fruits of recluseship, great higher knowledges, and the great ultimate meaning, Nibbāna. This phrase "lead to the state of great wisdom" is called great wisdom.

In the phrase "lead to the state of wide wisdom," what is "wide wisdom"? It is called wide wisdom because knowledge occurs in various and diverse aggregates. It occurs in various and diverse elements, in various and diverse bases (āyatana), in various and diverse instances of dependent origination, in various and diverse phenomena that are void of self and cannot be obtained as a self, in various and diverse meanings, dhammas, linguistics, inspirations, in various and diverse aggregates of virtue, aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation, in various and diverse right and wrong causes, in various and diverse dwelling attainments, in various and diverse Noble Truths, in various and diverse foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, in various and diverse noble paths, in various and diverse fruits of recluseship, and in various and diverse higher knowledges; therefore, it is called wide wisdom. Knowledge occurs in the ultimate meaning, Nibbāna, having well-surpassed the dhammas common to many various people; therefore, it is called wide wisdom. This phrase "lead to the state of wide wisdom" is called wide wisdom.
413:
In the phrase, “They lead to the state of having extensive wisdom,” what is “extensive wisdom” (vipulapaññā)? It is called extensive wisdom because it comprehends extensive meanings. ... It is called extensive wisdom because it comprehends the extensive ultimate reality, Nibbāna. This is extensive wisdom that “leads to the state of having extensive wisdom.”

In the phrase, “They lead to the state of having deep wisdom,” what is “deep wisdom” (gambhīrapaññā)? It is called deep wisdom because knowledge proceeds regarding the deep aggregates (khandhas). The detailed explanation should be understood as stated under wide wisdom (puthupaññā). It is called deep wisdom because knowledge proceeds regarding the deep ultimate reality, Nibbāna. This is deep wisdom that “leads to the state of having deep wisdom.”

In the phrase, “They lead to the state of having incomparable wisdom,” what is “incomparable wisdom” (asāmantapaññā)? For a certain person, through the determination of meaning, the analytical insight of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) is attained, realized, and touched with wisdom. Through the determination of the Dhamma, language (nirutti), and perspicuity (paṭibhāna), the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) is attained, realized, and touched with wisdom. In regard to meaning, Dhamma, language, and perspicuity, no one else is able to equal that person; since he cannot be equaled by others, he is one with incomparable wisdom (asāmantapañño).

The wisdom of a virtuous worldling (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) is far, very far, extremely far from the wisdom of the eighth person (one on the path of stream-entry); it is not near, not close. Compared to the virtuous worldling, the eighth person has incomparable wisdom. The wisdom of the eighth person is far from the wisdom of a stream-winner (sotāpanna). ... Compared to the eighth person, the stream-winner has incomparable wisdom. The wisdom of a stream-winner is far from the wisdom of a once-returner (sakadāgāmī); the wisdom of a once-returner from that of a non-returner (anāgāmī); the wisdom of a non-returner from that of an arahant. The wisdom of an arahant is far, very far, extremely far from the wisdom of a solitary Buddha (paccekabuddha); it is not near, not close. Compared to the arahant, the solitary Buddha has incomparable wisdom. Compared to the solitary Buddha and the world with its devas, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the supreme one with incomparable wisdom.

The Blessed One is skilled in the divisions of wisdom; he possesses analytical knowledge. ... Those kings, wise men, and others, having prepared questions, approach the Blessed One and ask about hidden and concealed meanings. Those questions are explained and answered by the Blessed One, and are pointed out with their reasons. They become those who submit to the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One shines forth in that assembly by means of his wisdom. Therefore, the Blessed One is the supreme one with incomparable wisdom. This is incomparable wisdom that “leads to the state of having incomparable wisdom.”
414:
“They lead to the state of having earth-like wisdom” (bhūripaññatā). What is earth-like wisdom (bhūripaññā)? It is called bhūripaññā because it overcomes lust (rāga); it is called bhūripaññā because it is an overcomer. It is called bhūripaññā because it overcomes hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), rivalry (palāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), stubbornness (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), negligence (pamāda), all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations, and all kamma leading to rebirth; it is called bhūripaññā because it is an overcomer. Lust is an enemy; because it is the wisdom that crushes that enemy, it is called bhūripaññā. Hatred, delusion, and so on, and all kamma leading to rebirth are enemies; because it is the wisdom that crushes those enemies, it is called bhūripaññā. The earth is called ‘bhūri’; because one is endowed with wisdom as vast and extensive as the earth, one is called a person with earth-like wisdom (bhūripañño). Furthermore, bhūri, medhā, and pariṇāyikā are synonyms for wisdom. This is earth-like wisdom that “leads to the state of having earth-like wisdom.”

“They lead to the state of having abundance of wisdom” (paññābāhulla). What is abundance of wisdom? Here, a certain person esteems wisdom, practices wisdom, is based in wisdom, is inclined to wisdom, has wisdom as his banner, has wisdom as his crest, has wisdom as his supremacy, investigates things much, investigates in detail much, perceives without distortion much, perceives well without distortion much, is one who reflects well on the Dhamma, and dwells in clarity. He is one who practices that wisdom, esteems that wisdom, has much of that wisdom, is inclined to that wisdom, leans towards that wisdom, is bent towards that wisdom, enters into that wisdom, and has that wisdom as his supremacy. Just as one who esteems a group is called ‘gaṇabāhulika’ or ‘gaṇagaruka’, or one who esteems robes, bowls, or lodgings is called ‘senāsanabāhulika’ or ‘senāsanagaruka’, even so, here a certain person esteems wisdom, practices wisdom, and so on, having that wisdom as his supremacy. This is abundance of wisdom that “leads to the state of having abundance of wisdom.”

“They lead to the state of having quick wisdom” (sīghapaññatā). What is quick wisdom (sīghapaññā)? It is called quick wisdom because it quickly fulfills the precepts (sīla). It is called quick wisdom because it quickly fulfills sense restraint, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. It quickly penetrates what is possible and impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna). It fulfills the meditative attainments (vihārasamāpatti). It penetrates the Noble Truths. It develops the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). It is called quick wisdom because it develops the right efforts (sammappadhāna), the bases of power (iddhipāda), the faculties (indriya), the powers (bala), the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Path. It is called quick wisdom because it quickly realizes the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). It is called quick wisdom because it quickly penetrates the direct knowledges (abhiññā). It is called quick wisdom because it quickly realizes the ultimate reality, Nibbāna. This is quick wisdom that “leads to the state of having quick wisdom.”
415:
"Conducing to the state of quick wisdom (lahupaññatāya saṃvattanti)." What is this? If it is asked, "What is quick wisdom (lahupaññā)?" it is the quick fulfillment of the precepts... This wisdom that conduces to the state of quick wisdom is called quick wisdom.

"Conducing to the state of joyful wisdom (hāsapaññatāya saṃvattanti)." What is this? If it is asked, "What is joyful wisdom (hāsapaññā)?" in this Dispensation, some person fulfills the precepts with an abundance of pleasant feeling, an abundance of satisfaction, an abundance of mirth, and an abundance of gladness... Realizing the ultimate Nibbāna is joyful wisdom. This wisdom that conduces to the state of joyful wisdom is called joyful wisdom.

"Conducing to the state of swift wisdom (javanapaññatāya saṃvattanti)." What is this? If it is asked, "What is swift wisdom (javanapaññā)?" it is the swift perception through knowledge of all form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—as impermanent. It is the swift perception as suffering and as non-self. Swiftly perceiving everything from the eye... up to aging and death, whether past, future, or present, as impermanent, suffering, and non-self is swift wisdom. Having weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest that form—past, future, or present—is impermanent in the sense of passing away, suffering in the sense of danger, and non-self in the sense of being coreless, the swift movement towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of form, is swift wisdom... The swift movement towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death, is swift wisdom. Having weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest everything from form... up to aging and death, whether past, future, or present, as having the nature of passing away, the nature of vanishing, the nature of fading away, and the nature of cessation, the swift movement towards Nibbāna, which is the cessation of aging and death, is swift wisdom. This wisdom that conduces to the state of swift wisdom is called swift wisdom.

"Conducing to the state of sharp wisdom (tikkhapaññatāya saṃvattanti)." What is this? If it is asked, "What is sharp wisdom (tikkhapaññā)?" it is called sharp wisdom because it quickly cuts off defilements. Not tolerating arisen sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty, and abandoning, removing, doing away with, and bringing to non-existence every evil unwholesome state as it arises is sharp wisdom. Not tolerating arisen greed, hatred, delusion... and all kamma that leads to rebirth, but abandoning, removing, doing away with, and bringing them to non-existence is sharp wisdom. Attaining, realizing, and touching with wisdom the four noble paths, the four fruits of asceticism, the four analytical insights, and the six direct knowledges in a single sitting is sharp wisdom. This wisdom that conduces to the state of sharp wisdom is called sharp wisdom.
416:
In the phrase 'They lead to the state of having penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññatāya saṃvattanti*)' (the meaning should be understood). 'What is penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhikapaññā*)?' Here, a certain person is full of trepidation towards all formations (*saṅkhāra*), full of terror, full of weariness, full of dissatisfaction, full of great dissatisfaction; facing outward [from formations], he does not delight in any formations. He penetrates and breaks through the mass of greed that was never before penetrated or broken through. Therefore, it is called penetrative wisdom. He penetrates and breaks through the mass of hatred, the mass of delusion, anger, malice... and all kamma leading to rebirth that was never before penetrated or broken through. Therefore, it is called penetrative wisdom. This is the penetrative wisdom referred to in 'They lead to the state of having penetrative wisdom'.

In this way, the meaning here should be understood by the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*. The only difference is that in that text, it is in the plural, whereas here [in the Aṅguttara Nikāya] it is in the singular. The rest is just the same. These sixteen great wisdoms are taught as a mixture of mundane and supramundane.

## Commentary on the Chapter on Mindfulness of the Body.

## 20. Commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless

600-611. 'Monks, they do not partake of the Deathless' means they do not partake of Nibbāna, which is free from death. Is Nibbāna not supramundane, while mindfulness of the body (*kāyagatāsati*) is mundane? How then can it be said that those who partake of mindfulness of the body partake of the Deathless? It is because it is attained by developing that [mindfulness]. One who develops mindfulness of the body attains the Deathless; one who does not develop it does not attain it. Therefore, it was stated thus. By this method, the meaning of all terms should be understood. Furthermore, here '*viraddhaṃ*' means failing or not attaining. '*Āraddhaṃ*' means being fulfilled. '*Pamādiṃsu*' means they are negligent. '*Pamuṭṭhaṃ*' means forgotten or lost. '*Āsevitaṃ*' means practiced from the beginning. '*Bhāvitaṃ*' means developed. '*Bahulīkataṃ*' means done repeatedly. '*Anabhiññātaṃ*' means not known by way of the 'known' direct knowledge (*ñāta-abhiññā*). '*Apariññātaṃ*' means not fully understood by way of the 'known' full understanding (*ñāta-pariññā*). '*Asacchikataṃ*' means not realized. The meaning of the remaining terms is clear in all places.
